articles.title: A missing config file triggered an AI agent to leak passwords
articles.text:
'I leaked secrets': An AI agent confessed to its own data leak — but others got around corporate protections
AI agents lack institutional memory and ignore past warnings
- An AI assistant exposed company passwords across 10 sessions spanning three weeks
- Another AI agent bypassed corporate restrictions using an alternative API connection
- AI coding assistants can expose confidential credentials while completing routine software development tasks
Artificial intelligence agents are gaining access to company systems, internal documents, and sensitive credentials to complete tasks assigned by employees.
However, two incidents uncovered by NordLayer AI Scout reveal how ordinary instructions can expose confidential information or circumvent organizational security restrictions.
In one incident, an AI coding assistant even acknowledged that it had exposed sensitive credentials after repeatedly accessing company files.
AI assistant exposed company passwords
In this incident, a quality assurance engineer instructed an AI coding assistant to examine proposed software changes.
The project's instructions directed the assistant toward a GitLab access token stored inside an environment configuration file.
However, that file also contained production passwords, an authentication token for an internal human resources system, and credentials belonging to a business intelligence service.
The assistant repeatedly accessed the entire file across 10 separate sessions over three weeks, transmitting its contents to an external AI service each time.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The situation became worse when the assistant encountered a fresh project copy without the expected configuration file.
Rather than stopping its search, it retrieved the computer's entire collection of environment variables, exposing additional passwords and authentication credentials.
After recognizing what happened, the assistant acknowledged its mistake and recommended replacing the exposed credentials.
“I leaked secrets into this session's tool output… I'd rotate them,” the AI coding agent confessed in a session observed by NordLayer AI Scout.
Vakaris Noreika, a cybersecurity expert at NordLayer, said engineers frequently instruct AI assistants to retrieve credentials directly, creating unnecessary exposure.
He explained that assistants can repeat such behavior across subsequent tasks, allowing security problems to continue unnoticed.
AI agent bypassed company restrictions through an alternative connection
A separate incident involved an employee attempting to use an AI assistant to retrieve information from the company's Confluence documentation platform.
The organization's Model Context Protocol (MCP) connection appeared to prevent the assistant from accessing those internal pages.
Instead of treating the restriction as final, the employee asked whether creating an API token could provide another route into the documentation.
The assistant confirmed that this alternative approach worked, effectively circumventing the restriction imposed on its official connection.
The employee might have been seeking convenience rather than deliberately compromising company security.
However, using an alternative connection without authorization can undermine restrictions established by an organization's security team.
“Security controls only ever cover the cases someone foresaw. Every company has rules, but agents simply don’t know them, because they are not employees who were trained at the company,” says Noreika.
“This is a current technology limitation: Agents don’t retain rules between sessions, and sometimes even after getting specific instructions not to do something, they still do it.”
The incidents raise concerns about organizations granting automated assistants access to sensitive systems without adequate monitoring.
Organizations should separate sensitive credentials, store valuable passwords in secure vaults, track which resources AI agents can access, and monitor their activities.
Companies should also provide approved access routes rather than relying exclusively on restrictions that employees might circumvent.
Such measures could help security teams identify unusual access and prevent confidential information from reaching unauthorized destinations.

articles.title: Italia multó a Meta con 805 millones de euros por acceder a las fotos de Facebook en teléfonos Android
articles.text:
La autoridad de protección de datos de Italia, el Garante, multó a Meta con 805 millones de euros por acceder a las fotos y los videos de usuarios de Facebook en teléfonos Android sin un consentimiento específico. La empresa tecnológica anunció que apelará.
El organismo concluyó que la aplicación pidió un único permiso del sistema para acceder a fotos y videos, válido para varias funciones, y que lo hizo con un aviso genérico. Ese permiso no bastó, según el regulador, para autorizar la función bajo examen: las sugerencias de publicación tomadas de la galería del teléfono.
La función se llama “Ottieni suggerimenti dalla galleria quando navighi su Facebook” (en español, recibir sugerencias de la galería mientras se navega por Facebook). Muestra fotos y videos guardados en el dispositivo como ideas para compartir en la red social. Según el Garante, está disponible desde 2023 y venía activada por defecto.
El Garante calculó que unos 20 millones de usuarios de Android en Italia podían estar afectados. La multa equivale a cerca del 0,47% de la facturación mundial del grupo, informó el organismo en su comunicado del 14 de noviembre.
Un permiso general para varias funciones
La resolución explica que, antes de la autorización, la app mostraba una pantalla según la cual el acceso servía para “compartir fotos y videos, recibir sugerencias sobre las fotos que se suben y habilitar otras funciones”. Para el Garante, ese texto no permitía entender que se autorizaba también la función de sugerencias.
Una vez concedido en su modalidad completa, el permiso de Android permite a la app leer todo el archivo multimedia del teléfono, por lo general de forma permanente. El usuario solo puede retirarlo desde los ajustes del dispositivo. El Garante añadió que ni el usuario ni la autoridad pueden comprobar qué información se usa realmente.
La norma aplicada es el artículo 122 del Código de Privacidad italiano, que traslada al derecho del país la directiva europea ePrivacy. Considera el teléfono parte de la esfera privada y exige un consentimiento libre e informado para acceder a lo que guarda, aunque los datos no se transmitan ni haya un daño.
El Garante rechazó además la objeción de Meta, que sostenía que el caso correspondía a la autoridad irlandesa por el mecanismo de ventanilla única del reglamento europeo de datos (GDPR). Según el regulador, la normativa ePrivacy no prevé ese mecanismo.
Qué deberá cambiar Meta y cómo se fijó el monto
Meta tiene 60 días desde la notificación para pedir el consentimiento con una solicitud separada y específica, explicar para qué sirve la función y mantenerla desactivada por defecto, también para quienes ya dieron el permiso. Debe informar de las primeras medidas en 30 días y de su aplicación en 90. Si no se adapta, la función no podrá operar sin consentimiento válido.
Para fijar el monto, el Garante tuvo en cuenta el número de personas implicadas, la duración de la infracción, una resolución de 2019 contra la misma empresa y la escasa colaboración durante la investigación. Consideró atenuantes los cambios que Meta introdujo después de la denuncia, aunque los calificó de tardíos y limitados a quienes actualizan la app.
El caso nació de una denuncia presentada el 10 de julio de 2025 por el Centro de Defensa del Consumidor de Bolzano. La denuncia planteaba un vínculo con el entrenamiento de sistemas de inteligencia artificial de Meta, pero el Garante precisó que no examinó ese punto, que la empresa niega.
Meta apelará y el Garante evaluará otra función
Un portavoz de Meta dijo que la empresa está “en total desacuerdo” con la valoración de los hechos y la aplicación de la norma, y que considera desproporcionado el monto. Según el vocero, se trata de una función simple, el usuario debe conceder un permiso en el dispositivo y puede cambiarlo cuando quiera. Meta afirmó que presentará un recurso.
El Garante se reservó la posibilidad de investigar por separado otra función, lanzada en la Unión Europea a comienzos de 2026, que procesa en la nube el contenido de la galería. La resolución indica que ese punto no formó parte de este procedimiento.

articles.title: Nvidia expands its Vera Rubin platform at SC26 supercomputing conference
articles.text:
Nvidia finally reveals new Rubin GPU with almost 3X more CUDA cores than the Nvidia RTX 5090 — but you will have to wait till 2028 to grab it
Nvidia unleashes a 50,000-core Rubin HPC GPU built to supercharge AI
- Nvidia's new Rubin HPC contains more than 50,000 CUDA cores
- Its core count exceeds the RTX 5090's 21,760 by over 28,240
- Nvidia expects Rubin HPC to reach deployed systems sometime in 2028
Nvidia has unveiled a new processor for scientific computing, with more than 50,000 CUDA cores contained within one graphics processing unit.
The Rubin HPC accelerator is intended for demanding simulations and data analysis, rather than consumer gaming or conventional desktop graphics applications.
Its core count exceeds the GeForce RTX 5090’s 21,760 CUDA cores by almost three times.
Over 50,000 CUDA cores with availability scheduled for 2028
Announced at the SC26 supercomputing conference, Rubin HPC will join Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform as a specialized accelerator for technical workloads.
Nvidia says the chip will help researchers run simulations examining materials, molecules, industrial designs, climate systems, and other complex scientific processes.
The company expects the GPU to become available in 2028, leaving organizations several years before they can evaluate its performance in deployed systems.
The chip design combines numerous processing cores with faster data movement between computing components.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Nvidia says this balance should prevent processing units from remaining idle while waiting for information, a problem affecting data-intensive scientific calculations.
Rubin HPC also incorporates sparse data acceleration, intended to improve operations that retrieve limited information from much larger datasets during calculations.
According to the company’s technical description, these operations occur in applications involving sparse matrices, stencil calculations, sorting, and reduction tasks.
Such calculations recur across simulation, analytics, and engineering software, where the time required to access information can influence completion speeds.
The accelerator also adopts seventh-generation Nvidia NVLink technology, which is designed to improve communication between GPUs operating together inside larger computing systems.
That connectivity matters when complex simulations are distributed across multiple processors, although Nvidia has not published throughput figures for this implementation.
Scientific simulations and AI drive the new GPU's development
Nvidia links the hardware to growing use of AI agents in scientific and engineering research, where software can propose possible candidates.
Researchers can use simulations to assess proposed materials, molecules, and designs before committing resources to laboratory experiments or physical prototypes.
Faster calculations could allow teams to examine more possibilities, although actual improvements will depend on software, system configuration, and measured performance.
“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA.
“Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”
Nvidia also cites its CUDA-X libraries, which provide optimized software implementations for algorithms used in simulation, scientific research, and data analysis.
The company says these tools can operate alongside Rubin HPC to accelerate calculations initiated by AI agents and other scientific applications.
However, independent testing has not established how much faster specific workloads will run, leaving the practical performance claims awaiting verification.

articles.title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms
articles.text:
Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.
Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.
OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.
The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.
The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.
The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.
The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.
One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.
On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.
"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.
The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.
The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.
One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.
A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.
A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint.
Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.
The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt.
In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings.
OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.
The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties.
The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week.
Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers.
Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted.
What the Providers Have Disclosed
An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections.
Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated.
A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window.
At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July.
The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts.
Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers.
Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three.
The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week.
What Users Should Do
The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price.
Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check.
Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys.
A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

articles.title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps
articles.text:
A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.
Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.
Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.
Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses.
The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files.
The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering.
Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor.
WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index.
Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory.
WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other.
Updating the Renderer
The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced.
Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system:
- Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable
- Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending
- SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress
- SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress
- openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected
The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix.
Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell.
One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point.
The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

articles.title: Netflix lanzará en marzo de 2027 su plan con anuncios en Colombia y Perú
articles.text:
Netflix lanzará su plan de suscripción con anuncios en Colombia y Perú en marzo de 2027, según la carta que la compañía presentó a sus accionistas el 20 de octubre ante la Comisión de Valores de Estados Unidos (SEC). Hasta ahora, no informó el precio ni el día exacto.
La carta indica que el servicio llegará a 15 países nuevos durante 2027. La primera tanda de lanzamientos será en marzo y reunirá a nueve países de Europa, Medio Oriente y África, además de Colombia, Perú y Nueva Zelanda.
Los nueve países de esa región son Austria, Bélgica, Dinamarca, Irlanda, los Países Bajos, Noruega, Polonia, Suecia y Suiza, según la lista que Netflix difundió en una presentación para anunciantes. La carta describe a Nueva Zelanda como una incorporación respecto del anuncio previo de la empresa.
En mayo de 2026, durante su presentación anual para anunciantes, Netflix había incluido a Colombia y Perú entre los 15 mercados de 2027, pero sin una fecha. La directora de Publicidad de la compañía, Amy Reinhard, habló de marzo en septiembre, durante un evento del sector en Brasil, según Produ.
Qué se sabe del precio y qué falta
Netflix no publicó cuánto costará el plan en pesos colombianos ni en soles. Tampoco detalló cuántos anuncios verá el suscriptor ni qué condiciones tendrá, por ejemplo, para descargar contenidos. La carta a los accionistas se limita a confirmar el calendario.
En Colombia, la plataforma vende hoy solo planes sin anuncios: el Básico cuesta COP 18.900 al mes, el Estándar COP 32.900 y el Premium COP 50.900, según Valora Analitik, que cita la página oficial de la empresa.
El medio calculó que, si Netflix aplica la proporción de otros mercados, el plan Estándar con anuncios costaría entre el 42% y el 60% del Estándar sin publicidad, lo que equivaldría a entre COP 14.000 y COP 19.700. Es una estimación del medio, no un precio de la empresa.
Valora Analitik recordó que en Estados Unidos, España y Brasil Netflix retiró después el plan Básico sin publicidad, de modo que la opción con anuncios quedó como la de entrada. No hay confirmación de que ocurra lo mismo en Colombia o Perú.
Brasil y México ya tienen el plan
El plan con anuncios ya funciona en Brasil y México. En mayo, Netflix informó que supera los 35 millones de usuarios activos mensuales en Brasil y los 28 millones en México, según la agencia peruana Andina. En todo el mundo, la compañía contó más de 250 millones de espectadores mensuales de esa modalidad.
Valora Analitik señaló que Argentina, por ahora, no ofrece este plan. La carta de Netflix no menciona al país entre los mercados de 2027.
La publicidad, un negocio que Netflix ajustó a la baja
La expansión llega junto con una corrección. En la misma carta, Netflix redujo su previsión de ingresos publicitarios de 2026 a unos USD 2.700 millones, frente a los cerca de USD 3.000 millones que esperaba antes. La empresa lo atribuyó a un despliegue algo más lento de algunas herramientas de publicidad.
En la conferencia con analistas, ejecutivos de Netflix dijeron que en mercados más nuevos, entre ellos Colombia, lo más importante es aumentar la cantidad de miembros, según la transcripción de la reunión que recoge PPC Land.

articles.title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
articles.text:
A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.
The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.
The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.
Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.
There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.
Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage."
In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up.
From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown.
That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent.
The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines.
Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through.
The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in.
The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

articles.title: Meta lanzó una extensión de Chrome para que su agente de IA Muse navegue con la cuenta del usuario
articles.text:
Meta publicó una extensión de Chrome que instala a su agente de IA Muse, un asistente que ejecuta tareas por su cuenta, en el panel lateral del navegador de Google. Alexandr Wang, director de IA de Meta, informó en X que 200.000 personas ya la usan.
La extensión, llamada “Muse from Meta”, figura en la tienda oficial de Chrome con una calificación de 4,5 sobre 5 en 257 valoraciones. Funciona en Chrome 137 o posterior y se abre con el atajo Alt+Shift+C. Para usarla hace falta una cuenta de Muse.
Según la ficha de la tienda, Muse puede completar formularios, comparar precios, hacer reservas y hacer seguimiento de reembolsos sin que el usuario salga de la página que tiene abierta. También puede conectarse con el correo, el calendario, Instagram, Facebook y datos de salud y finanzas.
Wang escribió que el aviso era “tardío”: la extensión ya estaba disponible desde antes. El sitio TestingCatalog la detectó el 13 de noviembre, cuando Meta todavía no había dicho nada.
Qué puede hacer Muse dentro del navegador personal
Muse navega con el Chrome del propio usuario. Abre sus pestañas en un grupo aparte y solo puede actuar dentro de ellas, según la página de ayuda de Meta. La empresa afirma que el agente no ve las contraseñas guardadas, el historial de navegación ni la configuración del navegador, y que las claves que aparecen en una página se eliminan del texto antes de que Muse lo lea.
La misma página de ayuda aclara un límite: Muse puede usar cualquier sitio en el que la persona ya haya iniciado sesión, sin pedirle de nuevo sus datos de acceso. Por eso Meta recomienda cerrar sesión en las cuentas que el usuario no quiera que el agente utilice, antes de conectar la extensión.
Meta también advierte que los sitios web y el navegador pueden registrar información a partir de la actividad de Muse y atribuirla al usuario. Esa actividad puede aparecer en su cuenta de Google y en su historial, y puede afectar los anuncios, las recomendaciones y los contenidos que ve dentro y fuera de los productos de Meta.
La ficha de Chrome Web Store declara que la extensión maneja información personal identificable, datos de salud, información financiera y de pago, datos de autenticación, comunicaciones personales, ubicación e historial web. El desarrollador indica que esos datos no se venden a terceros, salvo en los usos aprobados.
Los controles que ofrece Meta
Meta afirma que el usuario puede aprobar acciones antes de que ocurran, revisar un registro completo de actividad y revocar cualquier conexión cuando quiera. Para frenar al agente basta con hacer clic en la página, presionar Esc o sacar la pestaña del grupo de Muse. La extensión también puede desinstalarse desde la configuración de Chrome.
La empresa reconoce que Muse puede cometer errores o tomar acciones inesperadas, y pide al usuario que supervise su trabajo.
Un antecedente de fallas recientes
El lanzamiento llega pocos días después de una investigación de Reuters, publicada el 18 de noviembre, basada en más de dos docenas de mensajes internos de empleados de Meta. Los textos describían acciones de Muse que nadie había pedido, entre ellas un recordatorio sobre un mensaje de Signal que la empleada no había conectado al agente.
Reuters probó con personal de Signal y del AI Now Institute, una organización sin fines de lucro que estudia el impacto social de la IA, y replicó ese acceso en un teléfono Android y en una computadora Apple. Un vocero de Meta, Daniel Roberts, calificó los ejemplos de “incidentes aislados” y dijo que Muse accede a otras aplicaciones solo con permisos que el usuario concede de forma explícita.
Según The Next Web, Muse suma 10 millones de usuarios desde su lanzamiento en septiembre y llegó a Australia el martes 18 de noviembre. Meta no ha informado una fecha para nuevos países en el caso de la extensión; los medios leídos no precisan en qué mercados está disponible, más allá de que no funciona en Emiratos Árabes Unidos ni en Arabia Saudita, según el sitio tbreak.

articles.title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
articles.text:
A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.
The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.
The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.
Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.
The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.
Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says.
The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG.
When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details.
The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier.
What to Update
The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.
What to install depends on where the library sits:
- Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory.
- Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible.
- Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch.
- Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases.
- GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed.
The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

articles.title: Microsoft admitió que atacantes accedieron a correos de administradores de empresas por una falla en un servicio
articles.text:
Microsoft informó a sus clientes que sufrió una brecha de seguridad: atacantes aprovecharon una falla en Entra Connect Health, un servicio de la empresa, y accedieron a correos de administradores y a datos de configuración de organizaciones. Según BleepingComputer, que citó la notificación enviada a los administradores, la compañía corrigió el error el 19 de noviembre.
Entra Connect Health es un servicio en la nube con el que los administradores de sistemas vigilan el estado y las alertas de la infraestructura que gestiona las cuentas y contraseñas de sus empresas. Se usa desde el panel de administración de Microsoft Entra.
La notificación indica que Microsoft detectó la vulnerabilidad el 9 de noviembre, y que el error había entrado en el sistema el 23 de julio. El 20 de noviembre, la empresa concluyó su investigación y determinó que hubo acceso de solo lectura no autorizado a metadatos de las organizaciones. No encontró cambios de configuración indebidos.
Qué datos quedaron expuestos
Según la notificación, los atacantes pudieron ver los correos de los contactos técnicos y de las cuentas de administrador. También accedieron a identificadores del cliente, nombres, dominios iniciales, códigos de país y región, el nivel de licencia de Entra y el estado de sincronización del directorio.
Entre los datos figura además un certificado vencido que servía para registrar agentes del servicio ante un sistema interno de Microsoft, dado de baja a fines de 2024. Ya no se usaba, pero seguía guardado y la interfaz del servicio aún lo devolvía.
Microsoft afirma que no se expusieron contraseñas, huellas digitales de contraseñas, credenciales de sesión, claves criptográficas válidas, detalles de los servidores internos de las empresas ni información de suscripciones de Azure, su plataforma de servicios en la nube.
Lo que Microsoft no dijo
La compañía no reveló cuántas organizaciones resultaron afectadas, quién explotó la falla ni cuándo comenzaron los ataques. Más de una docena de administradores informaron en un foro de Reddit que recibieron el aviso, y algunos proveedores de servicios informáticos recibieron avisos por varios clientes a la vez.
Un vocero de Microsoft confirmó a BleepingComputer que la empresa avisó a los clientes afectados por medio de Azure Service Health, el sistema de avisos de la plataforma. La compañía declinó dar más detalles.
Qué recomienda la empresa
El aviso precisa que los clientes no deben instalar ninguna actualización, porque la corrección se aplicó en los servidores de Microsoft. Sí recomienda alertar a los equipos de seguridad sobre posibles ataques de phishing, es decir, mensajes falsos que buscan engañar a una persona para que entregue datos, dirigidos a los correos expuestos.
Microsoft también aconseja que las cuentas con privilegios usen una verificación en dos pasos resistente al phishing, que revisen la configuración de Connect Health y que examinen los registros de auditoría y de inicio de sesión de Entra en busca de actividad sospechosa.
La empresa publicó además un script de PowerShell que permite a los administradores ver qué tipos de datos de su organización pudieron quedar expuestos. El programa muestra los valores actuales de la configuración, no la información a la que accedieron los atacantes durante la brecha.
Vulnerabilidad en Outlook
Este mes, Microsoft corrigió una vulnerabilidad en Outlook, identificada como CVE-2026-124194, que atacantes ya explotaban para robar datos de acceso de los usuarios.
La falla permitía que, al abrir un archivo de mensaje manipulado, Outlook se conectara a una ubicación controlada por un atacante sin mostrar el aviso habitual de contenido externo, lo que exponía el hash NTLMv2 del usuario, un código vinculado a su contraseña de Windows.
El parche forma parte de la actualización mensual de seguridad de Microsoft, que corrige más de mil fallas en total, y afecta a Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise y a Office LTSC 2021 y 2024, por lo que requiere una actualización específica del paquete de Office además de la de Windows.

articles.title: South Korean candidate secretly used AI during professional exams
articles.text:
Smuggling AI into a national exam room: A South Korean candidate used a pinhole camera and concealed earpiece to score 159/160 before turning himself in
Han Won-seok scored 159 out of 160 in South Korea's tax exam before admitting to using AI
- Han Won-seok reportedly scored 159 out of 160 using AI assistance
- A miniature camera secretly captured questions inside South Korea's examination hall
- A concealed earpiece delivered answers generated by artificial intelligence
Artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities across education, professional training, and competitive examinations, but its misuse is becoming increasingly difficult to detect.
A recentcheating scandal in South Korea has exposed how candidates can combine miniature surveillance equipment, smartphones, and AI assistance to manipulate high-stakes assessments.
A 34-year-old man reportedly exploited this combination to achieve an almost perfect examination result before eventually surrendering through legal representation.
A concealed system helped produce an extraordinary examination score
The scandal covered both stages of South Korea's 63rd certified tax accountant qualification examination and the preliminary stage of its certified public accountant examination.
Han Won-seok reportedly used a miniature camera concealed in his clothing to capture examination questions without attracting attention from invigilators.
The images were transmitted through a smartphone to an artificial intelligence system, which generated answers that reached him through a concealed listening device.
According to Yonhap, the candidate explained his method during a public confession released through his attorney's YouTube channel.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“I cheated by taking pictures of the questions with a miniature camera, sending them to AI, and checking the answers on a smartphone,” he said.
The equipment reportedly allowed him to obtain answers without requiring another person to communicate directly with him.
However, available reports have not identified the camera manufacturer, the AI tools, or the specific smartphone model involved.
Investigators have also not disclosed how the photographs reached the artificial intelligence service or how responses were transferred into his earpiece.
The candidate reportedly answered 159 of the 160 questions correctly in the first stage of the tax accountant examination.
That result represents approximately 99.4% accuracy, although available reporting does not independently establish the precise circumstances behind his performance.
His unusually high score attracted attention as details surrounding the examination emerged publicly.
The candidate subsequently submitted a written statement describing his conduct to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency.
Explaining his decision, he said, “I wrote down everything I did in a statement of voluntary surrender and submitted it to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency.”
Police investigate the fraud
The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency has received the candidate's written confession through his attorney and assigned investigators to examine the case.
However, authorities have not announced any charges, prosecution or judicial decision, leaving the legal outcome unresolved.
Investigators may examine electronic devices, account records and examination hall footage to establish whether the candidate's account matches available technical evidence.
The incident also raises practical difficulties for professional examination administrators because increasingly compact electronic equipment can be difficult to identify during routine inspections.
Traditional restrictions on smartphones and communication devices may not adequately address equipment designed specifically for discreet image capture and wireless communication.
Professional licensing bodies could consequently face pressure to strengthen physical screening and reconsider how they assess candidates' competence.

articles.title: Cómo pasar tus cámaras y termostatos de la app Nest a Google Home para no perder el acceso en enero
articles.text:
Google dejará de ofrecer la app Nest el 25 de enero de 2027 y pasará la gestión de cámaras, timbres, termostatos y alarmas a Google Home. Quienes tengan una cuenta Nest anterior a agosto de 2019 deben migrarla a una cuenta de Google antes del 25 de marzo de 2027, o la perderán.
Así lo indica la página de ayuda oficial de Google Home y Nest. El cambio afecta solo a la aplicación y al sitio web home.nest.com: los dispositivos seguirán funcionando dentro de la casa, pero desde esa fecha no podrán verse ni controlarse desde la app Nest.
Los equipos compatibles incluyen el termostato Nest Learning de tercera y cuarta generación, el Nest Thermostat E, las cámaras Nest Cam IQ, el timbre Nest Hello, el Nest Hub Max, las alarmas Nest Protect de segunda generación y la cerradura Nest x Yale.
Las dos fechas que importan
La primera es el 25 de enero de 2027, cuando la app Nest (Android, iOS, televisores y web) deja de funcionar. Ese día, según Google, los dispositivos compatibles y su historial de video se transfieren de forma automática a Google Home y al sitio home.google.com.
La segunda es el 25 de marzo de 2027, el plazo final para migrar la cuenta Nest a una cuenta de Google. Hasta esa fecha todavía se pueden descargar o borrar datos. Después, Google comenzará a procesar las eliminaciones y la cuenta Nest, sus datos y sus suscripciones se borrarán.
No todos los usuarios tienen que migrar la cuenta. Quien empezó a usar Nest después del 19 de agosto de 2019 ya entra con una cuenta de Google. Para saberlo, basta abrir la pantalla de inicio de sesión de la app Nest: si el botón “Sign in with Google” muestra la casa, la cuenta ya está vinculada.
Si en cambio la app pide una contraseña propia de Nest, la cuenta es anterior y hay que completar el paso único “Migrate to a Google Account”. Google aclara que usar una dirección de Gmail para entrar a Nest no garantiza que la cuenta ya esté migrada.
Cómo migrar la cuenta paso a paso
Según la ayuda de Google, el proceso se hace desde la app Nest actualizada. Primero hay que comprobar que se dispone de una cuenta de Google válida o crear una nueva. Después, se abre la app Nest, se toca Configuración y luego Cuenta, y se verifica que la sesión sea la de la cuenta que se quiere migrar.
A continuación se toca “Migrate to a Google Account” y se elige “Continue with Google”. Hay que seleccionar la cuenta de Google, permitir el acceso a los datos que pide la app, elegir qué miembros del hogar conservan acceso, revisar la política de privacidad y los términos, y tocar “Complete migration”.
Google recomienda usar una cuenta personal y no una de Google Workspace, el servicio de cuentas para empresas y escuelas. Con Workspace, el administrador de la organización puede acceder al hogar y, posiblemente, a los dispositivos vinculados, y quien pierda esa cuenta pierde también el acceso a la casa.
La migración es opcional según la ayuda, pero no se puede revertir. Después de completarla, la app Nest deja de funcionar en Apple TV y Android TV. Si el dueño de un hogar Nest migra, los demás integrantes deben migrar y ser invitados de nuevo para conservar el acceso, por lo que Google sugiere hacerlo en conjunto.
Para verificar que el trámite funcionó, se intenta entrar a la app Nest con el correo y la contraseña de Nest. Si ya no es posible y sí funciona el botón de Google, la cuenta fue migrada.
Qué hacer con los videos y las suscripciones
Los clips guardados en la biblioteca web de home.nest.com no se transferirán a Google Home. Para cámaras y timbres más antiguos, Google pide entrar a ese sitio antes del 25 de enero de 2027 y usar el botón “Download All” para descargarlos a la computadora.
El historial reciente sí pasará solo: las grabaciones de eventos y el historial continuo se verán en Google Home hasta que venza su plazo habitual de 30 o 60 días. En el navegador, home.google.com permitirá ver transmisiones en vivo, recorrer el historial y descargar clips de hasta cinco minutos.
Los suscriptores de Nest Aware de primera generación, que se dejó de vender en 2023, pasarán a Google Home Premium Advanced desde el 25 de enero de 2027 sin costo adicional ni necesidad de volver a cargar una tarjeta. Los clientes de ADT, la empresa de alarmas, no se ven afectados porque sus sistemas no usan la app Nest.

articles.title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access
articles.text:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.
The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.
The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.
MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.
The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.
The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.
Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.
Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.
The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.
Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.
A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.
That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.
In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.
The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.
Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.
The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw.
What to Do Now
With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach:
- Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs.
- Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default.
- Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to.
- Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched.
- If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used.
The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described.
The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

articles.title: Future generations of AI systems will continue to accelerate': New report claims that by 2030, the world could generate approximately 317 billion AI tokens every second
articles.text:
Future generations of AI systems will continue to accelerate': New report claims that by 2030, the world could generate approximately 317 billion AI tokens every second
Five billion AI tokens a second today, 317 billion by 2030?
- SanDisk estimates AI systems will produce about 150 quadrillion tokens in 2026 and could hit 10 quintillion a year, or 317 billion per second, by 2030
- The 2026 baseline squares with Google's own disclosures and independent tallies, but the model's inputs are unpublished and labeled as 'illustrative'
- SanDisk's 2030 figure is roughly seven times Goldman Sachs Research's forecast of 120 quadrillion tokens a month
SanDisk has put a number on the AI boom, and it is a big one: in its Tokenomics 2030 outlook, the flash memory maker estimates AI systems worldwide will produce around 150 quadrillion tokens this year, or roughly five billion every second, and by 2030, it believes annual output could approach 10 quintillion tokens, or about 317 billion per second.
The figures come with a footnote that matters more than the headline: SanDisk says they are drawn from its own internal analysis and estimates and are "intended for illustrative purposes only," and the outlook names no outside data source.
This matters when you consider who is doing the counting: a company pitching its own enterprise SSDs as part of the infrastructure all those tokens will need.
How SanDisk built its number and why it has limitations
A companion post by SanDisk's Jeff Fochtman, says Eric Spanneut, the company's senior vice president of product management, put together the team behind the model.
Rather than starting from forecasts of how much AI people will want, the model asks how much token output the world's infrastructure could realistically support. Its inputs are described only in broad strokes: the power directed toward AI inference, the size and capability of the accelerator fleet, compute and memory bandwidth, networking and storage, and expected gains in utilization and software efficiency.
That makes 317 billion tokens per second closer to a capacity ceiling than a demand forecast, and SanDisk has not published the assumptions underneath it, such as how many gigawatts it expects to be serving inference in 2030.
The precise-looking figure is also less precise than it seems, ironically: 10 quintillion tokens a year divided by the roughly 31.5 million seconds in a year gives 317 billion, so the headline number is a unit conversion of a round estimate. The growth it implies is more than 60-fold in four years, meaning global token output would have to nearly triple every year until the end of the decade, an ambitious take to say the least.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The 2026 baseline, at least, looks plausible: At Google I/O in May 2026, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said Google alone was handling 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, up from 480 trillion a year earlier. Converting that to a per-second basis nets you roughly 1.2 billion tokens per second, or about a quarter of SanDisk's global estimate from a single company, with the caveat that Google talks about tokens processed, SanDisk about tokens generated, and neither spells out exactly what it counts.
Alphabet's Q3 2026 earnings remarks added that its first-party model APIs alone were running at nearly 32 billion tokens per minute, 40% more than the previous quarter and over four times the year-earlier rate. Independent tallies land in the same neighborhood. In July, I/O Fund cited a tracker putting industry-wide volume near 370 trillion tokens a day, or about 135 quadrillion a year, though it did not explain how it compiled that figure.
One could even argue that SanDisk is being restrained in its projections: Google's sevenfold year-over-year jump is far faster than the roughly 2.8x annual growth baked into the 2030 figure, so the outlook effectively assumes today's pace will cool in the near future.
On the other side of the spectrum, it seems extremely aggressive: In May, Goldman Sachs Research projected that token consumption would grow 24-fold between 2026 and 2030 to reach 120 quadrillion tokens per month, driven largely by AI agents. Converted to a monthly rate, Sandisk's 10 quintillion a year comes to about 833 quadrillion, roughly seven times Goldman's figure.
Part of that gap sits in the starting point: Goldman's multiple implies a 2026 base of around 5 quadrillion tokens a month, against Sandisk's 12.5 quadrillion, and Goldman's base already looks light given Google's own disclosure the same week. The rest comes from SanDisk simply assuming much faster growth.
The bigger question is what all of these tokens actually measure. SanDisk's own companion post presents tokens as a practical gauge of AI computational work rather than a measure of intelligence or value, and admits there is no universal formula for turning token output into storage demand.
Token counts also climb when reasoning models think at length or when people repeatedly re-prompt to get something usable, a habit one TechRadar Pro contributor recently branded as "tokenmaxxing." A world producing 317 billion tokens per second would certainly be doing more AI work. It would not necessarily be doing 60 times more useful work.
Why is a flash company interested?
The commercial logic behind the outlook is the KV cache, the attention state a model builds as it reads a prompt, which agents need to keep around across long, multi-step sessions.
SanDisk argues that keeping all of it in scarce, high-bandwidth memory will not always be practical or economical, and that enterprise SSDs can serve as a larger tier for selected cache data so systems avoid recomputing work they have already done. The PR pitch that accompanied the outlook goes further, casting SSDs as "token batteries."
The engineering case is real, but it is hardly unique to SanDisk. LMCache, Nvidia's Dynamo framework and BlueField-4 CMX platform, WEKA and Phison already persist KV cache to storage, and Nvidia argued after this summer's Future of Memory and Storage conference that storage now matters as much as the silicon it feeds, since serving KV cache from flash rather than DRAM lets each GPU support longer contexts and more simultaneous users.
The outlook's most important input is also ironically its weakest link: SanDisk's companion post calls power the starting constraint, and Gartner analyst Linglan Wang has warned that "AI capacity is now constrained by power availability."
Goldman's Jim Schneider expects chip shortages to last at least another year. Even the storage tier SanDisk is promoting is squeezed, with Phison CEO Pua Khein-Seng relaying a NAND maker's estimate that new capacity takes around four years to reach mass production, pushing supply difficulties out to 2030.
None of that makes the 317 billion figure wrong, but it does clarify what it is: a storage vendor's estimate of what the world's AI infrastructure could produce if it gets built, powered, and kept busy at full capacity. The baseline is credible, and the direction of travel is not in doubt. The destination, for now, rests on assumptions SanDisk has not published yet and therefore are not open to scrutiny at the time of writing.

articles.title: “Mil millones de muertes”: el temor de Bill Gates por el futuro de la inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
El cofundador de Microsoft, Bill Gates, advirtió que la inteligencia artificial podría facilitar hechos capaces de provocar mil millones de muertes si la tecnología cae en manos de personas con intenciones dañinas. “La IA es sin duda lo bastante poderosa como para impulsar acontecimientos que causen mil millones de muertes”, afirmó el empresario en entrevista con NBC News.
Gates sostuvo que la combinación entre actores maliciosos y las herramientas de inteligencia artificial más avanzadas representa una capacidad de daño sin precedentes. No afirmó que una catástrofe de esa dimensión sea inevitable ni estableció una fecha para un escenario de ese tipo.
Su advertencia se centró en el potencial de la tecnología para ampliar el daño que podrían causar individuos, grupos u organizaciones con objetivos criminales. “Nunca hubo un arma tan poderosa como la combinación de personas con malas intenciones y las últimas herramientas de IA”, dijo.
Gates reclama una regulación gubernamental del sector
El fundador de Microsoft cuestionó la capacidad de las propias empresas tecnológicas para controlar los riesgos de sus desarrollos. “Nadie piensa que la autorregulación sea suficiente”, señaló.
Para Gates, la respuesta pasa por una intervención legislativa. Según explicó, los gobiernos, las fuerzas de seguridad y los dirigentes políticos deben participar en la definición de las salvaguardas y de los mecanismos de monitoreo que tendrán que cumplir las compañías del sector.
La declaración se produjo en medio de un debate creciente sobre los límites, la velocidad de desarrollo y la supervisión de los modelos de inteligencia artificial. “Si alguien tuviera un plan creíble para frenar el avance de la IA a nivel mundial, probablemente lo apoyaría. Sin embargo, no creo que eso vaya a suceder.
Los incentivos geopolíticos y económicos presionan demasiado para avanzar a toda velocidad”, afirmó Gates en un ensayo titulado “La turbulenta era de la IA ya está aquí. Las decisiones que tomemos ahora son cruciales”, publicado el 26 de agosto de 2026.
“Para maximizar los efectos positivos de esta tecnología sin precedentes y minimizar los negativos, de modo que todos estemos mejor, necesitamos comprender tanto los beneficios como los riesgos”, agregó en ese texto.
Tres riesgos centrales en el análisis de Gates
En su ensayo, Gates planteó que la tecnología avanza con una rapidez capaz de transformar sectores enteros durante la próxima década y que el mundo aún carece de un plan para afrontar sus consecuencias sociales, políticas y económicas.
El primer riesgo que identificó es laboral. Gates prevé que la inteligencia artificial afecte empleos de oficina, ventas, atención al cliente, ingeniería de software y asistencia jurídica, y que, con el avance de la robótica, llegue también a tareas manuales. Le preocupa en particular la reducción de puestos iniciales para jóvenes y la concentración de los beneficios económicos en pocos actores. “Esperar a que las personas estén desplazadas o subempleadas será demasiado tarde”, planteó.
El segundo riesgo señalado es el uso de estas herramientas para fraude, desinformación, deepfakes, ciberataques y bioterrorismo. Según explicó, la inteligencia artificial puede facilitar que delincuentes con habilidades limitadas ataquen a individuos, empresas y gobiernos, mientras que los sistemas más poderosos podrían actuar de formas imprevistas.
El tercer riesgo se relaciona con los niños y los jóvenes. Gates advirtió que los compañeros virtuales pueden reemplazar vínculos humanos, generar dependencia y debilitar el aprendizaje. Citó un estudio con más de 1.100 usuarios de asistentes virtuales que asoció un uso más intenso y personal de estas herramientas con un peor estado de ánimo.
Su participación en la Asamblea General de la ONU
Gates participó en Nueva York de los debates sobre el impacto global y la regulación de la inteligencia artificial, en el marco de la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas de septiembre de 2026. Durante su intervención, defendió que la tecnología puede reducir desigualdades si se extiende su acceso a los países de menores ingresos.
A través de la Fundación Gates, destinó USD 1.000 millones para impulsar ese objetivo. La edición 2026 del informe anual Goalkeepers, elaborado por la misma fundación, puso el foco en los avances y los riesgos vinculados con la inteligencia artificial.

articles.title: Nearly all software teams admit to shipping AI-generated code as study finds verification 'has not kept pace with that shift'
articles.text:
Nearly all software teams admit to shipping AI-generated code as study finds verification 'has not kept pace with that shift'
What happened to verification before distribution?
- The majority of software development teams have merged code with AI contributions that they didn’t understand
- Some teams (55%) manually review code, while others use one AI model to review another, which has mixed results
- TestMu AI’s State of AI in Quality Engineering 2026 report has also found that only 13% of teams have an incident response provision for publishing AI-generated errors
Generative AI coding tool shave been wholeheartedly embraced by software development teams, to such an extent that 81% have admitted to merging AI generated code that wasn’t fully understood, new research has claimed.
TestMu AI’s State of AI in Quality Engineering 2026 report also found a mixed approach to reviewing AI code and very few teams employing an incident response procedure in the event of AI generated errors occurring on live projects.
These results raise some questions on how development teams are using AI and what steps are being employed to verify output. While some teams use manual review, others rely on a second LLM to review and judge the code. However, this appears to have increased the likelihood of code no-one understands being published.
LLM-as-a-judge
Revealed in the report is the notion of the verification gap, a challenge for teams relying on AI-generated code. Just 41% of teams use automated checks of AI-written code before merging it with existing, often live code. This gap is the beginning of the problem – there is simply too much code to efficiently check.
With 55% of development teams using manual review, or passing to a dedicated QA team (51%), it’s clear that with some teams, important measures are in place.
Employing a second LLM to grade the generated code might seem like a smart move. In terms of fixing issues, it probably is. But the result of this strategy is that teams using LLM-as-a-judge are shipping code they don’t understand at a greater rate – 29%, compared with 15% who don’t use AL grading.
Verify your output
Asad Khan, the Co-founder and CEO of TestMu AI said the key point that verification of AI-generated code is not keeping pace with the volume of output.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“Software teams now rely on AI to write their code, generate their tests, and increasingly determine whether both are ready to ship,” he noted.
“Verification, however, has not kept pace with that shift. We believe any output AI produces should be validated by a system independent of the model that produced it, before it merges and every time it changes.” The development teams that have put in place the procedures to do this are doing better, it seems.
“The teams in our survey that already follow this discipline see fewer defects reach production, and we expect it to become the standard for engineering organizations shipping with AI,” Khan added.
