articles.title: Content, AI, empowerment: test your business creativity with Edition 259 of our weekly quiz!
articles.text:
Content, AI, empowerment: test your business creativity with Edition 259 of our weekly quiz!
This insightful feature from YourStory tests and strengthens your business acumen! Here are 5 questions to kick off this 259th quiz. Ready?
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 259th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.
What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?
Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts.
Q1: Customer workflow
Most enterprises have tools to store customer records and manage calls – but employees often connect this data manually, leading to missed tasks and delayed resolutions. How can this gap be filled?
Q2: Enterprise content
Every enterprise is becoming a content enterprise – but many companies face challenges in creating relevant content quickly, accurately and at scale. Where is the entrepreneurial opportunity here?
Q3: Hemp
Hemp is a hardy crop, with many uses in fibre, food and oil. How can this business opportunity be tapped while also delivering an uplifting social impact?
Q4: Learning disabilities
Awareness of learning disabilities due to neurological conditions is rising in India, yet access to specialist care remains uneven. How can better care be provided here?
Q5: Audio entertainment
A growing number of listeners expect a wide range of audio content for entertainment, including blockbusters and hyper-personalised experiences. How can technology help create such content at scale?
Answers!
Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!
A1: Customer workflow
Founded by Henry Dag, Cogover brings CRM, built-in calling, workflows, and AI agents into one environment. This helps ensure that a customer interaction leads to a visible, accountable next step.
Customers can extract relevant information from a conversation, propose a record update or prepare a task. Read more here about how Cogover’s selection for NetApp Excellerator creates an opportunity to connect with a broader enterprise data perspective.
A2: Enterprise content
Founded and led by Prabhu Narasimhan, Brahma AI combines enterprise content intelligence and management with AI creation capabilities. They span visual AI, digital humans, voice, and multilingual performance.
The company works with customers such as Warner Bros, the NBA, and Mayo Clinic, with Google and Hakuhodo as distribution partners. Read more here about how it is reimagining the content supply chain in the age of AI, and its recent fundraise from Multiples Private Equity.
A3: Hemp
Founded by Pavitra Joshi, KumaonKhand is a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand. It has developed a multi-micro hub and spoke model with decentralised processing hubs that employ largely women workers.
KumaonKhand makes its own skincare range, hemp protein powder and hemp fibre textiles. Read more here about how its impact goes beyond creating a hemp market, and also enables women to earn independently and access opportunities closer to home.
A4: Learning disabilities
Founded by paediatric neurologist Dr Sonam Kothari and healthcare entrepreneur Dr Abhishek Sen, Butterfly Learnings is focused on India’s neurodevelopmental care system. Its platform combines therapy, diagnostics, digital therapeutics, and technology-enabled interventions.
It estimates that nearly 45 million children in India live with neurodevelopmental conditions, while only a small proportion receive timely intervention. Read more here about its solutions, and its recent fundraise from Inflexor Ventures, Enzia Ventures, Insitor Impact Asia Fund and IIMA Ventures.
A5: Audio entertainment
Founded by Rohan Nayak, Nishanth KS and Prateek Dixit, Pocket FM has more than 250 million listeners across 20+ countries, and more than 550,000 creators on its platform. “AI is creating an entirely new era of entertainment,” Nayak explains.
AI is increasingly used across content creation, production, personalisation, and distribution, reducing the time required to launch in new markets from about 12 months to two. Read more here about how its listeners now spend an average of 155 minutes a day on Pocket FM.
YourStory has also published the pocketbook ‘Proverbs and Quotes for Entrepreneurs: A World of Inspiration for Startups’ as a creative and motivational guide for innovators.

articles.title: Una pinza robótica que siente, interpreta y actúa en tiempo real
articles.text:
La empresa canadiense Robotiq presentó el 2FC, un dispositivo de agarre robótico con sensores táctiles e inteligencia artificial integrada que permite a los robots detectar deslizamientos, estimar la posición de los objetos y adaptarse a distintas piezas sin necesidad de cambiar el herramental. Su diseño apunta a entornos industriales de alta variedad, donde la adaptabilidad del agarre marca la diferencia.
La empresa, especializada en soluciones de robótica colaborativa, anunció en octubre de 2026 el lanzamiento del 2FC Physical AI Gripper, la versión con inteligencia física de su pinza 2F, uno de los sistemas de agarre adaptativo más utilizados en la industria, con más de 30.000 unidades desplegadas en todo el mundo.
El nuevo modelo incorpora sensores táctiles en cada dedo, procesamiento embebido en la muñeca del robot y un software propio denominado Contact Core, que transforma los datos de contacto en comportamiento en tiempo real, según los medios especializados Control Engineering y Robotics & Automation News.
Sensores, inteligencia artificial y funciones autónomas
El núcleo del sistema es un conjunto de sensores que toman mil lecturas por segundo. Cada dedo del 2FC mide presión, vibración, fuerza, velocidad, posición y propiocepción —la conciencia del propio movimiento del dedo—, distribuidos en 28 táxeles (unidades mínimas de captación táctil, equivalentes a los píxeles de una pantalla) por dedo.
Todos los datos se sincronizan con precisión de milisegundo en un marco temporal compartido y quedan disponibles para los sistemas de control a través de una interfaz unificada.
La información capturada fluye hacia el AI Hub, una pequeña unidad de procesamiento montada en la muñeca del robot, donde el software Contact Core analiza los datos en tiempo real y ejecuta cinco funciones de forma autónoma:
- Determina si la pieza quedó bien sujeta o corre riesgo de caerse.
- Detecta si está comenzando a deslizarse antes de que eso ocurra.
- Calcula en qué ángulo u orientación fue agarrada, sin necesidad de una cámara;
- Corrige el agarre si la pieza no quedó centrada entre los dedos;
- Verifica que la pieza agarrada coincida con la forma esperada.
A diferencia de los sistemas tradicionales, que envían números en bruto que un ingeniero debe interpretar después, el 2FC traduce toda esa actividad en conclusiones listas para usar, lo que reduce el trabajo manual y acelera el desarrollo de modelos de inteligencia artificial.
El sistema es compatible con los entornos de programación más extendidos en robótica industrial, y su código fuente está disponible públicamente en el repositorio de la compañía. Esto significa que cualquier equipo de ingeniería puede integrarlo en sus propios desarrollos, adaptarlo a sus necesidades específicas y construir sobre él sin depender exclusivamente del software de la compañía, algo que reduce la barrera de adopción para empresas que ya trabajan con herramientas estándar del sector.
Capacidades, aplicaciones y especificaciones técnicas
Una de las capacidades más destacadas del 2FC es su mecanismo de corrección activa. Cuando solo uno de los sensores detecta contacto con la pieza —señal de que el objeto está descentrado—, el sistema guía al robot para que ajuste su trayectoria de cierre hasta que el sensor opuesto también registre contacto. Una vez completado el agarre, el sistema informa la orientación, la fuerza aplicada y si la pieza coincide con la forma esperada.
El dispositivo apunta a aplicaciones de alimentación de máquinas, traslado de piezas y ensamblaje en entornos con alta variedad de partes, donde la adaptabilidad del agarre representa una ventaja operativa frente a los sistemas de visión o las soluciones de fijación a medida.
Está certificado para soportar dos millones de operaciones de agarre, lo que permite usarlo tanto en etapas de desarrollo y recolección de datos como en producción a escala, con el mismo hardware a lo largo de todo el proceso.
Se encuentra disponible en dos versiones —el 2FC-85 y el 2FC-140— diferenciadas por el tamaño de las piezas que pueden manipular y la carga máxima que son capaces de sostener (85 mm y 5 kg, y 140 mm y 2,5 kg, respectivamente). Ambas comparten la misma fuerza de agarre y se conectan al sistema mediante un único cable Ethernet, que gestiona a la vez la alimentación y la comunicación.

articles.title: Las viejas centrales cerradas de Europa han encontrado una segunda vida: los centros de datos
articles.text:
La empresa energética alemana Uniper está a punto de cerrar un acuerdo que puede dar un auténtico empujón a los centros de datos en Europa: quiere reconvertir sus centrales en desuso en la infraestructura de moda, como recoge el Financial Times. Y es que esas viejas centrales tienen todo lo necesario para ser el datacenter ideal: tienen espacio, accesos y lo más importante, una conexión a la red eléctrica asegurada.
El acuerdo. Hay mucho secretismo en cuanto al acuerdo, de hecho solo sabemos dos cosas: el primero es que la compañía está a punto de cerrar un acuerdo en uno de sus 10 emplazamientos sin uso, situados en Reino Unido, Alemania, Suecia y Países Bajos, para convertirlo en centro de datos, y mantiene negociaciones avanzadas sobre otros dos. El segundo es que su CEO, Michael Lewis, cifra en unos 700 MW la capacidad de red asegurada en esos emplazamientos, lo que según la Agencia Internacional de la Energía (AIE) bastaría para unos siete centros de datos de hyperescalers o unos 70 más pequeños.
Eso sí, desconocemos cuáles de esos 10 centros están entre los elegidos, si todas las papeletas están en el Reino Unido y Alemania, como deslizó su CEO en verano. Tampoco se conoce el precio, solo estimaciones: según UBS, el acuerdo rondará el millón de euros por MW, lo que daría unos 700 millones. Asimismo, ignoramos quién está al otro lado de la mesa, si bien entre los candidatos están gigantes como Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet o Meta.
Por qué importa. Porque entre la larga lista de burocracia necesaria para montar un centro de datos, esperar una conexión de red en la UE requiere entre dos y diez años en función del país. De hecho, la AIE calcula que por culpa de las limitaciones de red el 20% de la capacidad de los centros de datos previstos hasta 2030 pueden retrasarse. Así que quien ya tiene esa conexión se ahorra la espera. El quid de la cuestión es que los datacenters son auténticos tragones energéticos: la misma AIE proyecta que el consumo eléctrico de los centros de datos va a duplicarse hasta alcanzar unos 945 TWh en 2030.
Por tanto, el acuerdo es un win-win: Uniper rentabiliza instalaciones inactivas que tienen todo lo necesario y, a la vez, aumenta la demanda de su energía. Por otro lado, las empresas que montan centros de datos tienen el proyecto bastante adelantado para ponerlo en funcionamiento cuanto antes. Y además, sortea el problema de fondo: la red eléctrica europea no se diseñó pensando en la IA
El renacer de Uniper. Uniper fue en su día el mayor comprador de gas ruso de Alemania, pero en 2022 tuvo que ser rescatada por el estado, que inyectó 13.500 millones de euros para evitar su hundimiento. Después, el pasado mes de mayo Alemania anunció su intención de reprivatizarla, reduciendo su participación del 99% hasta un 25%. En julio, acordó invertir 5.000 millones de euros hasta 2030 en generación flexible y ha encontrado en esta reconversión de sus viejas centrales una nueva e inesperada fuente de ingresos.
No es la primera. Tampoco será la última. Uniper no se ha inventado nada con esta lucrativa reconversión, hace unos días se anunció el desarrollo de un campus de centros de datos en la central eléctrica de North Yorkshire a partir de la infraestructura existente de Drax, como detalla The Guardian. Y no hace falta ni cruzar la frontera: la también teutona PreussenElektra GmbH trabaja codo con codo con Nvidia para evaluar si sus viejas centrales nucleares pueden servir como centros de datos.
De generar electricidad a devorarla. Quédate con el nombre de la central de carbón inglesa Ratcliffe-on-Soar, propiedad de Uniper, porque tiene todas la papeletas para ser una de las elegidas. Esta central cerró en septiembre de 2024 pero según documentos municipales, Uniper ha solicitado a National Grid una nueva conexión de 720 MW para posibles centros de datos. Porque obviamente una central de carbón genera electricidad, pero un centro de datos la consume en grandes cantidades. Según Uniper, que anunció la demolición de las viejas instalaciones, ya tienen el permiso de planificación que permite la modificación para transformarla en un centro de datos.

articles.title: Sony's Patented Collar Would Blow Air on Players, Likely During VR Games
articles.text:
Saturday, November 21st 2026
Sony's Patented Collar Would Blow Air on Players, Likely During VR Games
If you're familiar with Sony's patents, you know they can be quite ambitious sometimes. Continuing that trend, Sony Interactive Entertainment recently filed a patent application for a curved neckband with air vents on the inner side that would blow air towards the wearer's neck, chin, and face. The filing (US 2026/0357800 A1), spotted by Patentlyze, went public on November 12. Sony itself describes the goal as a way to "increase the sense of immersion." Apparently, there is also a built-in communication unit that takes control signals from an external device and decides which vents fire and how hard. That external device would likely be a console or a PC.
Looking at the design, the filing shows eight tiny blowers spaced around the collar that would act as the outlets for air. Sony also mentions piezoelectric elements that vibrate a thin plate at high speed, apparently so the airflow can keep up with what happens on screen. Some of the diagrams are quite interesting too, including one where an enemy is approaching from the back, and the collar is supposed to alert the player to their existence. Apparently, some stimuli can trigger more frequent and stronger puffs of air, and there is also mention of wind effects for racing games. A schematic pairs the neckband with a VR headset, so maybe the PS VR2 or its successor is the target for this technology. Of course, a patent is not a finished product, and companies (especially Sony) file lots of them that go nowhere. Here's a similar one about turning game audio into visual cues for hearing-impaired players.

articles.title: This week on Tom's Hardware Premium: 21 November 2026 — AMD, Nvidia and more show off the future of high-performance computing at SC26
articles.text:
This week on Tom's Hardware Premium: 21 November 2026 — AMD, Nvidia and more show off the future of high-performance computing at SC26
The acceleration never stops.
In case you're worried about missing out on all the goodness on Tom's Hardware Premium, we've rounded up everything that we've published this week right here. The main theme for this week has been coverage straight from the show floor at the annual Supercomputing conference (SC26). If you've not yet caught up, you've been missing out, as all of our coverage from the conference is currently free to access. All you need to do is sign up or log in to your Tom's Hardware account to enjoy all of our coverage from the show.
First up, our resident CPU boffin, Jake Roach, has been on the show floor all week, offering us a direct line to all the goings-on at the conference, including an interesting back-and-forth from Nvidia and AMD on their CPUs. AMD claims that its latest EPYC Venice lineup is the best at agentic workloads, while Nvidia's marketing material characterized Nvidia's Vera CPU as being purpose-built for Agentic AI. At SC26, Nvidia CPU chief Ian Finder rebuked Nvidia's own marketing material, stating that the idea that Nvidia could have predicted the Data Center moment was "absurd," instead saying that the company's design know-how helped them develop the processor.
In this interview, we sit down with Finder to find out how Vera came to be, what agentic workloads mean for the CPU industry, and where Nvidia's headed next.
Nvidia's Vera CPU was a hot topic at SC26, as the company explained that existing software cannot always take full advantage of the processor without architecture-specific optimization. The company showed that under some workloads, Vera's performance can be optimized by up to 39% when taking its Olympus-based Arm cores into account. However, it remains to be seen how much performance can be gained from Olympus-specific hardware optimization workloads other than matrix multiplication.
Nvidia also announced a Rubin GPU variant, named Rubin HPC, a chip that the company claims is purpose-built for agentic workflows and scientific simulations that demand processing large datasets. While technical details remain scant, Nvidia says that Rubin HPC sports over 50,000 CUDA cores, or slightly below double the number of cores present in the standard-issue Rubin GPU. We explored all the details and possibilities that the newly announced chip might offer.
AMD is now featured in over 40% of the new TOP500 list of supercomputers, with a 14% boost to the company's position. Leading the company is Lux, a supercomputer developed in conjunction with the U.S. Department of Energy. The second supercomputer, Discovery, is expected to debut in 2028, sporting a suite of EPYC CPUs and Instinct accelerators.
Within the TOP500, not much has changed... at the top, with the top 10 systems remaining unchanged, as China's LineShine system in Shenzhen remains at the top of the list, with El Capitan remaining second. We take a look at the entire list and how the focus has seemingly shifted toward AI compute capacity. While the demand for HPC hardware is at an all-time high, it appears as though the vast majority of that hardware isn't being tested against the TOP500 benchmark.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
- AMD grabs over 40% of new TOP500 list for supercomputers, up 14% since last year — new Lux system developed between AMD and Department of Energy debuts at no. 14 with EPYC CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPUs
- China retains fastest supercomputer in the world crown as AI data centers soak up new hardware — Top500 records fewest new systems in 33 years
Despite AI clusters seemingly eating up compute capacity, AMD recognizes that the burgeoning segment will never wholly replace HPC computing, and that high-precision workloads will continue to be necessary. AMD's Scott Tease further suggested that building a heterogeneous compute stack would be the best path forward for tackling complex research problems. This point dovetails nicely into how AMD additionally touted that its MI430X's native FP64 operations will beat out emulated support for the full-precision data types seen in Nvidia's hardware. This is notable, as the company claims that Ozaki FP64 emulation could have cascading effects on memory usage, which is in notorious levels of undersupply.
- Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ says AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands
- AMD attacks Nvidia's FP64 emulation at SC26, touts native double-precision on Instinct MI430X — says Ozaki schemes fit less than 10% of HPC workloads and triple memory use and emulated FP64 is a poor fit for many HPC workloads
Not wanting to be left out of the conversation, Intel's next-generation Diamond Rapids CPUs surfaced at SC26, but not from Intel itself, curiously. On the ground, we saw the chips turn up at the CXL booth and at Bull, where the CPU was shown installed in a server. While there were no demos available, the company did show off demos for Xeon 6+ and its Crescent Island GPU.
Elsewhere at the show, PCI 6 devices and controllers have started to surface. First, Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was demoed at the show, armed with PerformaShape 2, which increases the number of quality-of-service sets from 256 to 512, alongside additional boons.
Elsewhere, Phison detailed two new enterprise SSDs: one that comes with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory, and another that is set to merge pSLC cache, with high QLC capacity on a single controller. We explore what makes these devices notable and why, though the company itself notes that the devices are very much still in development.
- Silicon Motion demos SM8466 PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, expected to ship by 2028 — controller boasts improved quality of service, samples imminent
- Phison details SSD with a built-in NPU and 64GB of 130 GB/s memory to run PyTorch and llama.cpp on-drive — claims up to 100x less data transfer alongside new mixed media pSLC and QLC design
VAST Data explained how petabyte-scale SSDs will outgrow the tried and true RAID parallel filesystems, according to a simulation the company ran on its own 900 PB system, which puts the odds of data loss at a staggering 1 in 11 over a decade. We explain all in detail about how it works.
As enterprise hardware and the titanic growth of AI superclusters push the limits of our existing material infrastructure, from interconnects to grid energy and raw materials, researchers from The Ohio State University discussed how high-performance networking could soon scale across entire regions. We explore how faster networking connections could spell a future where distributed computing systems communicate across vast distances.
While we have a few more articles waiting to be published from SC26, we've also been hard at work publishing stories from other corners of the industry. To read these, you'll need to first arm yourself with a Tom's Hardware Premium subscription.
This week, Anthropic debuted on the NYSE, but the frontier AI lab's debut is also colored by the backdrop of what seems like an endless barrage of new vulnerabilities, hacks, and AI-powered action by would-be malfeasants. The conversation around AI safety, sparked by OpenAI's HuggingFace incident, is also being used as a Trojan horse for safety legislation, and against this backdrop, we explore how the companies shaping AI safety might also be the ones warning against using competitors, like capable Chinese open-weight AI models.
Anthropic has also been busy bringing up more compute resources, notably publishing how it managed to get its Claude Mythos model to optimize its software stack to work with AMD Instinct hardware in around three days, with little human oversight. What once was a relentless task that took significant man-hours, an AI can now help complete in mere days. Such a feat could endanger Nvidia's highly lucrative CUDA moat, as AI continues to transform the hardware landscape.
Intel's acquisition of Quantum computing company Classiq is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027, and following it, Intel is poised to have a chance at becoming the first full-stack quantum computing vendor. The company also plans to manufacture quantum processors on its 18A process, offer foundry services, and eventually sell quantum computers.
An unmanned chip fab might be an unthinkable future today, but it's a future that chipmakers are already planning for. SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron, known rivals in the memory industry, have formed a body to standardize robotic charging, with the aim of having robots from different manufacturers share equipment and therefore cut the costs and complexity of deploying fleets of robotic workers.

To read any of the articles we mention above, as well as unlock Bench, you'll need to purchase a Tom's Hardware Premium subscription. Your support goes a long way in helping us to publish deeper, more insightful articles that might not otherwise be covered.
Sayem Ahmed is the Subscription Editor at Tom's Hardware. He covers a broad range of deep dives into hardware, both new and old, including the CPUs, GPUs, and everything else that uses a semiconductor. He has worked as a professional tech journalist since 2015 and has written for Gamespot, IGN, and Dexerto.

articles.title: Flipper One races to $15 million of backing on Kickstarter in 3 days — pocket device can set up Wi-Fi, 5G or VPNs anywhere and spot hacks too
articles.text:
Why did the Flipper One just raise $15 million on Kickstarter? Here’s what the pocket gadget does — and how it compares to the Flipper Zero
Another appealing gadgets for tech enthusiasts
Its makers are insisting it's not a direct successor to the Flipper Zero, but there's a new pocket-sized, mini-computer on the market that's going to appeal to tinkerers, hackers, and tech enthusiasts: the Flipper One.
A Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign for the device just went live: it raised $13 million on the first day, and currently stands at more than $14.5 million at the time of writing (and continues to go up rapidly).
Given that kind of financial backing and widespread interest, you might be wondering what the Flipper One is, what it can do, and whether it's going to cause as many security headaches as the Flipper Zero. Here's what you need to know.
Flipper One vs Flipper Zero: what is it?
Before we get to the Flipper One, it's probably helpful to do a quick Flipper Zero recap. Launched in 2020, the Flipper Zero is a tiny gadget that's still on sale and which can interact with a whole host of fundamental, low-level tech protocols: think Bluetooth, RFID, NFC, and the like. It can analyze and control devices like key cards, fobs, TV remotes, and electronic access points.
That's led to numerous security scare stories down the years, but it's not quite the hacker's dream that it's sometimes portrayed as — it can't really get into devices or systems that are competently protected. It's more for geeks and tech enthusiasts who are interested in customizing their gadgets and experimenting with electronics, which does admittedly include testing security vulnerabilities.
And so to the Flipper One. The two devices are "completely different projects built for different tasks" according to the team at Flipper. The Flipper One is a similar, compact size, but it runs regular software (Linux) and taps into more consumer-friendly technologies — so Wi-Fi and 5G rather than RFID and NFC.
The Flipper One is more powerful and is capable of running more complex software, but it doesn't tap into the raw wireless and wired signals that the Flipper Zero does. It's more interested in Wi-Fi networks, routers, and internet-connected devices — so, for example, the Flipper Zero could mimic a wireless garage door opener but the Flipper One can set up a VPN on a network.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
What can you do with the Flipper One?
So just how capable is this device? What's so appealing that over 27,000 (and counting) people have pledged money to bring it into being? The Flipper One's Kickstarter page lists many different things you can do with the device — and while it's not suitable for complete beginners, it should be accessible enough for anyone who's reasonably tech-savvy.
You can use it to set up a VPN on your network, as already mentioned, and it can act as both a Wi-Fi client and hotspot (with an Ethernet port, it'd work as a travel router in a hotel room). It's able to monitor Wi-Fi networks, so you could check up on the devices connected to your network and check for any security issues, and there's also eSIM capabilities so it can get on cellular networks without any other help.
It's helpful for analyzing traffic between smart home devices, and controlling them using custom configurations too. As it's actually a complete mini computer, you can use it as a portable TV media box, and it'll work as an actual desktop computer with the right peripherals attached — just don't expect too much in terms of performance.
There's also a lot of scope for expansion with the Flipper One, too. There are already add-ons for connecting to radio signals, so you could use it as a radio scanner, and off-grid communication protocols — the device can work as an off-grid walkie-talkie, for example. Of course, once the developer community gets access to the gadget, we can expect much more functionality to become available.
Should we be worried (again)?
We've already touched on some of the hacking concerns that have emerged around the Flipper Zero down the years, and they're not without merit. This is a compact device that's able to directly interface with electronics like access cards and key fobs, and test security protocols at basic levels.
Perhaps the most concerning capability of the Flipper Zero is its ability to intercept and repeat wireless signals — with a car key fob, for example. However, these kind of hacks have been largely exaggerated, and the Flipper Zero is far from being a magic hacking toy. The majority of systems will have enough security in place to keep it out.
The Flipper One can also be used as a hacking device, but in a different sort of way. It's more for prodding and pushing full computer systems and networks: you could test vulnerabilities in your Wi-Fi network or a web server, or even simulate some aspects of cyberattack. On the flip side, it can also be used as a honeypot, a way of trying to lure in and expose other hackers and malware.
As with the Flipper Zero though, there's no need to panic about the Flipper One. Its security testing and hacking prowess is not significantly different to a laptop or a Raspberry Pi system — it doesn't suddenly unlock security vulnerabilities in other systems and devices that weren't there before, and could be exposed in other ways.

Dave is a freelance tech journalist who has been writing about gadgets, apps and the web for more than two decades. Based out of Stockport, England, on TechRadar you'll find him covering news, features and reviews, particularly for phones, tablets and wearables. Working to ensure our breaking news coverage is the best in the business over weekends, David also has bylines at Gizmodo, T3, PopSci and a few other places besides, as well as being many years editing the likes of PC Explorer and The Hardware Handbook.

articles.title: How Illumine cracked the US SaaS market from India: AI, GTM, Growth playbook
articles.text:
How Illumine cracked the US SaaS market from India: AI, GTM, Growth playbook
In this episode of the Prime Venture Partners Podcast, Illumine co-founders Navneet Rastogi and Sourabh Agarwal share how they went from losing nearly 200 customers during COVID to building a global childcare SaaS business, competing with established US players and scaling sales from India.
Three months of advertising on Meta had produced disappointing results for Illumine, an Indian SaaS startup trying to establish itself in the competitive US childcare software market. The founders were close to abandoning the channel when they decided to run one final experiment. Instead of asking prospective customers to sign up immediately, they shifted their campaigns towards building awareness.
The results changed their approach to customer acquisition. Illumine went from generating approximately 20 leads a month to 400–500, with Meta eventually contributing 60–70% of its leads.
"The point was the awareness was not there," says Navneet Rastogi, Co-founder of Illumine.
It was one of several lessons that helped Illumine evolve from a bootstrapped Indian startup into a vertical SaaS platform serving preschools and childcare centres across more than 50 countries. Today, India accounts for less than 15% of its revenue, while the US has become a major focus for the business.
In a conversation with Gaurav Ranjan, Principal at Prime Venture Partners, co-founders Rastogi and Sourabh Agarwal discussed the company's international expansion, its experiments with go-to-market strategies and why customer understanding matters more than sophisticated technology.
From 200 customers to almost zero during COVID
Illumine began with a personal problem. As a parent, Rastogi wanted better visibility into his son's daily experiences at preschool. The founders subsequently discovered that even large childcare chains were struggling with outdated software designed for conventional schools rather than the operational complexities of early childhood education.
Their first customer, one of India's largest premium preschool chains, provided enough revenue for the founders to bootstrap the business. For nearly six months, they worked alongside teachers, administrators and finance teams to understand the workflows before building the product.
But COVID disrupted everything. Illumine had approximately 200 customers before childcare centres began shutting down. Unlike conventional education, childcare could not simply move online.
The crisis forced the founders to explore international markets where centres were still operating. Organic demand from the Middle East and Southeast Asia provided the initial opportunity, with Dubai eventually becoming an important market for the company.
The experience also prepared Illumine for the US. According to Rastogi, approximately 90% of childcare workflows were similar across geographies, with the remaining differences handled through product configuration.
Why Illumine chose Texas and Florida over California
Entering the US presented a different challenge. Established competitors such as Procare had decades of experience, strong customer relationships and substantial market presence.
Rather than following the conventional advice to begin in California, Illumine evaluated states based on three factors: market size, competitive intensity and customer purchasing power. Texas, Florida and New York became its initial focus areas.
The founders also realised that desk research could not replace understanding customers on the ground. During one visit, Rastogi and two colleagues walked approximately 30,000 steps across Manhattan, visiting childcare centres as prospective parents to understand their admissions and operating processes.
A particularly revealing experience came during a small event in Florida. An attendee questioned why customers should trust an unfamiliar Indian company over Procare, which had been operating for more than two decades.
Rastogi responded by asking whether existing providers had listened to customers' requests for improvements. The discussion revealed a simple but underserved requirement: communicating with Spanish-speaking families.
Illumine built the capability, helping it gain traction in Florida.
"Online will tell you the fancy thing to do, but it was not the reality there," Rastogi recalls.
The positioning mistake that was hurting conversions
Illumine's early US marketing attracted enquiries, but many came from small home daycare operators rather than established childcare businesses looking to replace their existing systems.
The founders realised that while their advanced features were attracting attention, they were not necessarily convincing customers to switch.
"Fancy is getting them into the call but not getting them to convert," Rastogi explains.
The team began mapping childcare centres across US states, studying their size, fees, existing software and purchasing power. It also changed how the product was positioned, balancing its AI capabilities with the core operational requirements customers expected from a childcare management platform.
This research informed the company's paid acquisition experiments. Google Ads was already generating leads from customers actively searching for solutions, but Meta was underperforming.
After three unsuccessful months, the team switched from lead-generation campaigns to awareness campaigns. Monthly lead volumes subsequently increased from approximately 20 to 400–500.
Importantly, Rastogi says the company also began attracting higher-value customers through the channel. The lesson was not simply about advertising optimisation. Illumine first needed to establish credibility as a serious alternative to established software providers.
Selling to US customers with a team in India
Illumine's US expansion did not depend on building a large American sales organisation. According to Rastogi, approximately 90% of its US revenue is generated by employees working from India.
However, adapting to American sales expectations required changes in how the team conducted conversations. Unlike Indian sales calls, which often move quickly into business discussions, US customers expected relationship-building, video interactions and a more consultative approach.
The company also recruited people with direct childcare industry experience, including former centre directors, who could speak to customers about their operational challenges rather than merely demonstrate software features.
This approach helped Illumine build trust in a market where customers were understandably cautious about adopting a relatively unfamiliar international platform.
The founders also learnt that implementation capacity had to grow alongside sales. A surge in customer onboarding around September required them to move experienced employees into customer success to support new deployments.
AI that reduces three hours of work to ten minutes
For Illumine, AI adoption has been driven by operational problems rather than the technology itself. Childcare teachers, for instance, spend considerable time documenting activities and sharing updates with parents, often sorting through hundreds of photographs after a full day of managing children.
Agarwal describes how a centre might generate 1,000 photographs daily, requiring teachers to identify children, organise activities and prepare individual parent updates. Illumine's AI now helps automate this process while allowing teachers to review and approve the output.
"So the 3 hours work went to 10 minutes now," Agarwal says.
The company is extending this approach to financial reconciliation, parent communication and front-desk operations. According to Rastogi, AI functionality can be upsold at nearly twice the base software price, creating an additional monetisation opportunity.
But the founders remain cautious about where automation belongs. Illumine declined requests to use AI-powered cameras to analyse children's emotions, preferring to leave observation and decisions involving children to educators.
Why the next SaaS moat is understanding the customer
With AI making software development increasingly accessible, Rastogi believes technology alone is becoming a weaker competitive advantage. What remains difficult to replicate is the accumulated understanding of complex customer workflows, from billing and payroll to occupancy management and regulatory compliance.
For Illumine, this knowledge has been built through years of working directly with childcare operators, including customers whose demanding requirements forced the company to improve its product.
Venture capital has also changed the founders' ambitions. After years of prioritising investments that delivered immediate returns, they could pursue longer-term opportunities and accelerate international expansion.
With the business growing approximately threefold year on year, according to the founders, Illumine is now exploring adjacent revenue opportunities in payments, insurance and compliance. Payments alone could eventually become several times larger than its core software revenue.
For a company that nearly lost its entire customer base during COVID, the ambition has changed considerably. Illumine is no longer simply trying to build better software for preschools. It wants to become one of the largest technology platforms serving the global childcare industry.
As Rastogi puts it, "I see a big opportunity to build."

articles.title: No tengo una consola y no sé por dónde empezar: cómo puedo jugar a 'GTA VI' gastando el menor dinero posible
articles.text:
Nadie puede decir que el lanzamiento de 'GTA VI' le haya pillado por sorpresa. Es el juego más esperado de la generación y, cuando las actuales consolas salieron en 2020, ya hubo gente que las compró esperando jugar algún día al juego (aunque ni siquiera se había anunciado por aquel entonces). Pero si te ha pillado el toro y el FOMO no te deja dormir porque quieres jugar a 'GTA VI' a toda costa, vamos a responder un par de preguntas:
- Cuál es la forma más barata de jugar a 'GTA VI'
- Cuál es la mejor
Ya te aviso que casi ninguna es barata porque "gracias" a la crisis de componentes debido a la situación de la inteligencia artificial, todas las consolas han subido vertiginosamente de precio, pero volvemos a lo que decía antes: si no te quieres quedar fuera de 'GTA VI', vamos a ver las opciones para entrar ahora mismo.
La versión del juego
Es lo principal porque hay dos 'GTA VI': el completo y el recortado. Por un lado, tenemos tanto la edición con caja (sin disco, recuerda) como la edición digital por 80 euros. Este es el juego base y el que nos permite disfrutar de las misiones de historia como ha sido concebido el título.
Sin embargo, luego está 'GTA VI' Ultimate Edition por 100 euros. Es la versión completa que tiene diferentes estéticas para algunas armas y vehículos, pero también algún vehículo exclusivo, diferentes estilos de ropa, peinados y tatuajes y, quizá lo más interesante: comercios exclusivos.
Entre estos están peluquerías, centros de tatuaje, tiendas de ropa, diferentes talleres de modificación de vehículos y una actividad para desmantelar una banda criminal. Ninguno es contenido de historia, así que si no te interesa, te puedes ahorrar esos 20 euros.
Ahora bien, lo que yo haría:
- Comprar el juego en versión de 80 euros.
- Si finalmente te gusta como para querer explotarlo más, comprar el contenido Ultimate por los 20 euros adicionales desde las tiendas de PlayStation o Xbox.
Familia PlayStation
Visto el precio del juego, vamos con las consolas. La decisión aquí es mucho más sencilla porque es, directamente, monetaria y ya dependerá de lo que te quieras dejar:
- PS5 Digital + el juego - 599,99 euros + 80 euros = 680 euros.
- PS5 con lector + el juego - 649,99 euros + 80 euros = 730 euros.
- PS5 Pro (no trae lector de serie) + el juego - 899,99 euros + 80 euros = 980 euros.
La decisión de PS5 sin lector o con lector es dura porque dependerá de cómo quieras disfrutar de los juegos. Si la preservación te importa, lo suyo es comprar la versión de PS5 con lector, pero también porque, aparte de 'GTA', tienes cientos de juegos en formato físico que han ido bajando de precio con los años, así como todo el catálogo de PS4.
Por 50 euros de diferencia y teniendo eso en cuenta, yo iría a por la PS5 con lector. La mejor versión ya veremos que es la de PS5 Pro, pero otro cantar es encontrar una unidad en tiendas.
Familia Xbox Series
En Xbox no hay tanta opción porque, básicamente, tenemos dos modelos:
- Xbox Series S + el juego - 499,99 euros + 80 euros = 580 euros.
- Xbox Series X + el juego - 799,99 euros + 80 euros = 880 euros.
Aquí tengo muy, muy claro lo que haría: si quieres Xbox sí o sí, Series X (si la encuentras, ya que ahí seguramente tendrás que recurrir a la segunda mano. La versión en Series S no sólo es la más recortada de todas, sino que tiene un rendimiento paupérrimo, como veremos más adelante.
Si 880 euros te parece mucho (porque, efectivamente, lo es), optaría por PS5 Digital. Son 100 euros más que la Xbox Series S más el juego, pero la diferencia vale la pena.
La opción más barata y con asterisco: la vieja Xbox One
El truco del almendruco es que, si tienes una Xbox One (en cualquiera de sus variedades), puedes jugar a 'GTA VI'. ¿Cómo? Gracias al juego en la nube.
Para ello, necesitarás:
- La Xbox One, One S u One X.
- Comprar 'GTA VI' para Xbox.
- Tener Game Pass.
Si ya tienes una One, la consola te sale totalmente gratis y sólo tendrás que pagar tanto Game Pass como el juego. Ahora bien, ¿qué Game Pass? Pues...depende. Debido a los recortes de horas de juego, Game Pass Essential sólo ofrece cinco horas de juego en la nube al mes, Game Pass Premium 10 horas y Ultimate apenas 15 horas.
Para un juego como 'GTA VI', esas horas dan para poco, aunque se pueden comprar paquetes de horas adicionales. Sacando la calculadora:
- Game Pass Ultimate con 15 horas de juego por streaming son 20,99 euros al mes (aunque tienes una oferta de 14 días por un euro). Luego, hay paquetes de 10 horas adicionales por 3,49 euros, 25 horas por 6,99 euros y 50 horas por 10,99 euros.
Haciendo cuentas:
- 80 euros de 'GTA VI' + 1 euro de Game Pass con esos 14 días de prueba y 15 horas de streaming = 81 euros que no está nada mal.
- 80 euros de 'GTA VI' + 75 horas para ir tranquilo = 98 euros.
Es, de lejos, la opción más barata para jugar ahora mismo a 'GTA VI', pero hay dos condiciones:
- La versión que se juega por streaming es la de Xbox Series S.
- Aunque sea streaming, está limitado para que no puedas jugarlo en un PC. Necesitas una Xbox One sí o sí.
¿La mejor opción? Ahí ya hay menos dudas
Teniendo todo esto en cuenta y, de nuevo, si vas a llegar de primeras a las consolas gracias a 'GTA VI', tienes que estudiar muy, muy bien tanto el dinero como la versión.
Yo estoy jugando en PS5 base. Llevo más de una decena de horas y, aunque hay momentos en los que rasca, estoy teniendo una experiencia muy buena. Se ve de escándalo, en persecuciones el frame-rate aguanta bien y sólo cuando se unen muchísimas cosas en pantalla (explosiones o locura con muchos coches estrellándose) la tasa se resiente un poco. Nada que lo haga injugable y en una PS5 digital se jugaría igual porque el hardware es el mismo.
La mejor versión en términos absolutos es la de PS5 Pro, pero estamos hablando de casi 1.000 euros ahora mismo. Una absoluta burrada. Y en Xbox Series X también rinde de maravilla gracias a que la consola es algo más potente que una PS5 base, pero volvemos a lo de antes: 880 eurazos.
La versión que evitaría es la de Xbox Series S. Con el aumento de precio, la máquina ha dejado de ser atractiva por completo y, además, ya no es que 'GTA VI' se vea mal en ella, sino que el rendimiento es muy, muy malo.
Sólo jugaría esta versión tan comprometida si no tuviese ninguna consola de las de actual generación por ser jugador de PC y siguiera con mi Xbox One. Ahí sí optaría por las horas de juego por streaming.

articles.title: L’Italie autorise le FSD de Tesla avant le vote européen
articles.text:
Le ministère de Matteo Salvini a ouvert les routes italiennes au système de conduite assistée de Tesla, l’ancien FSD, sans attendre le vote européen de décembre. Aucun grand pays de l’Union ne l’avait autorisé avant l’Italie, et la France le refuse toujours.
Et un de plus, un ! En avril, les Pays-Bas ont été les premiers en Europe à autoriser ce système, à titre provisoire. Dix autres pays de l’Union ont suivi depuis, sans attendre le feu vert de Bruxelles. Le ministère italien des Transports a donné le sien le 19 novembre, après des vérifications techniques. Avec ce système, le conducteur laisse la voiture tourner, accélérer et freiner, jusque dans les carrefours et les ronds-points, mais il doit garder les yeux sur la route et il répond de sa conduite, rappelle le ministère. Matteo Salvini a annoncé la nouvelle le lendemain sur X. Pour le ministre, l’Italie prend ainsi de l’avance sur une reconnaissance européenne « encore en cours de définition ».
L’Italie a renoncé à attendre Bruxelles
Le sénateur Carlo Calenda réclamait cette autorisation depuis fin avril. Le 29 octobre, après un échange « très positif et constructif » avec Elon Musk, Matteo Salvini demandait encore à l’Union européenne d’aller vite. Azione, le parti de Carlo Calenda, l’avait alors accusé de se cacher derrière Bruxelles, puisque rien n’empêchait l’Italie d’agir seule. Trois semaines plus tard, son ministère a tranché sans l’Union.
Entre-temps, Tesla a cédé sur plusieurs points. Le constructeur a abandonné le nom Full Self-Driving en Europe, à la demande de l’Allemagne. Le conducteur pouvait aussi régler sa voiture pour dépasser la limite de vitesse de 50 %, et Tesla a ramené ce plafond à 10 %, avec l’accord des Pays-Bas début novembre. Le 16 novembre, les autorités néerlandaises ont validé une surveillance plus stricte du conducteur, qui devra garder les mains sur le volant au-dessus de 130 km/h. C’est cette version, réservée aux Tesla équipées de l’ordinateur de bord HW4, que l’Italie a autorisée.
Sur X, Tesla Europe a seulement répondu « Approuvé en Italie, le déploiement commence bientôt », sous une vidéo où l’une de ses voitures roule seule dans Rome, rapporte Electrek. Mais on ne sait toujours pas quand les Tesla pourront rouler presque seules dans les rues de Rome.
Tesla a encore besoin de la France ou de l’Espagne en décembre
Avant l’Italie, onze pays de l’Union autorisaient le système. Ils rassemblent environ 70 millions d’habitants, soit 15 % de la population européenne, d’après les calculs d’Electrek. Avec ses 59 millions d’habitants, l’Italie porte cette part à près de 30 %.
Ce poids compte pour le vote de décembre. Pour autoriser le système dans toute l’Union, il faut l’accord d’au moins 15 des 27 pays, qui rassemblent au moins 65 % de la population. Le comité européen chargé des véhicules (TCMV) devait voter en octobre, mais il n’a consacré que 25 minutes au dossier et ne se réunira pas avant décembre.
L’Allemagne a promis en octobre de soutenir Tesla, en échange du changement de nom et du plafond de vitesse. Si Berlin tient parole, les pays favorables pèseraient environ 47 % de la population, selon Electrek. Pour franchir la barre des 65 %, Tesla a besoin de la France ou de l’Espagne, et de la plupart des pays encore indécis.
Pour rappel, l’Espagne n’a toujours pas autorisé le système, et la France l’a refusé en juillet. Le ministre des Transports, Philippe Tabarot, reprochait à Tesla de laisser le conducteur dépasser la limite de 50 % et de mal surveiller son attention. Tesla a revu ces deux points depuis. Après un échange avec Elon Musk, Philippe Tabarot a autorisé en septembre des essais sur route avec deux voitures fournies par le constructeur, mais la France n’a pas encore dit comment elle votera en décembre.

articles.title: Pour le Black Friday 2026, ce reflex Nikon noté 4,5/5 passe sous les 900 €

À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Nikon D7500 passe à 899,00 € chez Darty.com, soit une baisse d'environ 31 % et 400,00 € d'économie. Réactif grâce à son suivi autofocus efficace et sa rafale à 7,5 i/s, ce reflex affiche une note actuelle de 4,5/5 dans nos tests.
Le Nikon D7500 vient s'intercaler entre le D7200 et le D500 pour proposer un boîtier reflex expert centré sur l'image d'action. L'appareil mise sur un suivi autofocus précis, un traitement d'image soigné et une construction robuste. Ce modèle avait convaincu notre laboratoire lors de ses essais.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, ce reflex descend à 899,00 € chez Darty.com, soit environ 31 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (1 299,00 €). Cette baisse de prix permet d'économiser 400,00 €.
Réactivité et suivi autofocus pour l'action
Ce boîtier reflex se montre particulièrement vif pour capturer des sujets en mouvement rapide. Comme souligné dans notre test complet, sa cadence en rafale atteint 7,5 images par seconde, ce qui permet de décomposer précisément une action sportive ou animalière. L'autofocus assure un suivi continu du sujet sans décrocher, tandis que l'écran tactile orientable de 8 cm simplifie les cadrages au ras du sol ou en hauteur.
Nikon D7500
Points forts
- Qualité de construction.
- Réactivité générale.
- Suivi AF très efficace.
- Qualité d'image en hausse (sensibilité et ombres).
- Rafale à 7,5 i/s.
- Écran orientable et tactile.
- Wi-Fi et Bluetooth.
Points faibles
- Un seul emplacement SD.
- Fonctions vidéo limitées.
- Crop 2,2x en vidéo 4K/UHD.
- Définition de l'écran en baisse.
- Dégagement oculaire un peu faible.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Une sensibilité étendue malgré des limites en vidéo
Le traitement d'image garantit des clichés nets même lorsque la lumière vient à manquer, grâce à une plage de sensibilité allant de 100 à 51 200 ISO. Cette montée en sensibilité permet de conserver des détails précis dans les zones d'ombre sans faire exploser le bruit électronique. Il faut toutefois composer avec un seul emplacement pour carte SD et un recadrage de 2,2x en vidéo 4K/UHD, ce qui pénalise les vidéastes mais ne gêne en rien la pratique de la photo.

articles.title: Modder cools gaming laptop with a bounce house blower for a 35-degree drop
articles.text:
Modder cools gaming laptop with a bounce house blower for a 35-degree drop — airflow is so strong the laptop has to be taped down, extreme airflow delivers 19% gaming boost before hitting diminishing returns
Trash Bench is cooling laptops again, now using a bounce house blower fan and reaching temperatures below 50 degrees Celsius.
Experimental PC modder Trash Bench recently tested a laptop cooler and tried to beat it with increasingly powerful blower setups, eventually opting for a bounce house inflator blower to cool the i7-10750H and RTX 2070 MaxQ with a 90W power limit. He was able to bring temperatures down from 84 degrees Celsius to 48.8 degrees Celsius, with Cyberpunk going from 47 FPS to 56 FPS.
Trash Bench was asked to review a laptop cooling stand, but he said he doesn’t do reviews, so he proposed a video idea: He’ll test the laptop cooler and try to beat it with his creations—no opening the laptop, no sub-ambient cooling solutions, only airflow.
The Llano V12 laptop cooling fan sent to Trash Bench achieved an impressive 58.3 degrees Celsius average on the GPU at medium settings, dropping 27 degrees from the stock 84 degrees Celsius. The lower temperatures also improved gaming performance by an average of 19.4%. Pushing the Llano V12 to 100% made it incredibly loud, but it only reached 56.7 degrees Celsius with negligible performance gains.
His first attempt to beat the Llano V12 was using the Noctua NF-A20, a huge 200mm fan, and a 3D-printed duct with foam around the edges, like the Llano V12, to prevent air leaks. Unfortunately, the single 200mm fan didn't beat the Llano V12, with GPU temperatures averaging 66.3 degrees Celsius—still pretty impressive given the setup's simplicity, if you ignore the messy PC power supply and fan speed controller beside it.
His second attempt used six Arctic P12 fans at full speed, beating the Llano V12 by 0.9 degrees Celsius at medium settings and achieving an average GPU temperature of 57.4 degrees Celsius. However, it lost to the full-speed Llano V12, but only barely. The third attempt used two 4000 RPM server fans, which were even louder than the six full-speed Arctic P12S — but that finally did the trick, beating the Llano V12 at 100% by 2.6 degrees Celsius.
When do you start your Black Friday shopping?
And just to go extreme, like Trash Bench often does in his experiments, he used a powerful blower fan designed to inflate bounce houses. He took advantage of the larger foam gaskets the Llano V12 used and 3D-printed an interface at the bottom of the laptop cooler’s housing to fit a flexible duct. The sheer force of the air lifted the laptop off the stand, so it needed to be taped down to seal the air leak.
The bounce house blower produced an average GPU temperature of 48.8 degrees Celsius, but saw very little performance gain over the Llano V12 at 100%, six Arctic P12s, and the pair of server fans, with Time Spy benchmark results within 1% of each other. The Noctua was the weakest in the benchmarks, however, lagging by 3% behind the bounce house blower, but was much quieter.

Trash Bench admits that while lower temperatures are great, they reach diminishing returns once the thermal bottleneck disappears and another bottleneck takes over.
