articles.title: A 30 años de sus inicios, GTA VI convirtió el videojuego en una simulación de la vida contemporánea y batió los récords de Rockstar Games
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI ya no es solo un juego en el que se roba un auto o se huye de la policía. La nueva entrega de Rockstar Games convirtió su mundo virtual en una simulación de la vida cotidiana: el jugador puede ir al almacén a comprar comida, probarse ropa, hacer ejercicio, reparar una gotera, cargar combustible, abrir una cuenta bancaria, cazar caimanes o nadar en la playa. Esa escala define también el lanzamiento más grande en la historia del entretenimiento: el 19 de noviembre, GTA VI generó USD 3.790 millones en ventas durante su primer día, según Rockstar Games.
El juego cerró una espera de 13 años desde el estreno de Grand Theft Auto V. Su impacto excedió lo comercial: en el Reino Unido, tres empresas de gestión laboral y escolar registraron picos de ausencias que coincidieron con el día del lanzamiento, y departamentos de policía de todo Estados Unidos publicaron mensajes para recordarles a los fanáticos que los delitos del juego tienen consecuencias penales reales.
GTA VI lleva 30 años de evolución a una simulación de la vida contemporánea
The New York Times trazó una línea histórica desde los primeros títulos de la franquicia hasta la entrega actual. Grand Theft Auto III, lanzado en 2001, fue el primer juego de la saga en ofrecer una ciudad tridimensional inspirada en Nueva York. Grand Theft Auto IV marcó un giro hacia los personajes y la narrativa: su protagonista era un inmigrante que confrontaba la distancia entre el sueño americano y lo que encontraba al llegar. Grand Theft Auto V profundizó la vida virtual con hobbies y rutinas que no afectaban la trama principal.
GTA VI lleva esa fórmula a otra escala. Transcurre en Leonida, un estado ficticio inspirado en Florida, con una representación de Miami construida con un nivel de detalle que, según el diario, permite a quien haya visitado la ciudad real identificar puntos concretos del mapa: hay referencias a Miami Beach, a los murales de Wynwood Walls y a otros espacios urbanos reconocibles.
El mundo abierto de GTA VI va más allá de las misiones criminales
La propuesta de mundo abierto —término que define a los juegos sin un camino lineal obligatorio, donde el jugador se mueve con libertad por un entorno extenso— alcanza en GTA VI una dimensión inédita. El mapa es continuo: no hay pantallas de carga entre zonas.
Los protagonistas son Lucía Caminos y Jason Duval, una pareja ligada al crimen que intenta mejorar su situación dentro de Leonida. La campaña principal demanda entre 60 y 70 horas, según el periodista especializado Juan Lomanto. El modo en línea no está disponible y Rockstar no anunció una fecha para su lanzamiento.
Rockstar Games superó por amplio margen el debut histórico de GTA V
Los USD 3.790 millones del primer día sitúan a GTA VI en una categoría propia. Según Rockstar, el juego acumuló además 32,5 millones de unidades en preventa. Para dimensionar esas cifras: GTA V tardó tres días en alcanzar los USD 1.000 millones tras su estreno en 2013 y acumula más de 230 millones de copias vendidas —dentro de las 470 millones de unidades totales de la franquicia—, según Take-Two Interactive.
La edición estándar tiene un precio de referencia de alrededor de USD 80 en el mercado estadounidense. Lomanto estimó que el costo de producción ronda los USD 1.500 millones, aunque ni Rockstar ni Take-Two confirmaron esa cifra.
La policía de Estados Unidos advirtió que los delitos del juego tienen consecuencias reales
Desde Atlanta hasta Denver, decenas de agencias publicaron mensajes en redes sociales que combinaron advertencia y humor. El Departamento de Policía de Atlanta escribió: “GTA no es un lugar real, pero Atlanta sí lo es”.
La Oficina del Sheriff del Condado de Pima, en Arizona, apeló al lenguaje propio de los videojuegos: “Las leyes de la vida real no incluyen trucos, respawns ni reinicios de misión”.
El Departamento de Policía de San Juan, en Texas, optó por una fórmula directa: “Lo que pasa en GTA VI, se queda en GTA VI”. El de Denver aclaró que “ganar cinco estrellas no es un logro que nosotros entregamos”, en alusión al sistema del juego que mide el nivel de persecución policial.
Las ausencias laborales y escolares en el Reino Unido coincidieron con el día del lanzamiento
La firma BrightHR registró un aumento del 56% en ausencias por enfermedad el jueves 19 de noviembre frente al jueves anterior. La plataforma Deel también registró un alza en las solicitudes de día libre respecto al mismo día de 2025.
El proveedor escolar Arbor informó que 35.000 alumnos adicionales faltaron a clases ese día en más de 1.400 escuelas secundarias. BrightHR aclaró que esa semana coincidió además con un aumento de enfermedades respiratorias, por lo que ninguna medición establece una relación causal directa con el lanzamiento.
La escala de GTA VI plantea dudas sobre la sostenibilidad del modelo en la industria
El título recibió la clasificación M (Mature, mayores de 17 años) de la Entertainment Software Rating Board (ESRB), con advertencias por violencia intensa, lenguaje explícito, desnudez, contenido sexual y consumo de drogas y alcohol. The Guardian describió a GTA VI como “el mundo virtual más extraordinariamente detallado que hemos visto hasta ahora”.
Detrás de ese resultado hay ocho años de producción y un equipo cercano a las 4.700 personas, según reportajes de investigación de la industria. El podcast The Daily, del New York Times, estimó que el costo de desarrollo superó los USD 1.000 millones y que cerca de 10.000 personas participaron en distintas etapas del proyecto.
El diario planteó la pregunta que circuló entre especialistas: si una producción de esa magnitud es sostenible para el resto de la industria, o si el entusiasmo del estreno tendrá consecuencias en un mercado que ya atravesó una fase de ajuste tras la pandemia.

articles.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
articles.text:
It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.
(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.
Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.
Godzilla Minus One was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero.

articles.title: Typing 365 Turns PC Building, Technology and More into Typing Practice
articles.text:
Saturday, November 21st 2026
Typing 365 Turns PC Building, Technology and More into Typing Practice
Typing faster is useful, but what if practice could also teach you something? Typing 365 is a free native Windows app that combines structured typing lessons, educational content, and competitive challenges.
With over 100,000 installs and nearly 4 million typing races completed worldwide, Typing 365 has grown into more than a speed test. Its Albums Store offers themed collections covering technology, science, history, psychology, and more.Build Your PC: A Free Album for First-Time Builders
The new Build Your PC album features 40 free typing exercises about desktop hardware. It covers motherboards, component compatibility, assembly, first boot, operating system installation, and troubleshooting.
Here's the idea in practice: instead of just reading a guide, you type passages such as "Before buying a CPU, check that its socket matches your motherboard and that the board's BIOS supports it." By the end of the album, you've practiced thousands of keystrokes while picking up the fundamentals of building a PC.
You might already know your way around a PC case, but it's an easy recommendation for students, first-time builders, or that friend whose build you always end up helping with.
Why a Native Windows App?
Browser-based typing sites are great for a quick test. Typing 365 is designed for consistent practice, combining a dedicated Windows experience with structured courses, progress tracking, and detailed performance statistics.
Beginners can start with Typing 101, a free course that gradually introduces keys before moving on to complete sentences. Other courses cover keyboard rows, punctuation, and speed development.
During practice, an on-screen keyboard and optional hand guidance support finger placement. The app tracks words per minute (WPM), characters per minute (CPM), accuracy, and mistakes. You can also turn your own notes or technical material into typing exercises.Find Your Weak Spots with PRO Analytics
The free app offers plenty of practice material, while Typing 365 PRO adds detailed analytics for users who want to improve their skills. View speed trends, session history, and keyboard heatmaps, or identify slow words, characters, and letter pairs for targeted practice.
PRO also unlocks exclusive albums, advanced courses such as Typing 102, which focuses on building typing speed, plus additional fonts, keyboard sounds, avatars, and customization options.
PRO is available through a monthly subscription or a one-time lifetime purchase, with US pricing starting at $2.99/month or $29.99 lifetime. Prices may vary by region.
Race Against Other Typists
Prefer competition? Join ranked typing races, compare your results with other players, and climb the global leaderboards. Whether you're chasing a personal best or a higher rank, every race offers a new challenge.
Practice in Five Languages
Typing 365 supports English, German, Spanish, Russian, and Arabic, allowing users to practice across languages and keyboard layouts.
From learning keyboard basics to understanding how a PC comes together, Typing 365 turns everyday practice into something worth your time.
Download Typing 365 for free from the Microsoft Store and start typing.
Typing 365 is available for Windows PCs, with optional premium albums and PRO features.

articles.title: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro knocked the Kindle Fire-shaped chip from my shoulder, but unless you really like Amazon services, I’m not sure who it’s for
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
On paper, Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro might not seem terribly exciting; most specs are middling, Alexa’s inclusion is far from a selling point and, based on Amazon’s track record, the company’s services can do more to interrupt a product’s usefulness than inform it. However, between its gorgeous nanomatte screen, stylish design, and clever features (especially for Kindle fans), the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is a surprisingly exciting device and a solid start for Amazon’s post-FireOS era.
Reasons to buy
- + Finally, FireOS is laid to rest
- + Nanomatte display is among the best screens at its price
- + Svelte and functional design, barring weight
- + Great for reading, good for entertainment
Reasons to avoid
- - Specs might not offer longevity
- - Expensive peripherals
- - Not entirely clear of Amazon bloat
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: One-minute review
When Amazon announced its new Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, I found myself at a crossroads. On the one hand, despite my criticisms of the company’s product ecosystem, I’ve used Amazon Echo smart speakers and displays to control my smart home for several years, and I do appreciate the brand’s approach to providing a broad spectrum of price points in its device lineup.
But I don’t like that many of these devices are treated as billboards for Amazon’s wider products and services, and Kindle Fire tablets are (or were) the biggest offenders; FireOS was a sluggish, bloatware-loaded platform that barely functioned in itself, let alone as a tablet OS with its limited app store.
So, hearing that Amazon had launched an Android-based tablet came as a genuinely welcome surprise, and I was particularly excited to try its top-of-the-line 12-inch nanomatte screen model. I’ve spent two weeks testing the Alexa Tab 12 Pro, and while it’s still far from perfect, it’s a surprisingly competent and well-thought-out device for the price. With time (and perhaps a second-generation model), Amazon could finally be making its mark in the tablet market.
The Tab 12 Pro’s design is simple but slick, its specs are decent enough and help keep the price low, and some of the added features (including those that drive the user towards Amazon services) feel smartly integrated into the tablet. And the nanomatte display variant? It’s a triumph for Amazon: clear and crisp, defiant to most reflections unless under direct light and wonderfully vibrant.
I’ve not seen the non-nanomatte version of the Alexa Tab 12 Pro, but I can’t imagine it lives up to the model I tested; in all likelihood, nanomatte is every bit worth the $50/£50 upgrade. Equipped with it, the Tab 12 Pro’s 12-inch display is one of the best screens in its category, and really, that’s what a lot of everyday customers are looking for versus performant chipsets, high-spec cameras, and powerful speakers.
That being said, the cracks do show in some of the Tab 12 Pro’s lower-end specs, and it feels a little like Amazon’s focus on delivering a well-rounded product comes at the expense of the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro having a real, hard-hitting selling point — and perhaps its longevity, too.
For instance, while its blue light-reducing reading profiles, 3:2 aspect ratio, paperlike screen texture, and slick Kindle experience make it great for reading books and documents alike, it’s too heavy to use one-handed and stash away like a typical e-reader. For streaming video, the screen is bright and clear, but that vibrancy I mentioned before can mean colors are a little overblown, even if you tune them down with the different profiles in settings, and the tablet’s speakers are pretty flat if you want to listen aloud. Even for its main selling point, its productivity usecases, the chipset doesn't offer the longevity it needs to keep pace in 2-3 years time under heavy loads.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
This is a thread that will follow through much of my commentary on Amazon’s best-ever tablet; being a ‘jack of all trades, master of none’ device doesn’t really do much for me, even in a general-use tablet. Still, the Alexa Tab 12 Pro is far from a disappointment overall, and especially for Prime members, Kindle lovers, or those wanting a great household management-come-productivity slate, it’s a really solid Android tablet.
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Price & availability
- Starts at $499/£449 for the 12-inch model without nanomatte
- Alexa Tablet Pro keyboard is $149.99 / £129.99
- Alexa Tablet Pro Pen is $89.99 / £79.99
- Available at Amazon
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro comes in at $499/£449 in its base configuration with 128GB storage and its standard display; for $/£50 more you can add the nanomatte display, and for $/£100 more you can upgrade to 16GB RAM / 256GB storage.
There are optional peripherals to factor in too; sold separately, the keyboard costs $149.99 / £129.99, and the stylus is $89.99 / £79.99, but you can bundle these in with the tablet for an added cost of $150/£140. These are fairly steep standalone prices, so if you think there’s a chance you’ll benefit from these peripherals, I’d buy them outright.
While a lot of the Tablet 12 Pro’s specs are middling, at its price point and versus the competition, this is a pretty solid value proposition; Amazon will often trim the fat from its hardware to reach low prices, and it’s a similar story across the other smaller tablets in this lineup. The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $229.99 / £199.99 with 4GB RAM and 64GB storage, and the Tablet 11 comes in at $329.99 / £289.99 with 8GB RAM and 64GB storage. These smaller models can be bought without ads for an extra $20/£20 a piece.
By comparison, Samsung’s Galaxy Tab S10 FE is slightly less powerful, has a slightly smaller battery and a 90Hz screen, but does offer a slightly better front camera; it starts at $549.99 / £539. Apple’s latest iPad Air comes in at $749 / £749, and while it does offer the more powerful M4 chipset, it’s smaller at 11 inches and has a static 60Hz display versus the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro’s 120Hz.
I’ve seen a lot of discussion around whether the Tablet 12 Pro’s low price is worth paying for a product that will inevitably become more of an ad platform as new updates roll out. With the freedom of Android OS, it’s a little easier for consumers to have their say on what they see by downloading a different launcher, but I’d be doing a disservice to those who have been burned by aggressively targeted ads (especially on the Echo Show) if I didn’t at least acknowledge how ads may factor into the value proposition here. That being said, I’ve barely seen anything ads-wise in my time testing the Tablet 12 Pro…
- Value score: 4/5
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Specs
| Alexa Tablet 12 Pro Specs |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Alexa Tablet 12 Pro base model | Alexa Tablet 12 Pro (with nanomatte) I tested | 
| Starting price | $499/£449 | $549/£499 | 
| Operating system | Android 16 (17 coming soon) | Android 16 (17 coming soon) | 
| Chipset | MediaTek Dimensity 8400 4nm 8-core CPU 7-core GPU (Arm Mali-G720) | MediaTek Dimensity 8400 4nm 8-core CPU 7-core GPU (Arm Mali-G720) | 
| Storage | 128GB / 256GB | 128GB | 
| Display | 12-inch 2.8K touch screen 2.8K display, up to 120Hz refresh rate. | 12-inch 2.8K touch screen 2.8K Nanomatte display, up to 120Hz refresh rate. | 
| Cameras | 13MP main, 8MP front, both with 1080p Full HD video | 13MP main, 8MP front, both with 1080p Full HD video | 
| Battery | 9000mAh, Amazon cites up to 16 hours video playback | 9000mAh, Amazon cites up to 16 hours video playback | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 LE, USB-C 3.0 port with support for Wi-Fi 6E | Bluetooth 5.3 LE, USB-C 3.0 port with support for Wi-Fi 6E | 
| Weight | 550g | 550g | 
| Dimensions | 270.8 x 183.85 x 6.5 mm | 270.8 x 183.85 x 6.5 mm | 
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Design
- Slick and simple design
- A little on the heavier side
- Magnetic peripherals (added cost) for productivity
Amazon’s not changing the game with its Alexa Tablet design aesthetically, but there are a few things of note about its slate.
Its 3:2 aspect ratio (270.8 mm x 183.85 mm x 6.5 mm) makes it a great tablet for productivity; you can read documents and books with ease, and there’s plenty of room for multitasking in its horizontal orientation. It’s a little heavy at 550g, but it does feel well-built, offering IP52 dust and splash resistance. There’s an elegance here I’m not quite used to in Amazon’s products; from the cursive Alexa branding on the back panel to the premium-feeling aluminum casing, which is surprisingly smudge-proof.
Embedded into the right-hand side bezel, the 8MP front camera is positioned just off-center when the tablet is stationed horizontally, and on the rear of the tablet, there’s a 13MP main camera — both offer 1080p full HD video.
On the right side of the tablet’stop edge, there’s a fingerprint sensor lock button, and at the top of its right-hand side is the volume rocker. On the bottom edge, you’ll find its USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 port (the smaller screen models have USB-C 2.0, for what it’s worth) and along the left-hand side are four pogo pins for attaching the folio keyboard.
Speaking of which, Amazon sent me the keyboard casing and stylus to test for this review, and while the price to add them both is a little steep, they unlock a great deal of functionality in the tablet. I wish Amazon had added a backlight at this price point, but broadly speaking, I’ve very few complaints.
The chiclet keyboard is soft and clicky but sturdy, featuring a dedicated Alexa+ key in lieu of a right control button as well as a writing assist key in the top-right hand corner. The trackpad is responsive and smooth, and there are ample shortcuts for productivity users. I don’t love the magnetically attaching rear cover and its fold-out kickstand; a few too many times, this popped off of the tablet while I was adjusting the height, and it doesn’t offer much stability if you want to use the tablet on your lap, or indeed any uneven surface.
The stylus magnetically attaches and charges, and offers a nice weight for a natural drawing experience. Its top end can be used as an eraser, and if it’s missing, you can find it by triggering an admittedly soft and quiet ping.
- Design score: 4/5
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Display
- Optional nanomatte display is well worth the upgrade
- Smooth and super responsive
- Great features for reading
The finest feather in the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro’s cap is its main screen, an opinion which is colored, by and large, by my love for the optional nanomatte display.
The tablet’s 12-inch 2.8K LCD screen offers a 2800 x 1840 resolution, 280ppi (pixels per inch), and a buttery smooth 120Hz touchscreen. I’ve only seen and tested the nanomatte version, and that’s a real boon when it comes to anti-glare; in every circumstance barring direct sunlight or direct indoor light like nearby table lamps, it’s easy to see from most viewing angles, even despite only offering 500 nits of brightness.
The default color profile is Boosted; I found this to be a bit too vibrant in most settings, in particular while watching TV series, but the Natural profile is much better unless you’re in an especially bright environment.
The gritty, paper-like nanomatte texture makes it easy on the eyes when reading, too — and even offers a decent bite for drawing and writing with the Alexa Tablet Pro Pen. That being said, I noticed there’s poor palm detection while drawing in apps like Clip Studio Paint, so if you’re looking for the best possible tablet for drawing, you’re better off with more specialized slates like the iPad Pro or Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 Ultra.
- Display score: 4.5/5
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Performance
- Yay for Android…
- But app compatibility issues and remnants of Amazon bloatware remain
- Makes the most out of some middling specs
Unlock the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and you’re greeted by its default launcher with Amazon services and Alexa baked in; these elements are omnipresent, with a widget in the top-left corner for recently viewed media on Amazon platforms as well as the Ask Alexa search bar in the bottom-right corner, which pops out into a chat window when pressed.
I don’t hate these features as much as other reviewers and customers seem to, but that’s in part because I often do want to hop back into my last-read Kindle book or quickly dive back into playlists, movies and TV series. And besides that, the Tablet 12 Pro is far less egregious with its advertising (at least, for now) than other Amazon devices I’ve used. Plus, thanks to Android OS, you can just switch out to another launcher if you really hate Amazon’s footprint.
As well as Amazon's own apps, Google takes up a fair amount of real estate by default, with its own app folder as well as a Google search bar in the top right corner. Swipe left, and you land in the content center with recommended content from Prime, Kindle, and Luna, and swipe up for your app tray; all fairly standard for Android tablets overall.
The Kindle experience is a particular highlight. When you open books in the app, the screen will automatically toggle into reading mode, which reduces blue-light emission, silences distractions like notifications, and extends the battery life. Were the tablet a little lighter and more portable, I’d say it’s a great replacement for Kindle users who want more than just e-reading, but I wouldn’t personally stash this in my backpack to read while on the go quite as readily as I would Amazon’s latest thin-and-light e-readers. What’s more, most of these features are exclusive to the Kindle app.
As an entertainment hub, the Tab 12 Pro is decent enough; the 3:2 aspect ratio isn’t ideal, as you do see quite a bit of letterboxing while streaming content, and the sound quality from the built-in speakers is a little tinny and bassless.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is no powerhouse; it’s middling at best, but at its price and for vast swathes of its target market, that’s perfectly fine. Its MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor is perfectly capable for light multitasking, moderately demanding apps and some AI tasks, but don’t expect iPad Pro- or Samsung Galaxy S10 Ultra-grade speeds here.
Still, the Tablet 12 Pro is a very capable productivity machine, whether in split-screen or desktop mode, and especially with its peripherals in tow. I played games like Wuthering Waves and used Clip Studio Paint and, broadly speaking, performance was fine in both applications with some tweaks in settings – even in desktop mode with a hefty update running in the background for Wuthering Waves, YouTube playing in windowed mode and typing on GDocs, the tablet handled the load pretty well, though it did get a little warm in the process. Gaming will need lower performance presets, but at this price that's to be expected, to an extent.
In my time with the Tab 12 Pro, I also encountered some stuttering when switching between apps, a few crashes, and some software lag, which could be any combination of the less powerful chipset and Amazon’s software. This, plus the long-running woes of Android app compatibility limiting the library of optimized apps, can cause friction in use.
Generally speaking, though, the Tab 12 Pro is pretty capable. I’m not convinced that will be the case in 3-4 years, which does give me pause, but only time will tell how these specs hold up.
Other features
Battery
I struggle a little with Amazon’s promise of 16 hours of video playback; just 4 hours of streaming Netflix series wiped out 50% of my battery life, and I was completely out after 8 hours. Combined with the tablet’s 2-3 hour recharge time, this isn’t ideal, but it will still last you throughout the workday so long as you’re not running lots of power-hungry apps at once without turning on power-saving mode.
Alexa and AI services
Alexa has the same issues here as it does across Amazon’s platforms; namely, that it’s built more as a shopping assistant than anything else. For smart home control, timer setting, and simple requests, it’s broadly fine, and you can download third-party assistants if you want more demanding tasks completed. You can access Gemini’s writing tools natively from the keyboard peripheral, too.
Cameras
Far from being standout features, the tablet’s cameras are decent enough; the 8MP front camera is good enough for video calls, and the 13MP rear camera is fine for shooting a quick photo or video in a pinch, albeit the results will be quite saturated. This is far from a deal-breaker in a general-use tablet, but if you like a crisp video feed for business calls, you’re better off with a more pro-grade slate.
- Performance score: 3.5/5
Should I buy the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro?
| Score card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
| Display | Especially in its nanomatte variant, this is a surprisingly premium display for a mid-range device | 4.5/5 | 
| Performance | Nothing to write home about, and its longevity remains in question, but it can handle moderate loads | 3.5/5 | 
| Design | Slick and simple with broadly well-thought-out features | 4/5 | 
| Value | Very competitive until you factor in the rather expensive peripherals, but still a good price. | 4/5 | 
Buy it if…
You use a lot of Amazon services
If you’re a Prime subscriber who uses Kindle services, Prime Video and/or Luna, this is a great companion to fit into your wider Amazon device ecosystem.
You want a solid productivity tablet without a high price tag
At its price, this is a competitive productivity slate, even with the added cost of peripherals, and it’s capable of moderate loads as well as multitasking.
You do a lot of reading 
With its nanomatte coating in particular, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is great for reading in and out of its optimized Kindle experience. The 3:2 aspect ratio lends itself to documents and books in both horizontal and vertical orientation, and the screen is very easy on the eyes.
Don’t buy it if…
You don’t like Amazon services
Yes, you can switch to a different launcher, but at its core, this is an Alexa-first package. It’s in the name, and though there are limited ways Amazon can mess with Android’s open design philosophy, you might prefer something that’s less Amazon-y out of the box.
You want an entertainment hub before all else
Streaming is fine on the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, but its aspect ratio isn’t optimal for TVs and movies, and the speakers are middling at best.
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Also consider
Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE
It’s comparable in terms of specs and price; while it has a slightly less powerful chipset and a slightly smaller 90Hz screen, it does have better IP68 water and dust resistance, 45W fast charging, and comes with the S Pen included. Plus, it’s less Amazon-y. 
Apple iPad Air 
The smaller, 11-inch iPad Air is certainly more powerful than the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro thanks to Apple’s M4 chip, but it has a static 60Hz 264ppi display and, of course, runs iPadOS rather than Android. 
How I tested the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro
- I used the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro for two weeks
- I used it as a productivity device as well as an entertainment device
- I benchmarked against mid-range tablets
During my two weeks with the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, I used it to write much of this review while exporting files and using various productivity apps, as well as for gaming and streaming content and using apps like Clip Studio Paint to test the drawing experience. I tried its advertised features, including desktop mode and split-screen, the built-in Alexa chat function, and Amazon app experiences like Kindle.
I benchmarked the device against comparable mid-range tablets like the Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE and the iPad Air (M4), playing demanding games like Wuthering Waves and completing multitasking workloads to see how it performs under pressure. I ran the battery down to 0% while streaming content on Netflix and recharged the device fully to measure battery performance.
I’m a regular iPad Pro user and have tested a variety of mobile computing devices in my five years at TechRadar, including Android slates, drawing tablets and beyond.
- Read TechRadar’s reviews guarantee
- First reviewed: November 2026
Josephine Watson is TechRadar's Head of Video, and an award-winning (PPA 30 under 30 2024), NCTJ-trained journalist. Having previously written on a variety of topics from pop culture to gaming and even the energy industry, she joined TechRadar to support general site management in 2021. Now, Josephine heads up TechRadar's social and video team and strategy. Generally, you'll find her fiddling with her smart home setup, watching Disney movies, playing on her Switch, or rewatching the extended edition of Lord of the Rings... again.

articles.title: Momentum by Google and YourStory to bring India’s founders, investors, and policymakers into one room in New Delhi
articles.text:
Google India
View Brand Publisher
Momentum by Google and YourStory to bring India’s founders, investors, and policymakers into one room in New Delhi
Momentum by Google, in collaboration with YourStory, puts India’s startup future on one stage, with the people who will build, fund, and shape it.
India’s startup story is no longer only about how many companies are being built; it is about how far they can go. The answer increasingly depends on conversations that happen between the people building, funding, and shaping the rules for those companies.
Google, in collaboration with YourStory, is hosting Momentum by Google, an invite-only gathering bringing together leaders from India’s startup ecosystem and innovation economy, on November 23, 2026, in New Delhi.
The evening will bring together a select group of startup founders, technology leaders, venture capital investors, and policy stakeholders around one question: what will it take for India’s innovators to build and scale globally as AI becomes part of every product and every business?
Momentum is a forum where ideas, experience, and perspectives on policy can be exchanged openly and directly. The focus will be on celebrating India’s technological momentum, highlighting emerging innovation, and fostering the collaborative frameworks that digital enterprises need to scale globally.
Who will be in the room?
The keynote on catalyzing India’s next tech leap will be delivered by Amardeep Singh Bhatia, IAS, Secretary, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). The audience will also hear from Wilson L. White, Vice President of Government Affairs and Public Policy for Platforms and Devices at Google, who leads government affairs across Asia-Pacific.
The sessions will be led by Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, The Bharat Project and YourStory Media. Speakers include Prof. Dr. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, ZenteiQ.ai; Ritu Mehrotra, Founder and CEO, Shunya Labs; Rajesh Ranjan, Director and India Lead for Government Affairs and Public Policy (GAPP) at Google; and Siddharth Shekhar, Director at Google, who oversees Government and PSUs, BFSI, Fintech, Education, and Auto.
What will the conversations cover?
A fireside chat on building and scaling with frontier AI will look at what it means for a startup to build with advanced AI at its core, and what it takes to grow from a promising idea into a company that competes on a global stage. As frontier AI becomes part of how products are designed, built, and taken to market, the conversation will explore how founders can use it to scale.
Frontier AI is also changing what policymakers need to consider. The panel discussion, on driving innovation and policy alignment for India’s AI ecosystem, will bring founders, industry, and government perspectives together to explore how regulation, public policy, and industry can move together. It will look at how policy can support new entrants as well as established players, and how the ecosystem can keep growing responsibly and competitively.
An open Q&A will give the audience an opportunity to engage in dialogue with the speakers and seek their views on the issues shaping India’s startup ecosystem.
Bringing the ecosystem together
Policy and innovation are now part of the same conversation. As AI moves from experimentation to everyday infrastructure, founders are making decisions about how to build, what to invest in, and where to compete, while policymakers are weighing how to encourage growth while keeping the ecosystem responsible and trusted.
Momentum by Google aims to bring founders, technology leaders, investors, and policymakers into the same conversation, with discussions that move from the practical realities of building and scaling with frontier AI to the larger question of how regulation, industry, and entrepreneurship can move in step.
It is also built to be interactive, with room for attendees to engage directly with speakers and bring their own questions and experiences into the conversation. For founders, that means a chance to share what it actually takes to scale a company in India today. For policymakers and investors, it offers a view of the ground realities behind the headlines. It is an exchange that works best when the people on both sides are in the same room.
Why the room matters
India’s startup ecosystem has become a primary engine of the country’s economic and technological transformation, and Momentum by Google reflects a growing recognition that the most meaningful progress often happens when the right people are in the same room and willing to listen to one another.
By convening founders, investors, and policymakers around a shared interest in India’s technological future, Google and YourStory are creating that room in New Delhi. For attendees, it is an opportunity to gain perspectives beyond what any single keynote or panel can offer, and to build relationships that will carry the ecosystem forward.

articles.title: En 1984, Países Bajos construyó un barrio imposible como solución a la vivienda: vivir en pelotas de golf gigantes que siguen desafiando la arquitectura
articles.text:
Durante décadas, la arquitectura europea se acostumbró a construir viviendas cada vez más parecidas entre sí. Sin embargo, hubo una época en la que algunos gobiernos decidieron experimentar con formas completamente distintas de habitar el mundo. En una ciudad neerlandesa, aquella búsqueda de soluciones dejó un barrio que todavía hoy parece sacado de una película de ciencia ficción.
Una invasión extraterrestre en plena crisis inmobiliaria. En 1984, la ciudad neerlandesa de 's-Hertogenbosch, también conocida como Den Bosch, inauguró un barrio que parecía recién aterrizado de otro planeta: 50 enormes pelotas de golf blancas, elevadas sobre pedestales y salpicadas de ventanas circulares. Se llamaban Bolwoningen, literalmente “casas bola”, y no eran decorados futuristas, sino viviendas sociales concebidas para responder a la escasez de alojamiento.
Su creador, el artista y arquitecto Dries Kreijkamp, había convencido a las autoridades de que una esfera podía convertirse en una alternativa económica, eficiente y radicalmente distinta a las casas tradicionales. Más de cuatro décadas después, aquellas 50 estructuras siguen habitadas.
El Gobierno decidió que las casas cuadradas no eran suficientes. Durante los años 60, Países Bajos experimentó un fuerte crecimiento demográfico y económico que agravó la escasez de viviendas. El Gobierno necesitaba construir rápido, barato y a gran escala, pero también quería evitar que las ciudades acabaran convertidas en interminables urbanizaciones idénticas.
Desde 1968 comenzó a subvencionar proyectos de arquitectura experimental, un movimiento del que también surgirían propuestas tan singulares como las casas cubo de Róterdam. En ese contexto apareció Kreijkamp, convencido de que el futuro de la vivienda no tenía por qué seguir dependiendo de paredes rectas y habitaciones rectangulares.
Un arquitecto convencido de que nacimos para vivir en pelotas. Kreijkamp, nacido en 1937, era escultor, diseñador industrial y arquitecto, y llevaba desde los años 60 obsesionado con las formas esféricas. Su inspiración procedía de los iglús inuit, las chozas de barro africanas y su experiencia fabricando esferas de cristal. Defendía que las formas redondeadas eran más naturales para el ser humano y resumía su filosofía con una pregunta: “Vivimos sobre una esfera, nacemos de una esfera… ¿por qué no vivir en una esfera?”.
Primero construyó un prototipo de poliestireno y después consiguió que el Ayuntamiento encargara 50 unidades. El proyecto sufrió retrasos y dudas sobre su viabilidad, pero el empeño del concejal de Vivienda Ton Lensen permitió que finalmente se levantaran en 1984.
Una pelota de golf que se montaba en un solo día. Cada Bolwoning consiste en una esfera de 5,5 metros de diámetro apoyada sobre una base cilíndrica de hormigón que alberga instalaciones técnicas y almacenamiento. La estructura esférica se fabricaba industrialmente mediante moldes de acero, capas de fibra de vidrio, aislamiento de lana de vidrio y un revestimiento protector exterior.
Pesaba apenas 1.250 kilos y sus componentes prefabricados permitían montarla, según el proyecto, en una sola jornada. Las ventanas redondas estaban distribuidas para aprovechar la luz natural, mientras que su aislamiento y geometría buscaban reducir el consumo de calefacción. Los primeros inquilinos pagaban 375 florines mensuales, una cifra que reflejaba su carácter de vivienda asequible.
Vivir dentro de una bola tenía letra pequeña. Aunque cada casa ofrecía unos 55 metros cuadrados repartidos en varios niveles, la superficie realmente habitable rondaba los 25 metros cuadrados. Una escalera de caracol conectaba el dormitorio inferior, el baño intermedio y un pequeño salón con cocina situado en la parte superior, donde se concentraba la luz natural.
El problema aparecía al intentar amueblar el interior: las paredes curvas complicaban colocar armarios, colgar cuadros o aprovechar los rincones. Kreijkamp consideraba que eran viviendas ideales para personas solas o parejas sin hijos, pero su distribución también planteaba dificultades para quienes estaban acostumbrados a espacios convencionales.
El experimento que resultó demasiado caro para repetirse. Kreijkamp imaginaba un futuro en el que sus esferas podrían conectarse entre sí, convertirse en viviendas móviles e incluso flotar. Sin embargo, la realidad económica terminó imponiéndose: aunque el diseño prometía rapidez de montaje, aislamiento y bajo mantenimiento, fabricar aquellas casas resultó demasiado complejo y costoso para extender el modelo.
La financiación y el interés por construir nuevas unidades desaparecieron, y las 50 Bolwoningen quedaron como una experiencia prácticamente irrepetible. El arquitecto falleció en 2014 sin ver materializadas sus propuestas más ambiciosas.
40 años después, los extraterrestres siguen viviendo allí. Lo que nació como una solución experimental a la escasez de viviendas terminó convirtiéndose en una de las curiosidades arquitectónicas más reconocibles de Países Bajos. Las Bolwoningen siguen agrupadas junto a un canal, conectadas por senderos peatonales y rodeadas de vegetación, mientras los turistas se acercan para fotografiar unas casas que parecen desafiar cualquier idea convencional de urbanismo.
Si se quiere, su supervivencia demuestra que una propuesta arquitectónica puede fracasar como modelo industrial y, aun así, convertirse en un éxito cultural. En 1984, Países Bajos quiso descubrir si era posible vivir dentro de una pelota de golf gigante. Más de cuatro décadas después, hay 50 respuestas afirmativas.

articles.title: À partir de quand un devoir fait avec ChatGPT devient-il de la triche ?
articles.text:
Si vous avez fait écrire votre devoir par une IA sans l’accord de votre enseignant, vous avez triché, au regard des règles de l’Éducation nationale publiées en juin 2025. Mais le prouver est une autre affaire. Et faute de détecteur fiable, les professeurs doivent changer la façon de concevoir leurs devoirs.
L’Éducation nationale a fixé des règles claires pour l’IA générative, mais leur application reste délicate. Un devoir fait à la maison ne témoigne plus de ce que l’élève a réellement compris d’une leçon. Et un simple soupçon ne suffit pas à sanctionner.
Une fraude à deux conditions
Le ministère a publié son cadre d’usage de l’IA en éducation à la mi-juin 2025, après une consultation de janvier à mai. Nous rapportions que l'IA générative, capable de produire du texte, des images ou du son à partir d’une instruction écrite, le « prompt », serait autorisée à partir de la 4e, avec une règle simple pour les devoirs. Sans autorisation explicite de l’enseignant, pas d’usage.
Sur un devoir, il faut donc faire une différence entre se faire aider à comprendre une leçon ou se faire livrer une copie. Le cadre parle de fraude quand deux conditions se cumulent. La première : l’élève confie tout ou partie du travail à l’IA sans l’accord de l’enseignant. La seconde, c’est quand il ne fait aucun travail personnel d’appropriation, c’est-à-dire qu’il ne relit pas, ne retravaille pas et ne cherche pas à comprendre ce que la machine a produit. Certaines fiches académiques résument la règle plus brutalement et parlent de fraude dès qu’il n’y a pas d’autorisation, mais le texte du cadre fait foi.
Et l’usage de l’IA va graduellement selon l’âge de l’élève. En primaire, les élèves découvrent l'IA sans toucher à un outil génératif. À partir de la 4e, l'usage reste limité à la classe, sous l’encadrement de l’enseignant. Au lycée, il peut devenir autonome, dans un cadre que le professeur définit.
Pix IA, la formation qui accompagne le cadre
Le cadre s’accompagne d’une formation proposée par Pix, le service public qui évalue les compétences numériques. Testée de septembre à décembre 2025 dans 140 établissements, auprès de plus de 7 000 élèves, elle est ouverte aux volontaires depuis le 5 février 2026.
Pix propose deux parcours de 30 à 45 minutes, découpés en modules de 7 à 10 minutes. Les élèves y découvrent comment fonctionnent les IA génératives et comment rédiger un prompt, mais aussi les biais, les deepfakes et l’impact environnemental de ces outils.
Le parcours est obligatoire pour les élèves de 4e, de 2de générale et de première année de CAP. Depuis cette rentrée, les académies indiquent que les parcours sont en place dans les établissements. Ils se font en classe, sans attestation ni certification.
Un devoir à la maison témoigne-t-il encore de ce que l’élève a appris ?
Sans surprise, l’IA est déjà entrée dans les habitudes. Selon un sondage mené en Nouvelle Aquitaine et cité dans un rapport du Sénat d’octobre 2024, 90 % des élèves de seconde disent avoir déjà utilisé une IA pour leurs devoirs. Il s’agit d’une déclaration, pas d'une mesure, mais on peut facilement comprendre l’inquiétude des enseignants.
Le problème va d’ailleurs au-delà de la simple triche. Une consigne de 4e comme “écrivez un texte sur vos vacances préférées” peut être confiée à une IA en quelques secondes. Une bonne note sur un devoir fait à la maison ne dit alors plus ce que l’élève a compris, et le professeur perd un repère pour savoir ce qu’il doit reprendre en classe.
Pour le ministère cela crée une « illusion de compréhension » chez l’élève qui se retrouve devant une réponse claire et pense d’emblée l’avoir comprise. Une étude slovène, publiée en 2024 dans Applied Sciences, portait sur 32 étudiants de licence en informatique. Plus ces derniers recouraient souvent à des modèles de langage, plus leurs notes finales étaient basses. Reste qu’il s’agit d’une corrélation, pas de la preuve d’un effet de l’outil, et les auteurs soulignent eux-mêmes la petite taille de l’échantillon.
Une autre expérience, menée à l’université de Maribor, ne confirme d’ailleurs pas ce lien. 182 étudiants de première année en informatique ont été répartis au hasard en deux groupes, l’un encouragé à utiliser ChatGPT, l’autre non, sans différence significative de performance. Dans les deux cas pourtant, ce sont des étudiants, pas des collégiens. Difficile, donc, d’en tirer des conclusions pour une classe de 4e.
Les détecteurs d’IA, un soupçon et pas une preuve
Face à ce doute, un détecteur paraît tentant pour trancher. Les inspecteurs conseillent pourtant de ne pas s’en servir et de ne jamais sanctionner sans preuve matérielle. D’ailleurs, nos essais remettent en cause la fiabilité de ces outils. Nous avions soumis Pangram et GPTZero à dix textes en français, dont quatre générés par ChatGPT. Les textes humains ont été correctement classés, mais les deux outils ne s’accordaient pas sur tous les textes de machine. Pour l’un d’eux, GPTZero hésitait à 40 % d’IA quand Pangram annonçait 100 %. Pour un article humain très réécrit par ChatGPT, Pangram voyait 38 % d'IA tandis que GPTZero le jugeait humain à 98 %.
Ces divergences n’ont rien de surprenant. Un détecteur ne sait pas qui a écrit un texte. Il se contente d'estimer à quelle famille de textes un passage ressemble. Puis, il transforme cette estimation en verdict, avec des seuils fixés par l’éditeur. Imaginons 10 000 copies, dont 100 rédigées par une IA, et un détecteur qui repère 90 % des copies générées tout en accusant à tort 1 % des copies honnêtes. Il signale alors 90 copies à raison, mais aussi 99 copies écrites par des élèves, soit 189 alertes au total. Plus d’une alerte sur deux vise donc un élève innocent. Quand le phénomène est rare, une petite erreur suffit donc à produire beaucoup d’accusations injustes.
Et des cas existent déjà au bac avec des candidats soupçonnés d’avoir triché avec une IA, parfois sur la foi de détecteurs.
Écrire la règle dans la consigne
Faute de pouvoir prouver l’usage après coup, mieux vaut donc tenter de le cadrer en amont. Les mêmes repères demandent de préciser, pour chaque travail, si l’IA est autorisée, interdite ou prescrite, c’est-à-dire demandée par l’enseignant.
Cette règle écrite a aussi un poids juridique. Nous rapportions en septembre que le tribunal administratif de Toulouse avait suspendu en urgence la sanction d’une étudiante exclue cinq ans de l’enseignement supérieur, qu’il jugeait disproportionnée, sans toutefois se prononcer sur la triche. Le tribunal administratif de Paris a de son côté débouté une université qui contestait la relaxe d'une étudiante soupçonnée d’avoir rédigé son mémoire avec une IA. Après tout, sans règle écrite en amont sur l’usage de l’IA, aucune faute ne pouvait être retenue. Ces décisions concernent le supérieur, mais elles rappellent qu’une sanction suppose des consignes connues à l’avance.
Une fois la règle posée, il faut donc concevoir des devoirs qui la soutiennent. Les inspecteurs conseillent des fiches de révision écrites à la main, des capsules audio, des présentations orales, une alternance entre devoirs à la maison et travaux guidés en classe, et des traces intermédiaires, comme un brouillon ou un plan annoté. C’est donc le processus d’apprentissage dans sa globalité qui est mis en avant. La démarche et la justification comptent alors davantage que la seule production finale. Finalement, c'est la même approche que ces professeurs de mathématiques qui nous obligeaient à poser les étapes logiques d’une opération avant de présenter le résultat final pouvant être facilement obtenu avec une calculatrice.
Il existe déjà des pistes concrètes pour repenser les devoirs. Un enseignant peut demander de préparer à la maison une fiche sur un sujet en particulier, que les élèves présentent ensuite en classe en trois minutes. Il peut aussi soumettre sa consigne à une IA avant de la donner. Si l’IA elle-même obtenait une bonne note sans effort, il doit pouvoir adapter sa consigne, par exemple en ajoutant une explication à l’oral ou une étape à faire en classe. En 4e, l’élève peut comparer la correction produite par une IA à sa propre démarche, puis explique à l’oral laquelle est la plus rigoureuse. S’il n’y arrive pas, l’adulte reprend la notion avec lui. L’objectif étant toujours de comprendre, pas de recopier.
Au bac, l’IA pèse peu, mais la sanction se module
Qu’en est-il à l’échelle de l’examen ? En 2025, le ministère a recensé 1 208 cas de fraude au bac, dont 833 poursuivis devant la commission de discipline. Selon L'Étudiant, l’IA représente 8,5 % des cas, ce qui fait une centaine de dossiers environ, soit trois fois plus qu’en 2024. Les téléphones et montres connectées restent loin devant avec 55 %, suivis de l’antisèche à 24 %.
Face à ces fraudes, la réponse peut désormais être plus nuancée. Depuis le décret du 27 février 2026, la commission de discipline peut adapter la sanction à la gravité des faits. Elle peut par exemple n’annuler que certaines évaluations du contrôle continu, c’est-à-dire celles de l'année qui comptent dans la note finale.
Reste la correction. Le ministre Édouard Geffray a dit le 19 mai 2026 qu’il refusait de voir l’IA se substituer aux professeurs. Pour lui, « corriger, c'est apprécier la qualité d'un raisonnement au-delà du résultat », rapporte Ouest-France. Des expérimentations ont toutefois lieu dans des lycées d’Île-de-France pour tester une aide à la décision des professeurs, notamment pour l’évaluation continue.
Un assistant souverain, mais pas encore pour les enseignants
Dès que des copies et des données d’élèves entrent dans l’équation, la question de la confidentialité se pose. Le cadre rappelle que les services d’IA grand public ne garantissent pas la non-réutilisation des données saisies. Il demande de n’y saisir que des informations pouvant être rendues publiques, et d’y renoncer dès qu’une donnée personnelle est en jeu. Nous détaillions d’ailleurs dans un dossier que supprimer une conversation n’efface pas toujours tout.
Du côté des enseignants, le ministère a autorisé des IA grand public en attendant un outil souverain, avec un appel à projets de 20 millions d’euros annoncé via France 2030. Un assistant interministériel est ouvert depuis juin 2026 à tous les agents de l’État, avec leurs identifiants académiques. Selon l’académie de Bordeaux, il peut traiter des données personnelles ou sensibles sans les utiliser pour entraîner les modèles. Une version pour les enseignants est en développement, avec un déploiement progressif prévu en 2026-2027.
Dans l’intervalle, le risque concerne surtout les copies puisqu’un enseignant qui confie le texte d’un élève à une IA grand public l’envoie chez un éditeur. Le respect de la règle repose donc, pour l’instant, sur la vigilance de chacun.
Rapport Calvez et heure d’IA, ce qui reste ouvert
Le débat n’est pas clos pour autant. Le 1er juillet 2026, la députée Céline Calvez a rendu public un rapport d’information de 26 recommandations, consultatives, qui n’engagent pas le gouvernement. Le rapport propose d’autoriser l’usage encadré dès la 6e plutôt que la 4e. Selon LCP, la députée juge les seuils actuels en décalage avec les pratiques puisque beaucoup d’élèves de 6e et de 5e disposent déjà d’un smartphone.
Le texte veut aussi renforcer la place de l’oral et garantir, à terme, des temps d’enseignement sans IA. Il évoque une « hybridation des évaluations » pour les travaux de recherche, une « IAgraphie » qui signale les usages de l’IA, et une formation continue obligatoire des enseignants.
Du côté du gouvernement, le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu a annoncé le 19 juin, au salon VivaTech, une heure d’IA par semaine pour tous les élèves de seconde. Elle démarrera à la rentrée 2027, intégrée au cours de SNT, les sciences numériques et technologie, et abordera le fonctionnement des modèles, l’éthique et l’esprit critique face aux fausses informations. L’emploi du temps reste flou, et le syndicat Snes-FSU craint une surexposition des élèves.
En attendant, les enseignants peuvent s’appuyer sur deux gestes simples : préciser la règle dès la consigne, et faire expliquer le travail à l’oral en classe.

Plus resserrée, plus rythmée et portée par des personnages inédits particulièrement convaincants, cette saison 3 des Anneaux de pouvoir permet à la série de gagner en maturité et donne enfin toute sa mesure à la fresque imaginée par Tolkien. articles.title: IShowSpeed terminó GTA 6 en 52 horas, sin dormir y transmitió por Twitch
articles.text:
IShowSpeed completó la historia principal de GTA 6 después de una transmisión en vivo que se extendió por más de 52 horas. El creador de contenido dedicó el maratón a avanzar por la campaña del juego y compartió el reto con su audiencia a través de Twitch.
Durante la emisión, el streamer hizo pausas breves para comer e ir al baño, pero no durmió. El desafío atrajo la atención de sus seguidores y de la comunidad de videojuegos, tanto por la duración como por la rapidez con la que llegó al desenlace de uno de los lanzamientos más esperados del año.
La sesión también dejó ver el desgaste que implicó permanecer frente a la pantalla durante tantas horas. Al terminar, IShowSpeed habló del cansancio físico y mental que acumuló y de la dificultad para asimilar que había completado un título de esa magnitud en un periodo tan corto.
Un maratón centrado en la campaña principal
El objetivo del creador fue completar la historia principal de GTA 6 lo antes posible. Para ello, priorizó las misiones de la campaña y dejó en segundo plano buena parte de las actividades opcionales que suelen ocupar a los jugadores en el mundo abierto.
La decisión implicó recorrer menos el mapa y dedicar menos tiempo a las misiones secundarias y los minijuegos. En los títulos de Grand Theft Auto, esas actividades suelen formar parte importante de la experiencia: permiten conocer la ciudad, descubrir personajes y situaciones imprevistas, además de avanzar a un ritmo propio.
El formato de maratón transformó la partida en una prueba de resistencia y en un espectáculo en directo. La audiencia pudo seguir los avances y las reacciones del streamer mientras completaba los objetivos de la campaña. Así, la transmisión convirtió el final del juego en un acontecimiento compartido por sus espectadores.
El impacto emocional de la historia
La llegada al desenlace también provocó una reacción intensa en IShowSpeed. El streamer expresó su sorpresa y frustración ante el rumbo de la historia y comentó que esperaba un resultado distinto para los protagonistas, Jason y Lucía.
Su respuesta generó conversación entre quienes siguieron la transmisión, en especial porque el desenlace contrastó con la inversión de tiempo y emoción que había dedicado a la partida. Sin revelar detalles concretos de la trama, el episodio mostró cómo las decisiones narrativas del juego pueden afectar a los jugadores, incluso cuando avanzan con rapidez.
Una forma distinta de vivir GTA 6
El reto de IShowSpeed refleja una tendencia habitual en las transmisiones de videojuegos: convertir una partida en un evento con una meta clara y un límite de tiempo. En este caso, completar la campaña en directo permitió a los espectadores acompañar cada etapa del recorrido y reaccionar junto al streamer.
Sin embargo, terminar la historia en poco más de dos días no equivale a descubrir todo lo que ofrece GTA 6. El juego incluye un mundo abierto pensado para que cada persona explore a su ritmo, realice actividades secundarias y encuentre contenido fuera de la trama principal. Al concentrarse en la campaña, IShowSpeed dejó pendiente una parte de esa experiencia.
El maratón terminó con la campaña completada y con el creador reconociendo el cansancio acumulado. Su transmisión quedó entre las más comentadas del estreno de GTA 6, no solo por las horas que duró, sino por la reacción que generó el desenlace entre él y quienes lo acompañaron en Twitch.

articles.title: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
articles.text:
At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).
These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.
These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.
What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.
This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.
How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?
Scientific shortcomings: biology and genetics
Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons. They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behavior and intelligence between human groups—such as races—over purely environmental differences.
Yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people.” No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology, or psychology.
In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously showed that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one another. There is genetic variation—though we’re actually a relatively genetically similar species compared to closely related primates. But this variation doesn’t fall neatly into clusters that correlate with how we typically categorize races.
Skin tone and color do vary between geographical locations. So do some other physiological features like hair texture, or the ability to process oxygen or milk products. But these differences are associated with characteristics of the environment rather than with racial groups. Some genetic variants associated with white skin color, for example, may have originated in Africa. Similarly, the ability to digest milk is seen in some populations in Europe, Africa, and Asia, rather than being an exclusively “Aryan” characteristic, as far right groups sometimes claim.
We now know considerably more about the human genome than Lewontin did in the 1970s, but his conclusions are supportedtoday. Knowing someone’s race just doesn’t tell us a great deal about their genetics.
Recent scientific advances allowing us to examine ancient DNA from archaeological sites help explain why genetic differences do not fall neatly along racial lines. This research paints a picture of constant mixing between human groups, as waves of migration washed to and fro across the globe. It ultimately makes any belief in the genetic “purity” of European or African populations meaningless.
While human genetics is fascinatingly complex, race scientists ignore this complexity in favor of a far-too-simplistic view of humanity. And this view is not supported by the work of scientists who have used rigorous scientific methods to further our understanding of our species.
Challenges from social science
When race scientists say that black people have lower intelligence than white people, they typically base that on claims of differences in IQ test results. But the data underlying these claims is often shaky, to say the least.
Hereditarians have relied heavily on a database that claims to provide average IQs for countries worldwide: the “national IQ” database. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that this database is deeply methodologically flawed. It isn’t possible to measure intelligence in the same way in very different cultures, with different exposure to formal education. That’s because we know that education is one of several other factors linked to differences in IQ.
The methods used to put the database together did not come even close to meeting typical standards of scientific rigor. There’s even analysis suggesting that low IQ samples were deliberately chosen to represent sub-Saharan Africa, to make the IQ for black populations artificially low.
Meanwhile, the Flynn effect, showing that IQ has risen considerably during the 20th and 21st centuries, clearly demonstrates that IQ scores are heavily determined by the environment we’re in. Such a rapid rise over a short period of time must have environmental, not genetic, causes.
What’s more, intelligence is a contested topic—something that is hard to define and measure. IQ tests only measure specific cognitive abilities, ignoring things like social intelligence or creativity, for example. In fact, social intelligence features heavily in mainstream research on the evolution of human intelligence.
As one of us recently outlined in a peer-reviewed paper, race scientists are largely silent on the social brain hypothesis—the view that humans evolved remarkable intellectual abilities to manage social issues. In every group, there is strong social competition around resources, mating, and status. These are the things humans spend the most time navigating—the complexities of our rich social lives.
Not one of the prominent mainstream views on the evolution of human intelligence concludes there are innate cognitive differences between racial groups. Factors that have been put forward range from our cooperative child rearing to our heavy reliance on culture and learning. These all involve our social relationships, and all have received equal lack of attention from race scientists.
Mainstream opinion in the evolutionary behavioral sciences is that cognitively, all human groups are the same, though of course individuals within groups differ. Our amazing behavioral diversity stems from our species’ ability to adapt flexibly to our environment. This is especially because of our reliance on culture and social learning—not because we have evolved different psychologies to suit different environments.
Rather than drawing on this mainstream research, race scientists use simplistic “just-so” stories to explain how race differences in traits such as intelligence supposedly evolved. Their “cold winters theory,” for example, claims that the challenges of cold winters in Europe and east Asia created evolutionary selection pressures for greater intelligence after human groups migrated out of Africa. In doing so, they make unsupportable assumptions about environmental differences between Africa and the rest of the world. They also fail to acknowledge half a century of research on the evolution of human cognitive ability.
Yes, we needed to learn new food gathering practices and methods for dealing with environmental challenges as we migrated across the world. But the same was true as humans migrated across the large and ecologically diverse continent of Africa. Race scientists provide no evidence for their arguments. They don’t rely on archaeological evidence, nor do they use typical methods from evolutionary biology to understand evolutionary processes. Using the methods of race scientists, it would be equally easy to make the argument that challenges posed by hot summers drove the evolution of higher intelligence, and equally without scientific backing.
No matter which way you look at these issues—from the view of genetics, anthropology, evolutionary biology, or psychology—hereditarianism does not hold up.
A short history of race science
To understand the potential consequences of these views, it is important to see them in historical context. Early in the 20th century, race science was mainstream. Overly simplistic and biologically deterministic views about the origins of differences between human groups—not just race but class—were widespread (if not universal) and important to the eugenics movement.
If disadvantaged groups owe their disadvantage to some fault within them, and not to the structural conditions they experience, then some argue society is not responsible for helping those people. Such arguments led to eugenic sterilization laws that aimed to “improve” society by preventing—without their consent—the reproduction of those considered likely to pass on their innate “defects” to future children. And it was ultimately behind the Nazis’ “solution” of trying to eliminate “undesirables” entirely.
In the decades after the Second World War, the horrors of the Nazi regime led to a decline in the popularity of eugenics in mainstream research and a rejection of race science. But the belief that science supported eugenic claims was already collapsing, even as the Nazis were trying to implement a race-based society. As we learned more about human biology and genetics during the 20th century, it became obvious that human genetic variation was too complex to be mapped into socially recognized racial (or class) categories. Advances in science meant race science dropped out of mainstream thinking.
Yet those committed to a belief in a biological hierarchy of races, regardless of what the science said, wanted venues in which they could continue their discussions. In the 1960s, the pseudo-scientific journal Mankind Quarterly became their venue. Mankind Quarterly was funded by the Pioneer Fund, a nonprofit foundation set up in the 1930s by a US textile magnate who chose to use his fortune to fund research on race science and fight desegregation in the US.
The Pioneer Fund continued to fund race science into the 21st century—including supporting Mankind Quarterly—when it was taken over by the current network of race scientists. They channeled its remaining funds into a new company, the Human Diversity Foundation, subsequently rebranded as Polygenic Scores LLC.
How race science still persists
Given all this, how is race science still being published in mainstream academic journals? To be clear, race science does not typically get published in genetics or evolutionary biology journals. Most academic journals operate peer review, meaning papers only get published after evaluation by experts in the field. The overall absence of race science in genetics or biology journals is a clear signal that it does not meet contemporary standards of scientific rigor in genetics or biology.
Instead, race scientists continue to publish in para-scientific journals. But race science also makes it into a growing number of mainstream social science or humanities journals. Psychologist Andrew Winston, an expert in the history of race science in psychology, has described it as a “community project… with its own networks, mentorships, journals, funding, conferences, heroes, origin myths, martyrs, defenders, and historiography.”
Behind the network of writers producing race science sits a community of editors, peer reviewers, and others in gatekeeping roles, which too often allows race science to be published in mainstream journals. This is particularly in the subfields of psychology interested in intelligence and individual differences, and evolutionary psychology.
Editors of Intelligence, the mainstream journal that has probably published the largest quantity of race science, have occasionally publishededitorials defending their publication of race science in the name of ensuring robust academic debate even on controversial topics.
There have been sanctions. Philippe Rushton, one of an earlier generation of race scientists, faced sanctions from his university in Canada but kept his job apparently owing to the intervention of Edward O. Wilson, arguably the most famous biologist toward the end of the 20th century.
Cofnas created justified controversy over his call for a “hereditarian revolution” after which it will be acknowledged that black people are innately intellectually disadvantaged compared to white people. But he kept his postdoctoral fellowship at Cambridge University (though his affiliation with a Cambridge college was ended). He has also kept his postdoctoral position at Ghent University after using the opportunity provided by excessive news coverage of Arday to publicize his hereditarian views (though some sanctions have been imposed, such as restrictions on teaching). Cofnas has defended his views by saying he’s been misunderstood and is entitled to free inquiry.
Moreover, when University College London discovered that the race science community had been holding conferences on its premises (the “London Conferences on Intelligence”), without their knowledge of the subject of the conferences, they acted to prevent further such conferences being held. The publisher of the journal Intelligence, Elsevier, has recently appointed new editors, who have stated their commitment to publishing both rigorous and socially responsible science. Race scientists are increasingly publishing in evolutionary psychology journals rather than Intelligence.
However, the London Conferences on Intelligence continue, though not at UCL. Race scientists also have a media arm, Aporia magazine, which promotes race science using much more overt language and with more obvious policy focus than publications in academic journals. One Aporia article, for example, argued for eugenics as a solution to Africa’s lack of economic development, noting in a post that some may find it “distasteful.” It claimed—relying on race science’s unscientific arguments—that artificial selection for higher intelligence is needed to improve the continent’s innately unintelligent populace.
Race science may not have the respect of the scientific community, but it does have funding and influential backers. A report by Hope not Hate revealed that the network of race scientists received significant funding from the US businessman Andrew Conru, who withdrew his funding after the report was released.
The US Ambassador to Belgium even intervened when Ghent University set up an investigation into how Cofnas was hired.
Race scientists are far from the victims they claim to be. Race scientists in this and previous generations have worked hard to ensure their messages are heard beyond academia. And in this generation, they are successfully using social media to spread their beliefs, especially Elon Musk’s X.
But what about academic freedom? Isn’t it good for science to discuss any hypothesis to ensure free exchange of ideas? Academic debate is productive only if it involves methodologically rigorous research. Science will not progress if one side of any debate consistently uses poor-quality, methodologically flawed work. Nor is it necessary to continually debate topics that have long since been settled.
We believe it is unequivocal that race science is fundamentally pseudoscience. In our view, it’s critical to call attention to not only the scientific flaws underlying this body of work but also the real target it’s aimed at: political actors and everyday readers who ultimately decide the direction that science, and society, goes in.
The Conversation is an independent source of news and views, sourced from the academic and research community. Our team of editors work with these experts to share their knowledge with the wider public. Our aim is to allow for better understanding of current affairs and complex issues, and hopefully improve the quality of public discourse on them.

articles.title: 28-Core Intel "Nova Lake-S" Appears in Testing Running at 5.2 GHz
articles.text:
Saturday, November 21st 2026
28-Core Intel "Nova Lake-S" Appears in Testing Running at 5.2 GHz
Intel's single-compute die "Nova Lake-S" variant has been spotted with a 28-core configuration and a boost frequency of 5.2 GHz, according to the OpenBenchmark testing suite. During the tests, a processor named Intel 0000 appeared with the "NVL" identifier, suggesting that a "Nova Lake-S" SKU with this configuration is indeed present. The processor's identification as Intel 0000 implies that the rumored four-number naming scheme is real, as confirmed by the benchmarks. This naming scheme could easily become standard, moving away from the three-digit SKU naming we've seen in the past.
Interestingly, the submission also identifies the integrated graphics as Intel NVL-S, indicating that the engineering platform is being tested beyond just CPU workloads. The tests include various graphics and compute applications, such as Quake II RTX, Unigine benchmarks, Hashcat, and multiple OpenCL workloads. While the 5.2 GHz figure is promising, it should not be taken as confirmation of the processor's final boost frequency. Engineering samples can operate with different firmware, power limits, and clock configurations than retail products. The listing also does not disclose whether the reported frequency represents a sustained operating clock or a maximum observed value.The system information lists 28 CPU cores, likely indicating a configuration with 8 P-Cores, 16 E-Cores, and 4 LPE-Cores, along with a reported operating frequency of 5.20 GHz. The motherboard is identified as an Intel "Nova Lake-S" reference platform, specifically an NVL-S UDIMM 1DPC CRB Fab2 configuration running an early BIOS build. The system was tested with 32 GB of memory under Ubuntu 26.04, suggesting that it could be Intel's internal engineering teams testing the system, or one of their OEM PC partners.
Source:
