If there’s one thing that the MO27Q2A leaves out, it's LED lighting. There’s no colorful show to dazzle your opponents with. But nothing else has been sacrificed. A pair of five-watt internal speakers delivers good audio, or you can use the 3.5mm headphone jack.
The screen is super colorful with over 108% coverage of DCI-P3 thanks to a Quantum Dot layer. Color is very accurate, so much so that I found calibration completely unnecessary. You get sRGB and Adobe RGB options as well. Brightness is solid at 250 nits for a full field and over 1,000 nits for a 3% window pattern. You can use variable brightness for SDR and HDR content to pump up small highlights for even more dynamic range.
High-performance gaming is the primary goal here, and for that, the MO27Q2A comes with a reliable 280 Hz refresh rate, Adaptive-Sync with certifications from Nvidia and AMD, and a host of Game Assist features like aiming points, sniper modes, flash suppression, timers, and a frame counter. Like all OLEDs, it has lightning-fast reflexes with super smooth motion rendering.
Gigabyte pays plenty of attention to panel care with a host of options like pixel refresh and logo detection. There’s extensive passive cooling (no fans) and AI control that tracks usage at the pixel level to keep everything in balance. The end result is longevity and reliability, which is backed by a three-year factory warranty that includes burn-in.
The MO27Q2A’s value is the most impressive part. At this writing, it sells for $399 online. It wasn’t long ago that you’d pay that for a 240 Hz QHD LCD. That category has dropped in cost as well, with some screens coming in around $200. But spending an extra $200 for an OLED seems like a no-brainer to me. Let’s see how the MO27Q2A fares in my tests.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Assembly and Accessories
Gigabyte offers a bit of fanfare on the MO27Q2A’s carton with colored graphics that set it apart from the plain brown wrappers more commonly seen at the big box store. A clamshell lid opens to reveal blocks of crumbly foam containing the panel, upright, and base, which assemble without tools. The power supply is internal, so you get a selection of IEC cords plus cables for HDMI, DisplayPort, and USB. A little clip goes on the stand to tidy up the wiring.
Product 360
The panel is minimalist from the front with a thin flush bezel and a metal backing that wraps around the edges. A narrow trim strip crosses the bottom with a tiny Gigabyte logo in its center. The controls are under the center point and consist of a backlit joystick and two keys. One is the Tactical Switch, and it changes resolutions on the fly. More about that below.
The stand is above average in quality with all-metal construction and smooth ergonomics. It includes 5.2 inches of height range plus 5/21 degrees tilt, 15 degrees swivel, and a 90-degree portrait mode. There is no hint of wobble or play. It is one of the better stands I’ve encountered, and I’ve encountered many.
From the side, you can see the panel-on-bulge design that is shared by many OLEDs. Not only does this look cool, but it actually is cool. The MO27Q2A’s panel is backed by metal, which acts as a heat sink. The bulge is also well ventilated, enough so that no fans are needed. A graphene layer behind the OLED contributes to cooling and hence, longevity.
Underneath is a well-appointed I/O panel with two HDMI 2.1s, a DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC, a USB-C that supports video and 18 watts of power, and USB 3.2, one upstream and two down. They can be bound to different video inputs using the KVM feature in the OSD. You also get a 3.5mm headphone jack and a pair of internal speakers with five watts of amplification.
OSD Features
The MO27Q2A’s OSD presents complete information with signal status at the top and current settings shown at the bottom.

The Gaming menu includes a black frame insertion feature called Ultra Clear. It works at 280 or 120 Hz and is effective at removing motion blur. If you can run at 180fps or higher, you won’t need it. Other options include Black Equalizer, which increases shadow visibility, super resolution (edge enhancement, do not use), display mode for aspect ratio control, and a VRR toggle.
The MO27Q2A includes 10 picture modes mainly aimed at different game types. It comes out of the box in Eco, which limits brightness. Choose Standard to unlock the maximum light output. Within this mode, you can adjust color temp and gamma and choose a color space. My sample was nearly perfect out of the box, so good, in fact, that I could not improve it with calibration. If you want sRGB or Adobe RGB color, those choices are in the Color Space submenu. For sRGB, there’s an sRGB picture mode. HDR signals get their own five modes. Peak 1000 is the brightest and best choice there.
You can use the KVM Wizard to bind USB ports and video inputs. That way, one keyboard, mouse, and monitor can service multiple sources like a PC and a gaming console, for instance. You can also view two sources at once using the PIP/PBP options.
Quick Switch lets the user program the functions of the joystick directionals. It provides quick access to commonly used functions like brightness or crosshairs.
A separate screen comes up for the MO27Q2A’s OLED care options. This is where you’ll find APL Stabilize, which has two levels of variable brightness or a constant setting. Its terminology is counterintuitive because Low means off, while Middle and High modulate light output more aggressively. High has the most dynamic range, with 1,000 peaks possible in HDR mode. If it were up to me, APL Stabilize would be in the Picture menu and be called Variable Brightness. Additional care options include pixel orbiting, panel refresh, and dimming for logos and corners. You turn any or all of these off if you wish.
Press the joystick and click right for the Game Assist menu and its plethora of play aids. You get four crosshairs, a timer, stopwatch, refresh rate indicator, and positioning of the information window. Also included are sniper mode and night vision. Flash Dimming suppresses your weapon’s muzzle flash if that becomes a distraction.
Gigabyte’s Tactical Switch is a unique feature that switches the MO27Q2A’s resolution on the fly. You can have FHD or HD in 16:9, 4:3, or 5:4 aspect ratios. The refresh rate remains at 280 Hz, but by shrinking the image, you get higher frame rates with no significant sharpness penalty.
Gigabyte MO27Q2A Calibration Settings
There isn’t much to the MO27Q2A’s calibration because it isn’t necessary. In fact, I could not improve my sample with calibration. It measures nearly perfect out of the box for D65, 2.2 gamma, and coverage of DCI-P3. The sRGB mode, which is also very accurate, is found in the picture mode list. For Adobe RGB, go to the Color Space sub-menu. For gaming and daily use, I settled on Standard mode, Native color space, and left everything else at default settings. My recommendations are below.
For HDR signals, HDR is the default mode, but I found the same excellent accuracy and high brightness in the Peak 1000 mode. It delivers the promised 1,000 nits for a 3% window, which in my tests equated to 445 nits for a 25% window pattern. You get a number of sliders for brightness and contrast, but they are not needed unless you want a different look for HDR content.
| Picture Mode | Standard | 
| Brightness 200 nits | 75 (APL Stabilize Low) | 
| Row 2 - Cell 0 | 40 (APL Stabilize High) | 
| Brightness 120 nits | 41 | 
| Brightness 100 nits | 33 | 
| Brightness 80 nits | 25 | 
| Brightness 50 nits | 13 (min. 22 nits) | 
| Contrast | 50 | 
| Gamma | 2.2 | 
| Color Temp | Normal | 
| Color Space | Native | 
Gaming and Hands-on
A great way to evaluate a monitor’s HDR accuracy is by viewing static content that covers the full dynamic range of both color and neutral tones. Doom Eternal has such a screen in its HDR adjustment menu, and I use it for every review to verify detail rendering. The MO27Q2A showed every nuance in this torture test, which told me that it is very color accurate and tracks luminance correctly. In simple terms, you’ll see everything the game creators put in.
This gives gameplay a heightened sense of realism, especially in textures like stone, metal, and dirt. The MO27Q2A let me almost reach out and touch them. I had to remind myself that its resolution was QHD and Ultra HD because it rendered so finely. I also saw rich color that was perfectly balanced. You’ll see in the SDR and HDR tests that this is a seriously precise monitor.
Gameplay was up to the premium OLED standard with smooth motion that was completely free of blur. I had no trouble maintaining a constant 280fps. If you can’t hit that speed, Gigabyte includes Ultra Clear, which is a black frame insertion feature. It will remove motion blur at lower rates like 120 Hz. I noted that it was available at 280 Hz as well, which is unusual. It cuts brightness by around 40%, but you can partially compensate for that with the brightness slider. It operated artifact-free.
Another way to increase frame rates is with the Tactical Switch, which changes resolution and picture size on the fly. It doesn’t increase the refresh rate, but by shrinking the image, it maintains a favorable pixel map so that sharpness doesn’t take a huge hit.
Gameplay was addictive during my numerous frag fests. Input lag and response are super quick, which helped make my aim more precise. The MO27Q2A was so fast that it made me overconfident. I rushed into the melee rather than picking off enemies one by one. It was truly difficult to stop playing.
The MO27Q2A excels as an everyday screen with 109ppi pixel density in its 27-inch form factor. It’s significantly less expensive than an Ultra HD monitor if you can accept a small reduction in clarity. And that resolution is a sweet spot for frame rates. You won’t need a giga-hauler video card to achieve its full potential.
Accurate color out of the box meant I could rely on the MO27Q2A as a reference for graphics and photos. I found excellent results in my initial tests, and I could not improve upon them with adjustments. This monitor is pro-level for sure.
It’s impressive ergonomically too, with a solid all-metal stand and rugged panel construction. There are no missing features except for flashy LEDs. The internal speakers play loud and clear in the upper midrange, or you can plug in headphones. Users with a PC and console will appreciate the USB ports and KVM functions.
Takeaway: The MO27Q2A is a truly full-featured gaming monitor that can double as an everyday screen or a professional display. It games on par with the very best screens I’ve reviewed and delivers performance equal to more expensive OLEDs with higher refresh rates. It also matches those products in build quality with a solid stand and metal construction. For $399, you’ll be hard-pressed to find better.

Christian Eberle is a Contributing Editor for Tom's Hardware US. He's a veteran reviewer of A/V equipment, specializing in monitors. Christian began his obsession with tech when he built his first PC in 1991, a 286 running DOS 3.0 at a blazing 12MHz. In 2006, he undertook training from the Imaging Science Foundation in video calibration and testing and thus started a passion for precise imaging that persists to this day. He is also a professional musician with a degree from the New England Conservatory as a classical bassoonist which he used to good effect as a performer with the West Point Army Band from 1987 to 2013. He enjoys watching movies and listening to high-end audio in his custom-built home theater and can be seen riding trails near his home on a race-ready ICE VTX recumbent trike. Christian enjoys the endless summer in Florida where he lives with his wife and Chihuahua and plays with orchestras around the state.
- truerock I purchased my first OLED display this year. I fooled around with various power settings for it because it was my first OLED and thought it was something to worry about... screen burn-in, etc.
Anyway, what I re-discovered was the Windows "Screen Saver". I have it set to "Blank" and 2 minutes.
It's great because it allows the screen to be instantly turned on with the slightest touch of the mouse or keyboard... because the monitor is still powered "On" even though the pixels are powered "Off".
You won't find "Screen Saver" in Windows Settings. You will find it in the old "Control Panel"
Using Power Settings to save an OLED display is very annoying because it takes the screen several seconds to recover and turn back on... sometimes it won't turn back on at all and you have to reboot your PC. Power settings in PCs have always been unreliable and I have accepted they will always be unreliable.
If you want to also do power settings, you can do that - but, almost nobody is going to power-down their monitor every 2 minutes. Reply

articles.title: A tale of two Nvidias | TechCrunch
articles.text:
We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.
Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.
What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.
A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.
Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.
Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.
And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.
Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.
It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.
So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.
Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.
It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”
So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.
Kirsten: Sure, never say never.
Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.
Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.
Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.
Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

articles.title: Which earbuds should I buy this Black Friday? I’m an audio editor and I tested five best-selling options to find the ultimate winner
articles.text:
Apple AirPods 5, Bose QC Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2), Technics EAH-AZ100, Nothing Ear (a) or Shokz OpenFit Pro: I've found the earbuds you should buy this Black Friday
I put five of the best wireless earbuds of 2026 in a group test for sound, ANC, stamina and features — and there's one clear winner
It's been a massive year for earbuds — and not only for wireless models, but also for the influx of wired options and open designs, either arc-shaped to sit behind your ear, or ear cuff-style, to clip around it.
I’ve personally reviewed many of the best earbuds and best open earbuds in our respective buying guides, and I have to tell you that the work is only ramping up as 2026 draws to a close.
With Black Friday deals very much on our (Tech)radar, I think we need a little group test to work out which of the likely discounted earbuds is most worthy of your money, don't you?
Under direct a/b comparison (and of course c/d, d/e and every possible parallel in between), I'm going to tell you which buds feel the best, look the most premium, sound the most zealous and detailed, have the best stamina, sport the best on-ear controls, and include some of the neatest features — some of which you perhaps weren't aware you could get for the money.
Don't know if you want buds or cans? Stop everything, and take my quick quiz below… then come back here!
All five models in this group test earned glowing 5-star or 4.5-star ratings under TechRadar's rigorous review process, as carried out by yours truly.
But here's the thing: often, it isn't as simple as, "Okay, this set gained the full five; this pair's half-a-star off perfect — so this one's best!" Why not? First, because cost and value play vital roles; and second, because each of us is different. Something with a fantastic battery life that's slightly less impressive for audio than the Apple AirPods 5, say (which will only last five hours with ANC on), might be better for an individual who regularly flies from London to Tokyo. See what I'm saying?
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
That said, these are all winning buds — often literally, because they've won awards at this very publication. So a part of me knows that whichever of this little quintet you pick, you won't be disappointed. Then again, as TechRadar's Audio Editor, a huge part of my job is finding the ideal set of buds for you, or whomever you're buying for.
So let's work out which of this little lot that is! Meet the contenders: 
Apple AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging; unveiled September 9, '26 — $149 / £139 / AU$249
Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2); arrived June 12, '25 — $299 / £299 / AU$450
Nothing Ear (a); unveiled April 18, '24 — $99 / £99 / around AU$192
Shokz OpenFit Pro; unveiled January 6, '26 — $249 / £219 / AU$399
Technics EAH-AZ100; unveiled January 7, '25 — $299 / £259 / AU$478
Right then. Let's step to it…
Design, fit and battery life
We're not here to mess around — time is precious as we run up to Black Friday and 2026's gift-giving season. The easiest thing is for me to list the earbuds, with their perks and pitfalls, in various key areas. So here we go.
Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging
The good: without question the smallest case of the quintet. And said case still emits useful, findable noises (much like Apple's far pricier buds), despite its bijou proportions. The AirPods themselves are easy to access and simple to fit. There's a beauty — not to mention a popularity — in the simplistic, function-first design here; I wore them for hours on end without issue. Also, an IP57 rating means they'll survive full immersion in water for a limited time.
The bad: you only get up to five hours of stamina (with ANC enabled) or up to 22 hours including the case, which is the least impressive battery life stat in this roundup. Also, these buds are Apple's "open-fit" design — i.e, there are no ear tips to fit. This results in a bud that isn't as intrusive in the ear canal, which many wearers prefer (I happen to really like the shape of this particular iteration). But the fit is a little less secure than solutions that create a seal using your ear canal and the tip fitted onto the neck of an earbud.
Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2)
The good: this "sonic sangria" color is the most winsome and elite-looking of the crop in my opinion. Also, the fit is very secure, because as well as three different-sized ear tips, you also get three different silicone "stabilizer fins" to add to the driver housing to create a more bespoke fit. An IPX4 rating means they're splash-proof, too, although not tested against dust ingress.
The bad: battery life is better than the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging, but not by much. At 6 hours from the buds or up to 24 hours with the case, it's acceptable rather than excellent — and this is premium territory. Also, while I had no issue with the fit here (even with my storied smaller ears), it's worth noting that the earpieces do look a little big in the ears, because they protrude a tad. It's a small issue, but it's my job to notice.
Nothing Ear (a)
The good: they're a little older, with an April 2024 launch date, and they've been superseded by the Ear (3a) – don't worry, you haven't missed a (2a), although it's not easy to explain why — but I didn't like the 3(a) nearly as much as I love these. And I'm listing it as a Good Thing because even at their original MSRP, they were the cheapest in this roundup. I'm fairly sure you can find them for up to half-price in early Black Friday deals now, and the specs still hold up just fine in 2026. The design is delightfully transparent with accents of color, especially if you get the yellow set I reviewed. And for me these earbuds fit securely, while the pinch stems (also a feature of the more expensive AirPods) add real value. An IP54 rating means they're as splash-proof as the Bose buds above, but there's a level of dust-ingress protection, too.
The bad: the stamina is in-between the two options above, at 5.5 hours (although it does jump to 9.5 hours without ANC) or a total with case of 24.5 hours (42.5 hours without ANC), which isn't a great deal to write home about, unless you're giving up ANC. Also, while I found the case very pocketable and fun, it does occasionally pick up scratches if you're slinging it in a pocket with your keys, say.
Shokz OpenFit Pro
The good: as open earbuds go, these are the most elite-feeling I've ever tested. There's a sense of pride in ownership about them, especially when you feel the little aluminum, red-accented nub on the underside of the driver that slips around your ear just so. The case is of course a little bigger, to accommodate each earpiece, but it's still slender and one of the more durable in this roundup — and I should know, because it lives in either my dance bag or my other half's tennis racket bag and still looks new. Also, the extra bands for stability aid with a more sporty fit. Battery life? It's good: 12 hours (earbuds, noise reduction disabled), or 50 hours in total with the case before it too needs to be charged. An IP55 rating means they're splash-proof and dust-ingress resistant.
The bad: it's a small thing, but we find that when wearing the extra stability bands for longer periods of time (ie. not playing sports), they can begin to irritate your ear. All this means is that you have to remember to remove the bands after playing sports — and then not lose them because you were in a hurry…
Technics EAH-AZ100
The good: the "concha fit" design that Technics created for its earbuds (initially for the older, also superb Technics EAH-AZ-80) may look fairly deep, but it's the absolute business. Technics worked really hard on it, and it shows. They fit securely, aided further by five different sizes of ear tip to choose from, and they look (and feel) like elite-level earbuds — because that's what they are. Stamina is also good: 12 hours (earbuds, ANC off) or 10 hours with it on.
The bad: although the battery life from the buds is good, you only get up to 28 hours from the charging case, which is perhaps a little disappointing given the initial figure. That said, it's hardly a bad stat given the competition here. Also, an IPX4 rating, while certifying the buds as resistant to droplets of water from any direction, is the lowest IP rating in this roundup.
- Design/aesthetics winner: Nothing Ear (a)
- Comfort/security winner: Technics EAH-AZ100
- Stamina winner: Shokz OpenFit Pro
Features and active noise cancellation
Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging
The good: if you have an iPhone, the ANC here can only be touched by Apple's more expensive AirPods Pro 3 or AirPods Max 2. It is excellent for the money. Apple has finessed these buds for the iOS ensconced — and to that end, if you have a newer iPhone with Apple Intelligence, you'll also get Live Translation on the cheap. Apple's famed head-tracked Personalized Spatial Audio is also present, as is head gesture support, an excellent Conversation Awareness perk, and volume swipe functionality from the stems.
The bad: Don't have an iPhone? Sadly, I do think you'll need to look elsewhere — you simply cannot get them at their best with an Android phone. Also, it's worth noting that even with an iPhone, you won't get Apple's top-tier heart-rate monitoring, or hearing tests to generate those hearing-aid-like features. For that, you need the latest Pro model. Oh, and this is Apple, so you must forget LDAC or aptX codec support (you knew that).
Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2):
The good: Bose wrote the book on ANC, and while the company intends on charging you for that expertise, I cannot deny that the noise cancellation here is expert. And it isn't just a case of on or off either; you also get "Modes". Essentially, you can combine as much of Bose's excellent ANC or ambient passthrough you want on a slider, along with Immersive Audio (aka spatial audio) to create a head-tracked experience with ANC to boot, to create sonic profiles. If they didn't work, I might say they were surplus to requirements — but the thing is, you're getting truly device-agnostic, head-turning, laugher-inducing joy. Musical strands either present themselves all around you, or slightly in front of your temples, depending on the mode you select. It's really something.
The bad: although this all sounds excellent for Android, there's no LDAC support or aptX on the spec-sheet, so lovers of higher-resolution audio aren't very well served.
Nothing Ear (a) 
The good: When I tested these earbuds I couldn't believe how effective the ANC was for the money, and despite the two years and change since their release, I remain convinced the Ear (a) still offer some of the best active noise quashing at the level. Also, you get LDAC support for better quality audio from supported Android handsets, and even ChatGPT via the stems if you're using a Nothing Phone with the app downloaded. Often at this level you start losing a few perks, but wearer detection is still included, as is a low-lag toggle for gaming, fuss-free multipoint to two devices, a good ear-tip fit test, and a Find My Earbuds feature that issues a (pretty fun, I have to say) rattlesnake-style sound from whichever bud you're trying to locate.
The bad: there's no wireless charging support, unlike all of the other buds in this roundup. Also, you don't get Nothing's flagship hearing tests for personal sound curation — although you do get a three-band EQ tab.
Shokz OpenFit Pro
The good: the headline-grabber here is that Shokz's open earbuds do boast a level of noise "reduction". And make no mistake, this is active noise-cancellation software; Shokz just didn't want to give it that full title because, in a fully open design, there's only so much it can do. That said, I happen to think it's very, very good. You also get Bluetooth 6.1 (the newest version in this list) and wearer detection, multipoint to two devices, five preset EQ modes, and a detailed 10-band custom equalizer in the app. Impressive.
The bad: sure, closed earbuds have a bigger feature set in general (you'll find no spatial audio or hearing tests here) — but the fact that noise reduction exists in a set of open earbuds is impressive.
Technics EAH-AZ100
The good: the headline-grabber here is multipoint to three devices, not two, and if you've never experienced how useful that is, you won't want to go back once you've tried it. Next up is Sidetone, Technics' excellent voice-boosting feature for calls, which allows you to hear your own voice better so that you never have to shout. If taking calls on your buds is the norm, look to these Technics buds. There's wearer detection to pause your music, plus ANC that can either be set to "Adaptive" to automatically adjust, or simply "On" to tweak manually as you move to busier environments. For me, dialling up the ANC to 100% or close to it gives very good results — better than the Nothing option, if not quite as good as AirPods or Bose. Also highly competent is the device- and service-free spatial audio offering, which can be deployed with head-tracking.
The bad: you'll get no hearing tests, hearing aid perks, or scope for nodding to summon your voice assistant here. I don't miss these features, but it's still my job to note their absence.
- Features winner: 
iOS — Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging
Android — Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2)
- ANC winner: 
iOS — AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging
Android — Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2)
- Call-handling and multipoint connectivity winner: Technics EAH-AZ100
Sound quality
Apple AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging
Sonically, Apple's almost-cheapest buds are a triumph for the level, and I write this despite their lack of higher-quality codec support. Okay, they're not for critical listening — those who want neutral, untouched detail should look elsewhere — but for expanse, impact and good old-fashioned fun, they won't let you down. There's space around each musical instrument, underpinned by the kind of layering you'd normally find in much dearer options. If I switch out to the much pricier Technics buds in this list, there's an extra ounce of detail for sure, but given the price difference, that's hardly a fair test. For an energetic listen that has you living in your head, these unassuming little Apple buds really wowed me. And given my "fine, not fantastic" take on AirPods 4's sound, I didn't expect to like them as much as I do.
Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2)
Taking the excellent ANC performance as read (click back to "ANC and features" if you missed that), sonically, the QCUE 2nd Gen are also a treat across the frequencies. Their layered and expansive soundstage allows bass registers ample space to rumble without muddying any of the higher frequencies — and again, this has been achieved without any higher-quality codecs onboard. For detail, they're also very good. Yes, there will always be that old argument about an integrated, neutral hi-fi sound versus fun and excitement (Bose's buds sit in the latter camp) – but for me, the sonic treatment here is splendid. In terms of detail and neutrality, you'll get just a smidgeon more from the aforementioned Technics EAH-AZ100, but for snappy bass impact, the Bose buds take it.
Nothing Ear (a) 
These buds gained five stars overall, so it will come as no surprise to learn that the Ear (a) don't lack in the sonic department for the money — and here you're getting LDAC codec support, too, if your Android can access it. But even when I stream lossy Spotify tracks (or much better Apple Music songs), the Nothing Ear (a) buds handle them very well indeed, with ample texture and space around each musical artifact. Sonically, the Nothing Ear (a) are best described as meaty and arresting. It's not that they lack refinement exactly, just that they prioritize fun and energy over that integrated hi-fi listen. For me, there's so much here to celebrate that I can't pick fault. No, they're not better than buds at nearly three times the price, such as the Technics I mention above, but for the budget category, Nothing has tweaked its recipe to near-perfection here.
Shokz OpenFit Pro
The difference in price between the Shokz OpenFit Pro and the vast majority of their open-ear competitors can be explained by how they sound. Lack of bass is a criticism often dished out to this design type, but I can't hand it out here because it wouldn't be true. The detail at the low end — especially with the EQ preset Bass Boost turned on in the Shokz app — is dynamic and weighty enough to almost make you forget that these are open buds. One note on all this: you can create your own EQ in the app, which does do a good job at establishing a Goldilocks setting specific to you. However, I listened almost exclusively in Bass Boost mode and found it solved any issues concerning a regimented, snappy low end, without getting too fiddly in the app. Is the sound here as good as an in-ear bud? Almost — and make no mistake, it's as close as this type of earbud has ever come to achieving that.
Technics EAH-AZ100
If you've read this far (I appreciate that, by the way), you'll know that these buds have become a reference set for me — and with good reason. I cannot hand the sound quality win here to another set of buds. We can have the value debate below, but for detailed, neutral, integrated audio quality despite the cost, these earbuds win hands-down. The Technics EAH-AZ100 are never less than "very good indeed", no matter whether they’re dealing with a 16bit/44.1kHz FLAC file via AAC or a 24bit/96kHz file using LDAC. They're respectably dynamic without ever straying too far into fun-and-frivolous territory. Technics wants to convey every last detail in your tracks with these flagship earbuds and, my goodness, you're getting some of the best sound a Bluetooth transmission can achieve here.
- Sound quality winner: Technics EAH-AZ100
Overall winner (ahead of Black Friday deals)
Selecting one winner is an incredibly difficult task, especially given the price differences in this roundup. But while I can't give you a simple "it's these earbuds, no question" answer, I can give you a few concrete answers to work with.
My quick-as-I-can-make-it verdict is this: for excellent audio above all else, you go for the Technics EAH-AZ100 — and thanks to their January 2025 launch date, they'll be ripe for a few discounts over Black Friday.
The Technics EAH-AZ100 are my top pick for Black Friday and the set I use every day. And I've just seen them dip to $199 in the US (was $299) as long as the silver finish suits, or £179 in the UK (was £259) whichever finish you prefer — a new lowest-seen price and one I've no hesitation recommending!
Not in these regions? Scroll down to see the best prices where you are
Does the silver finish work for you? Good, because this $100-off deal is by far the cheapest these earbuds have ever dropped to (their lowest-seen price was hovering around $210 until now), and for this money the AZ100 are so much better than any rival at the level. These January 2025-issue beauties are still among the only buds to offer multipoint to three devices simultaneously, plus there's Technics' excellent sidetone tech for hearing your own voice in calls. You're getting some of the most neutral and detailed audio in an even smaller, even more premium-feel design. Highly recommended.
A new lowest-seen price! The excellent EAH-AZ80 that came before this model basically tore up the rule book on sound quality and features in wireless earbuds – and the AZ100 are even better. Released in January 2025, these little beauties are still among the only earbuds to offer multipoint to three devices simultaneously, plus excellent sidetone tech for hearing your own voice in calls, as well as some of the most neutral and detailed audio in an even smaller, even more premium-feel design. Oh, and this deal is £10 cheaper than our price trackers have ever seen. A no-brainer if your budget will stretch to them.
Hold on just a minute, though! if affordable ANC and/or Spatial Audio performance is your top priority, it has to be the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging — provided you have an iPhone. Okay, they're the newest buds in this list thanks to a September 2026 launch date, but we often see a few minor discounts across Apple's more entry-level buds in big sales events.
No iPhone but want the best ANC? Go for the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2), which may also see some bigger discounts owing to their June 2025 launch date. Yes, Bose products rarely see discounts — but Black Friday isn't like any other sales event. They have briefly dipped to $229 and £199 before now (regular prices $299 / £299), so those are the figures to look for.
Looking for the cheapest bargain around that doesn't mean sacrificing on features or sound? I'd look to the Nothing Ear (a). They have actually been superseded twice, if you count the flagship Ear (3) set as well as the (3a), but their popularity endures for the plethora of features they offer at budget money — and I wouldn't be surprised if they dip to a new silly-low asking fee this Black Friday. Remember, they were only $99 / £99 to start with, and have seen a fair few discounts since then, so anything approaching 50% off those prices (it has happened before!) would be an easy recommendation.
And I'm still not done! If you've been looking just a little at open earbuds this Black Friday, well done you. The Shokz OpenFit Pro should emphatically be on your list. They arrived in January, and while we haven't seen anything in the way of price cuts on them yet, if they start seeing discounts then I'd recommend them without reservation.

Becky became Audio Editor at TechRadar in 2024, but joined the team in 2022 as Senior Staff Writer, focusing on all things hi-fi. Before this, she spent three years at What Hi-Fi? testing and reviewing everything from wallet-friendly wireless earbuds to huge high-end sound systems. Prior to gaining her MA in Journalism in 2018, Becky freelanced as an arts critic alongside a 22-year career as a professional dancer and aerialist – any love of dance starts with a love of music. Becky has previously contributed to Stuff, FourFourTwo and The Stage. When not writing, she can still be found throwing shapes in a dance studio, these days with varying degrees of success.

articles.title: FritzOS 8.50 und 8.51 kommen auf weitere Fritzboxen: Was die Updates bringen
articles.text:
FritzOS 8.50 und 8.51: Was das Fritzbox-Update bringt
Schon seit geraumer Zeit warten Fritzbox-User:innen auf das große Update FritzOS 8.50. Hersteller Fritz hatte erste Neuerungen zunächst mit der Labor-Version 8.40 testen lassen. Jetzt ist die Beta-Phase für erste Fritz-Router vorbei und die finale Version von FritzOS 8.50 wird in immer größeren Schritten für einzelne Geräte freigegeben.
Welche Fritzboxen bekommen FritzOS 8.50 und 8.51 jetzt?
Die Liste der Fritzboxen, die jetzt mit der Release-Version FritzOS 8.50 ausgestattet werden, ist mittlerweile schon stark angewachsen. Unter den Kandidaten befinden sich auch Router und Repeater, die direkt ein Update auf die Version FritzOS 8.51 erhalten. Am Funktionsumfang ändert sich dadurch nichts. Der Hersteller verweist bei den Ankündigungen auf X stets auf die Übersichtsseite von FritzOS 8.50.
In den kommenden Wochen und Monaten dürfte Fritz noch mehr Modelle für die Aktualisierung freigeben. Wer nicht so lange warten möchte, kann wie erwähnt bei manchen Modellen das Labor-Update zu FritzOS 8.40 installieren, das erste Funktionen von FritzOS 8.50 mit sich bringt. Beachte allerdings, dass es sich um Testversionen des Updates handelt, die noch Probleme bereiten können. Diese Modelle dürfen schon die finale Version von FritzOS 8.50 laden:
- Fritzbox DSL/Fiber 7-90 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 7530 AX
- Fritzbox 7690
- Fritzbox 7682 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 7630 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 7632 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbx 6690 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 6690 Pro (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 6670 Cable (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 6660 Cable (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 5630
- Fritzbox 5690
- Fritzbox 5690 XGS (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 4690 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 4630 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 4050 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritz Repeater 3000 AX (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritz Repeater 6000 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritz Mesh Set 4200 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
Was steckt in FritzOS 8.50?
Die größte Neuerung von FritzOS 8.50 ist ein DNS-Filter. Dadurch kannst du Werbeeinblendungen auf einer Vielzahl von Geräten im Netzwerk einfach ausblenden. Das gilt etwa für Smartphones, Tablets und verbundene Smart-TVs. Daneben bietet die Myfritz-App in Verbindung mit FritzOS 8.50 einen Smart Check. Darüber wird dir in der App der Status deiner Fritzbox und deines gesamten Netzwerks angezeigt. Die App gibt dir zusätzlich Empfehlungen, mit denen du dein Heimnetz verbessern kannst.
Ferner integriert Fritz mit FritzOS 8.50 eine automatische Priorisierung, die Echtzeitverbindungen wie Videoanrufe vor alle anderen Verbindungen stellt. Dadurch wird die nötige Bandbreite für Meetings und Co. freigegeben, falls andere Verbindungen die Leitung belasten. Für alle Smarthome-User:innen integriert FritzOS 8.50 vordefinierte Routinen wie beim Verlassen des Hauses. Bei selbsterstellten Routinen lassen sich künftig auch mehrere Auslöser festlegen und das Geofencing wurde verbessert.
Mit den Fritz Repeatern 3000 AX 6000 sind erstmals zwei WLAN-Verstärker unter den Update-Kandidaten. Anders als die zahlreichen Router profitieren die Gadgets unter anderem laut Winfuture jedoch nicht von neuen Funktionen. Demnach soll das Update vor allem Stabilitätsverbesserungen und Optimierungen beim Speicherbedarf liefern. Außerdem werde die Zusammenarbeit mit Amazon-Geräten und die WLAN-Stabilität beim Wechsel der Verbindungseinstellungen verbessert.

articles.title: Design, data, delight: how to get your message across at tech business exhibitions
articles.text:
Design, data, delight: how to get your message across at tech business exhibitions
In this photo essay from BTS at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre, we showcase highlights from the exhibition halls along with insights for innovators.
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) wrapped up its 29th annual edition this week at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre. See our BTS exhibition showcases from earlier editions in 2025 and 2024, and YourStory’s TechSparks exhibitors from 2026 and 2025.
Such leading global exhibitions bring together investors, business owners, industry experts, government, and academia. Innovators can present their ideas and attract financial support to develop their inventions, as well as learn how to improve their presentation, marketing and communication skills.
Exhibitions allow startups to assess their competition and potential partners, understand market trends, and identify opportunities to make their solutions better. Furthermore, displaying innovative solutions can motivate students, aspiring entrepreneurs, researchers, and other visitors to think creatively and develop their own ideas.
In this photo essay, we feature the BTS startups and tech firms Cloud Victor, WorkSuite, DPDPsuites.AI, Bramma, AIsphere, Inbound, Umber, DialGrid, SuperAgent, NuWare AI, Tyrios, IT Idol, and others. We also showcase booths and pavilions of other states such as Keralam, incubators (Jain LaunchPad, K-Heal), and countries like Germany and Denmark.
CloudVictor is a cloud technology and infrastructure management company specialising in helping businesses optimise, secure and scale their Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. It aims to help organisations reduce cloud expenditure, improve infrastructure performance, and strengthen security while ensuring business continuity.
WorkSuite is an integrated enterprise management platform by MJC GlobalTech, designed to bring multiple business functions together within a unified digital ecosystem. The platform incorporates AI-powered capabilities such as lead qualification, candidate screening, automated interviews, and workflow management.
DPDP Suites is an AI-powered data privacy and regulatory compliance platform developed to help Indian organisations comply with the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023. One of its key features is an AI-powered agent which acts as a privacy assistant by identifying compliance gaps, assessing risks, and providing actionable insights.
Bramma is an AI-powered workplace intelligence solution developed by Glymph Technologies. It combines specialised room hardware, multilingual speech recognition and AI to interpret conversations taking place in meeting rooms and workplaces.
AIESPHERE is an AI-powered CareerTech platform to support professionals in navigating their career journeys. The platform focuses on helping individuals identify suitable career opportunities, understand emerging industry requirements, develop relevant skills, and explore global employment prospects by leveraging AI and automation.
Umber is a technology company offering Digital Asset as a Service (DAaaS), an infrastructure solution designed to simplify the management and delivery of digital assets across different environments. By providing centralised asset management and controlled content delivery, Umber aims to reduce technical complexity and make digital content management more reliable.
DialGrid is an AI-driven business communication platform that helps organisations manage and automate customer interactions through voice, chat and messaging solutions. Its AI capabilities can improve response times, reduce customer service workloads and create more personalised customer experiences. DialGrid is particularly relevant to call centres and customer support teams.
NuWare Systems helps businesses modernise their technology infrastructure and accelerate digital transformation. Its experience across industries such as banking, financial services, retail, and healthcare positions it as a partner for organisations looking to adopt AI at an enterprise level.
TYRIOS is an integrated enterprise software platform developed by Repalogic, part of the Germany-headquartered Deepbyte Technology group. It helps businesses manage customer relationships, business operations, marketing activities, and organisational data through a modular digital platform.
IT IDOL Technologies is a CMMI Level 5-certified custom software company that helps startups and enterprises scale their digital products. By combining software engineering expertise with AI-driven solutions and cloud technologies, it helps organisations automate processes, improve business performance and build scalable digital products.
As shown in this photo essay, innovators can make an impression (and an impact) with attractive and innovative booth design. An eye-catching layout, creative branding, and attractive lighting help here, with clear displays of logo and key messages.
Live demonstrations and interactive experiences help showcase real-world applications. Interactive displays, VR/AR experiences, or hands-on activities enable visitors to experience the innovation rather than just read about it.
Young innovators need to master the communication of innovation by explaining key problems addressed, uniqueness and benefits of their solutions. Simple language, visual infographics and concise presentations go a long way here.
Having an engaging and knowledgeable team at the booth or pavilion is important, for welcoming questions and catalysing meaningful conversations. They need to be prepared to explain technical details, business potential and future possibilities.
Beyond the exhibition, exhibitors need to strengthen their networking and follow-up opportunities via brochures, business cards and QR codes. They should collect visitor enquiries and potential collaboration leads, and follow up with interested visitors after the exhibition.
As seen in this photo essay, it is not just exhibitors who compete with one another, but large exhibitions themselves who compete with other events across the country and overseas. BTS has completed 29 editions, but there are other large tech business conferences in India and abroad.
To differentiate itself, BTS has created a unique theme and identity. It develops a distinctive annual theme that reflects the exhibition's vision and purpose. It includes experiential demonstrations, breakthrough technologies, real-world solutions, and innovation challenges.
There are dedicated zones where visitors can experience emerging technologies. Bringing together diverse stakeholders creates meaningful collaborations. Facilitating structured B2B meetings and investor–innovator interactions helps create opportunities for partnerships, technology transfers, and joint ventures. Flagship programmes, startup pitch competitions, and hackathons take the momentum to the next level.
Memorable visitor experiences are strengthened by attractive and thematic art installations, local cultural performances, and messages on environmental sustainability that promote selfies and social media buzz. Finally, in this day and age, AI-powered visitor recommendations, digital navigation, and smart registration are indispensable in creating curated visitor journeys.
Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?
(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at BTS 2026.)

articles.title: Une étoile morte située à plus de 5 000 années-lumière envoie un mystérieux signal radio toutes les huit minutes en tournant autour d’une étoile semblable au Soleil
articles.text:
Une étoile morte située à plus de 5 000 années-lumière envoie un mystérieux signal radio toutes les huit minutes en tournant autour d’une étoile semblable au Soleil
Des astronomes australiens ont identifié l'origine d'un mystérieux signal radio qui se répète toutes les huit minutes à plus de 5 000 années-lumière de la Terre. Les impulsions viennent d'une étoile morte qui tourne autour d'un astre semblable au Soleil. Un duo pareil n'avait jamais été associé à ce type d'émissions.
C'est le 12 novembre que la revue Nature Astronomy a publié l'étude de l'ICRAR, un centre de radioastronomie d'Australie-Occidentale. Le signal provient du système GPM J071507-114153, situé dans notre galaxie. L'étoile morte est une naine blanche, le cœur très dense qui subsiste quand un astre a épuisé son combustible. Sa compagne est une étoile de type G, comme le Soleil.
Une naine blanche qui tourne sur elle-même en 7,9 minutes
Les impulsions radio reviennent toutes les 7,9 minutes, au rythme de la rotation de la naine blanche sur elle-même. En revanche, elle met 1,3 jour à faire le tour de sa compagne, soit environ 31 heures. La fenêtre de détection dépend de l'alignement des deux astres et ne dure qu'environ six heures par orbite.
Ce système appartient aux transitoires radio à longue période, des sources aux impulsions espacées de quelques minutes ou heures. C'est en 2021 que l'ICRAR a repéré la première et les chercheurs en connaissent aujourd'hui une douzaine. Certaines associent une naine blanche à une naine rouge, une petite étoile froide. Mais les astronomes ignoraient laquelle des deux étoiles émettait les ondes.
Le radiotélescope australien Murchison Widefield Array a capté le signal lors d'un relevé de la Voie lactée. Le réseau sud-africain MeerKAT a ensuite localisé précisément la source et l'observatoire Keck à Hawaï a confirmé la présence de l'étoile de type G.
Les chercheurs ont suivi la naine blanche autour de sa compagne grâce à ces impulsions. Selon sa position, chaque signal arrive jusqu'à quatre secondes plus tôt ou plus tard car la distance jusqu'à la Terre varie. Ce décalage a permis de mesurer la taille de l'orbite.
Des tempêtes magnétiques détectées sur la compagne de l'étoile morte
"C'est la première fois que les impulsions sont assez nettes pour voir la naine blanche se déplacer", a expliqué Sam McSweeney, auteur principal de l'étude. Selon lui, ces pulsations proviennent d'une zone très proche de l'étoile morte, voire de l'astre lui-même.
La naine blanche est aussi passée derrière une région au champ magnétique intense, sans doute une protubérance de plasma à la surface de sa compagne. L'équipe a également repéré des éruptions comparables à celles qui provoquent les aurores sur Terre. "C'est incroyable de pouvoir détecter les tempêtes d'une étoile à plus de 5 000 années-lumière grâce aux ondes radio", a souligné Natasha Hurley-Walker, co-autrice de l'étude.
Sam McSweeney, aujourd'hui scientifique à l'observatoire SKA, s'attend à découvrir d'autres systèmes similaires avec les radiotélescopes SKA en construction en Australie et en Afrique du Sud.

articles.title: El Reino Unido escanea un volcán del Caribe con terremotos y encuentra una sopa de metales críticos a dos kilómetros bajo tierra
articles.text:
En el Caribe está la isla Montserrat y allí hay un volcán llamado Soufrière Hills. Pues bien, bajo ese volcán hay algo que podría ser un depósito de fluidos calientes cargados de metales. ¿Podría? Sí, porque a ciencia cierta, no lo sabemos: nadie lo ha perforado y por supuesto, tampoco lo ha tocado. La Universidad de Oxford lo ha "visto" analizando terremotos.
El hallazgo. El equipo de investigación ha reconstruido una imagen en 3D del interior del volcán a partir de cómo viajan las ondas P y S de los terremotos. Estas se propagan a diferente velocidad en función del material que atraviesan. Así encontraron un potencial tesoro: un reservorio de magma que parece rico en metales. Tiene una anchura de 1-1,5 kilómetros y está a unos dos kilómetros de profundidad.
Esa salmuera caliente concentrada en sales y con capacidad para transportar metales es, según el equipo, un ejemplo de depósito de material en proceso de formación, es decir, antes de que los materiales se vuelvan sólidos y se conviertan en yacimientos como los que se explotan después.
Por qué importa. Como explica el equipo, "los volcanes no solo son fuentes de energía geotérmica, sino que también contienen metales necesarios para las tecnologías modernas y la transición de carbono". Hablamos de metales críticos necesarios para paneles solares, aerogeneradores o los vehículos eléctricos, y bajo los volcanes pueden concentrarse en salmueras magmáticas.
El principal problema es encontrarlos: perforar cerca de un volcán activo es caro y peligroso. Ahí es donde esta investigación es clave: la imagen sísmica pasiva ofrece resolución suficiente para detectarlos minimizando los riesgos.
La búsqueda del tesoro. Oxford lleva años con esta idea entre ceja y ceja: ya en 2021 el mismo grupo propuso que la salmuera atrapada bajo volcanes es un "mineral líquido" con metales como oro, cobre y litio. De hecho, en Montserrat un sondeo previo ya había encontrado restos de estos fluidos en cristales de cuarzo a 1.480 metros a partir de una muestra de testigo, pero ahora los han visto a mayor escala y sin necesidad de perforar nada. Para descubrirlo, esta vez han empleado datos de 1.039 sismos registrados entre 1996 y 2007 por el Observatorio Vulcanológico de Montserrat.
Las incógnitas. La sísmica ha detectado que hay algo, pero no mide cuánto metal hay, de qué tipo y en qué proporciones: para eso hacen falta otras técnicas e idealmente, perforar. Por otro lado, que el volcán tenga actividad hace que cualquier extracción y las infraestructuras montadas para tal fin, sean arriesgadas. Por eso, a día de hoy este estudio tiene más interés científico por la técnica en sí que económico: tal y como está todo, en la actualidad esa sopa de metales difícilmente se va a poder aprovechar.

articles.title: Cómo preparar tu PS5 y Xbox para descargar GTA 6 a la mayor velocidad
articles.text:
GTA 6 ya está disponible, pero su descarga puede tomar desde menos de una hora hasta casi dos días, según la velocidad y estabilidad de internet. El juego ocupa alrededor de 212 GB, por lo que diferentes guías advierten que el tiempo estimado de descarga presupone una conexión constante, sin interrupciones ni otros equipos saturando la red.
Antes de comenzar, revisa cuánto espacio libre tiene la consola -ya sea PS5 o Xbox- y compara ese dato con el tamaño que aparece en la tienda digital. Si falta espacio, borra juegos que ya no uses, contenido descargable o capturas antiguas. Deja margen para que la consola complete la instalación y descargue posibles actualizaciones.
Conecta la consola directamente al router
La manera más estable de descargar GTA 6 será conectar la PS5 o Xbox Series X|S al router con un cable Ethernet. La conexión por cable reduce las interferencias que pueden afectar al wifi y ayuda a mantener una velocidad más constante durante una descarga tan grande.
Si no tienes un cable a mano y usarás wifi, acerca la consola al router. Procura que el equipo esté al descubierto, sin muebles que bloqueen la señal. Si tu router ofrece redes de 2,4 GHz y 5 GHz, la banda de 5 GHz puede ser más rápida a corta distancia, aunque su señal atraviesa peor las paredes.
Reduce el uso de internet en casa
La velocidad de descarga puede disminuir cuando varios dispositivos comparten la conexión. Mientras el juego se descarga, pausa las películas en streaming, las descargas de archivos y las actualizaciones en otros equipos. Si otras personas necesitan internet, elegir un momento de menor actividad —por ejemplo, durante la noche— puede ayudar.
También conviene evitar ejecutar otros juegos o aplicaciones que usen la red en la consola. Revisa que no haya actualizaciones pendientes del sistema esperando instalarse, pues podrían interrumpir o ralentizar la descarga de GTA 6.
Cuánto puede tardar la descarga
Diferentes guías calculan que descargar 212 GB tomaría cerca de 56 minutos con una conexión de 500 Mbps, poco más de tres horas con 150 Mbps y unas seis horas y 17 minutos con 75 Mbps. Con 30 Mbps, el cálculo sube a casi 16 horas; con 10 Mbps, se acerca a dos días.
Son estimaciones teóricas, no una promesa sobre cuánto tardará en tu consola. La velocidad contratada no siempre coincide con la que recibe el dispositivo: la distancia al router, la congestión de la red y la actividad de otros equipos pueden prolongar el proceso. La consola también puede descargar más despacio en algunos momentos, aunque la conexión parezca rápida.
Recuerda que Mbps significa megabits por segundo. No es lo mismo que MB/s, que significa megabytes por segundo; por eso, el número que muestra una prueba de velocidad puede diferir del que aparece en la pantalla de descarga.
Comprueba el avance antes de volver a jugar
Cuando inicies la descarga, mira el tiempo estimado en la consola y comprueba que avance con regularidad. Si se detiene o baja mucho la velocidad, pausa y reanuda la descarga, verifica la conexión y reinicia el router si fuera necesario. Mantener la consola y el juego actualizados también ayudará a evitar interrupciones por instalaciones pendientes.
La recomendación final es liberar espacio, usar Ethernet cuando puedas, fortalecer la señal wifi si no tienes cable y reducir el tráfico de otros dispositivos. Estas medidas no harán que una conexión lenta alcance la velocidad de una rápida, pero pueden evitar pérdidas de rendimiento mientras PS5 o Xbox descarga los más de 200 GB del juego.

articles.title: Trump says reported FBI database hack is ‘not good’ | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press.
The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.
A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”
President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”
In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack.

articles.title: New semi-autonomous 911 drones will cover nearly all of Knoxville in 90 seconds or less — 12 Skydio docks launch within seconds, purge video after 15 days
articles.text:
New semi-autonomous 911 drones will reach nearly all of Knoxville in 90 seconds or less — 12 Skydio docks launch within seconds, purge video after 15 days
Launched as part of the Drone as First Responder program, the drones can be deployed within seconds of a 911 call being received.
The Knoxville Police Department has announced its “Drone as First Responder” program, or DFR, with semi-autonomous drones set to be launched from 12 docks located around the city. The docks will allow drones to be dispatched within seconds of a 911 call being received, and they will be able to reach nearly any area of the city within just 90 seconds, according to a page on the police department's website. It's hoped that the drones will be able to reduce the risk to the community as well as police officers, while providing real-time situational awareness during "rapidly evolving events."
While the police department hasn't confirmed which drones will be used, we do know that they will be launched from Skydio docks located at city-owned facilities. It's expected that the drones will, in some cases, reach the scene more quickly than the police officer they are supposed to accompany. This should give officers vital information related to the scene that they are about to attend.
While drones won't be dispatched to all 911 calls, the department says that they will be sent in response to 911 calls in which aerial coverage may be of use to the overall response. That includes enhancing the safety of the officers attending as well as public safety.
The new drones will no doubt raise concerns about privacy. The department says that they will not be used for surveillance, pointing out that department policy and state law prohibit the drones from being used for random patrols or surveillance. They also don't possess any kind of facial recognition or license plate reader technologies. While the drones will, of course, capture video, the department's FAQ page notes that any recorded footage will be purged after 15 days. That is, unless it is retained as evidence for use in an ongoing criminal investigation or prosecution.
Knoxville isn't the first to turn to drones in this way. Several cities were reportedly experimenting with using Flock's own DFR system last month. Companies have also been advertising Starlink-connected first responder drones for some time.
