articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI makes nearly $4 billion on day one, biggest launch in entertainment history
articles.text:
Bottom line: GTA VI was always expected to be a blockbuster, but Take-Two's first-day numbers show just how far past a typical hit the universally praised open-world crime simulator has gone. The launch was big enough to rewrite the entertainment record books and, apparently, to empty a fair number of offices and classrooms. Other reports point to skyrocketing work and school absences, surprising no one.
Take-Two has confirmed that day-one retail sales of Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI reached an estimated $3.79 billion, cementing the highly anticipated game's status as the most successful launch in any entertainment medium. GTA VI also set a new record for pre-orders across all platforms, reaching 32.5 million.
Circana's Player Engagement Tracker shows that on the game's November 19 launch day, 61% of active US PlayStation 5 owners and 56% of active Xbox owners worldwide played GTA VI. PS5 players averaged 513 minutes (8 hours and 33 minutes), while Xbox players averaged 8 hours and 14 minutes. GTA VI players still made time for the usual chart-toppers in the run-up to launch, including Fortnite, Call of Duty, GTA V, Roblox, and NBA 2K27.
Reports also confirmed an expected spike in sick leave from work and school. Provisional attendance data from school management firm Arbor suggests roughly 35,000 more secondary school pupils were absent on launch day than earlier in the week. Meanwhile, BrightHR reported a 56% increase in sickness absence across the UK on November 19 compared to the previous Thursday. Another firm, Deel, reported a 21% jump in requests for the day off compared to the same day last year.
Pre-loads for the game, which weighs in at about 212GB on PS5 and 209GB on Xbox, also broke internet bandwidth records for several providers. On November 18, GTA VI pushed Virgin Media O2's evening traffic 9.4% above the record set during pre-loading a week earlier, while the game accounted for up to 24% of all Comcast traffic at peak. BT and EE networks also reported new home broadband peak records the same day.
GTA VI earned a 99 Metacritic score, to tie the original 1998 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game ever, albeit across a far larger pool of reviews. IGN, The Guardian, GameSpot, Eurogamer, and other outlets awarded GTA VI a perfect score for its immersive world-building and engaging storyline.
With the game now out on consoles, many likely await the PC version, which Rockstar has not formally announced. Prior Rockstar games have taken more than a year to transition from consoles to PC, but rumors suggest GTA VI could reach PC as soon as the first quarter of 2027. Some will also certainly try to vibe-code a PC port before then, and modders have already found a workaround to apply DLSS to the console versions' video output.

articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
- November 13, 2026
- Source:
- Princeton University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Princeton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- John Mark P. Martirez. A Chemist’sGuide to Solid-State Qubits: DiamondColor Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules. ACS Central Science, 2026; 12 (10): 1578 DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548

articles.title: Style meets serious versatility with the The Smeg MOC02 Combi Microwave — a compact four-in-one appliance that grills, bakes, and air fries to perfection
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Smeg MOC02 looks great on the countertop, and packs a capable grill, fan oven and air fryer into a compact body. Setup was easy, the grill impressed me and the air fryer impressed my son, but some interface icons were confusing and the snug cavity makes turning food fiddly. At £449.95 (about $590 / AU$880) it's not cheap, but it offers more value for money than its price suggests. Especially when you factor in all of the cooking modes, presets and performance.
Reasons to buy
- + Smart, compact countertop design
- + Excellent grill performance
- + Versatile modes and programmable stages
Reasons to avoid
- - Some icons are hard to decipher
- - Tight cavity makes turning food fiddly
- - Expensive if you don't use all of its functions
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Smeg MOC02: 30-second review
The Smeg MOC02 looks every bit a Smeg appliance, with rounded corners, a band of color around the door and an aluminum control panel. I tested the Storm Blue version and it looked great on my countertop.
Of course, at £449.95, it needs to do more than look good and for the most part, it succeeds. There's a microwave, grill, fan oven and air fryer inside, a series of combination modes that let you double up the functions, plus defrost and keep warm settings. And that's before the 25 automatic presets.
Getting started is relatively easy, even if some of the icons aren't obvious and there’s also a little more waiting around than I expected. After preheating, the Smeg waits for a press of the dial to start cooking, and my microwave-to-air-fry sequence needed another press between stages. The presets and multi-step options help with choosing settings, but you’ll still need to stay nearby and check the food.
Performance-wise, the air fryer made a good first impression. My eight-year-old declared the fish fingers the "best he’d ever had", and breaded chicken bites came out evenly browned with juicy meat inside. The grill was another highlight, making quick work of melting cheese and browning toppings, although some breadcrumbs on my mac and cheese burned before others. I preferred the microwave and oven combination for a jacket potato, while the cake preset left a runny middle that needed another five minutes on the oven setting.
The compact size suited my kitchen but it did mean turning food on the rack or air-fry plate was fiddly, and the ventilation clearances mean it needs more space than its dimensions suggest. If you’ll regularly use its range of cooking modes, there’s plenty here to justify giving the MOC02 a spot on your counter. If you mainly reheat leftovers, much of what you’re paying for will go unused, but at least it will look the part.
Smeg MOC02: price and availability
- Price: £449.95 (about $590 / AU$880)
- Available in blue, white, black and green
- The Smeg MOC02 isn't yet sold in the US or Australia
The Smeg MOC02 costs £449.95 in the UK. It's sold in White, Black, Emerald Green and Storm Blue and is available from Smeg directly, AO and Amazon. That works out at about $590 / AU$880, thought it's not currently sold in the US or Australia.
At first glance, the Smeg looks expensive for a combi microwave. It’s about £90 more than the £359.99 Ninja Crispi Microwave, £50 more than the Sage Combi Wave 3 in 1, and roughly three times the price of the £149 IKEA GÅTEBO.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
That said, when you consider what you get for that extra money, the Smeg is better value. For starters, the Ninja can microwave, air fry and bake but its FusionCrisp mode follows a sequence, whereas the Smeg gives you more choice over which modes you use together.
Ninja lists 14 functions, but that figure includes presets within its three modes. Smeg, instead, has six distinct functions, three combined modes for each recipe, plus 25 automatic programs, making the headline numbers a tad misleading.
Compared to the Sage, the Smeg offers more automatic cooking programs. Compared to IKEA's model, the Smeg lets you queue up tasks and has a dedicated Keep Warm setting. All of which expands the Smeg's capabilities considerably.
Of course, if you mostly reheat leftovers or defrost food, a basic microwave will do those jobs for less but if you'll regularly switch between reheating, grilling, baking and air frying and want a machine to handle it all, the Smeg stands out.
Value for money: 4/5
Smeg MOC02: specifications
| Model tested | MOC02SBMUK, Storm Blue | 
| Installation | Freestanding countertop | 
| Capacity | 27 liters | 
| Dimensions (W × D × H) | 19.87 × 16.73 × 12.01 inches | 
| Turntable | 11.02 inches | 
| Microwave output | 900 W | 
| Cooking functions | Microwave, grill, fan oven, air fry, defrost, keep warm, microwave + grill, microwave + fan oven, and fan oven + grill | 
| Automatic programmes | 25 | 
| Controls | Color LCD, dial and buttons | 
| Accessories | Air-fry basket, crisp pan and grill rack | 
Smeg MOC02: design
- Storm Blue finish, brushed aluminum controls and a soft-close door
- Compact enough to fit on my worktop
- Easy to set up, although some cooking icons and modes take getting used to
If you've ever owned, or seen a Smeg appliance in real life, you'll know they have a distinctive design, and the MOC02 is no exception. Even if the Smeg logo wasn't emblazoned across the front, I’d still recognize the rounded corners, icon design and the band of color around the door.
I tested the Storm Blue version, which has a dark glass window and a strip of brushed aluminum down one side. That strip holds the colored LCD display above three buttons and a round dial. These buttons include:
- Chef’s hat: This button opens the automatic programs menu. You then use the dial to cycle between meat and poultry, fish and shellfish, vegetables, cakes and sweets, and bread, pizza and cereals
- Plus: This is used to line up multiple cooking modes
- Curved arrow: This works like a back button on a browser.
Across the five categories are 25 presets, numbered P01 to P25, covering everything from roast chicken and frozen fish fingers to jacket potatoes, mug cakes and reheating pizza.
| Chef Menu automatic programmes |  | 
|---|---|
| Preset | Program | 
| P01 | Meat | 
| P02 | Chicken | 
| P03 | Bacon | 
| P04 | Roast chicken | 
| P05 | Chicken wings | 
| P06 | Chicken nuggets | 
| P07 | Thick fish fillets | 
| P08 | Thin fish fillets | 
| P09 | Prawns | 
| P10 | Frozen fish fingers | 
| P11 | Potatoes | 
| P12 | Hard vegetables | 
| P13 | Soft vegetables | 
| P14 | Frozen vegetables | 
| P15 | Frozen chips | 
| P16 | Popcorn | 
| P17 | Melting butter or soft cheese | 
| P18 | Mug cake | 
| P19 | Cake | 
| P20 | Muffins | 
| P21 | Toast | 
| P22 | Rice | 
| P23 | Reheating pizza | 
| P24 | Frozen pizza | 
| P25 | Lasagna or pasta bake | 
The whole unit is surprisingly compact given the range of features it offers. I found a spot for it in the corner of my worktop which kept it out of the way, but also gave me the 11.8-inch clearance needed overhead, and the 7.9-inch gap between the oven and my walls. The door opens to the left, so you'll also need to leave yourself enough room to swing it open and lift a dish straight out.
There's then a glass turntable in the bottom and Smeg includes a raised grill rack, crisp plate and round, shallow air-fry plate in the box. The air-fry plate has holes in it to let hot air reach the food, and the rack lifts your dishes closer to the grill.
In terms of space, I could easily fit a small chicken inside. There's also enough room, height-wise, for a dish on the raised rack. How much room you have to work with though, depends on where the food sits. With the rack or air-fry plate, I found it a bit fiddly to reach in and turn food halfway through cooking. With a pull-out air fryer, I can put the basket down and get at the food from above. Here I was reaching through into a fairly snug — not to mention hot — space.
If you tend to cook in a wide rectangular dish that won't fit as the turntable rotates, you can turn the rotation off in the settings.
Getting started was easy and I soon got the hang of the controls. I turned the dial to pick a mode, used the back button if I went past what I wanted, and pressed the little chef’s hat to open the automatic program.
When I used the cake preset, I could see the program number, weight and time left on the display. Air frying took me longer to find. The icon isn't instantly recognizable and although I could work it out, by process of elimination, I ended up looking it up in the manual to make sure.
The plus button then does three things, depending on when you press it. Before you start cooking, it lets you line up a second mode with its own settings, so you can set both stages in advance. This has its pros and cons, which I detail more in the Performance section.
Once the Smeg is running, pressing the button adds 30 seconds to the time. And if the display is showing the clock, the same plus button starts the microwave at full power, which is handy when you just want to warm something up quickly.
While trying to figure out what each of the icons and presets were, I tried scanning the QR code inside the door, which is a shortcut to the My Smeg Assistant. This is Smeg's AI chatbot. However, when I asked it cooking questions, it often didn’t understand what I was asking. It was better at helping me troubleshoot general appliance problems but not that useful all things considered.
Smeg recommends washing the grill rack, air-fry plate and crisp plate by hand in warm soapy water with a soft sponge or cloth. If you’re using the air fryer a lot, that means washing up the plate after cooking and checking the glass turntable for any crumbs or drips that have fallen through. Smeg also recommends wiping out the cavity once it’s cool, before splashes have a chance to dry on.
Design: 4/5
Smeg MOC02: Performance
- The grill was quick, although mac and cheese browned unevenly
- Air fry worked well for frozen food but I preferred the oven for a jacket potato
- The cake preset needed extra time
For an appliance with such a wide range of features, it can be overwhelming knowing where to start, but as fish fingers are my eight-year-old's favorite food – much to my dismay — the air fryer function was first up.
I spread them out in a single layer in the shallow plate and selected the P10 — frozen fish fingers — preset. They cooked well, with a crispy outer shell and a fluffy inside. Frozen fish fingers have a habit of falling apart easily or being soggy when cooked, but my son exclaimed they were the "best fish fingers" he'd ever had. High praise indeed for Smeg. This is the sort of quick freezer dinner I’d use the MOC02 for regularly, especially when I only need a small batch.
I also used the air fryer for some breaded chicken bites. They cooked evenly across the basket, with a browned coating and juicy meat inside. I was pleased with the balance, because getting enough color on breaded chicken can mean leaving it in long enough for the meat to dry out.
As I mentioned in the Design section, turning both the fish fingers and chicken bites was fiddly. I had to work through the door, with less space to angle my tongs around the plate or remove the plate completely. This isn't enough to put me off, but it was noticeable.
Next up was a jacket potato, which let me try the microwave and air fryer together using the plus button feature. I set the microwave stage first, then lined up air fry to finish and crisp up the skin. Entering both stages before starting was simp[le and quick, and I assumed that would be the last input it needed from me.
Instead, the Smeg beeped when the microwave stage finished and didn't start the air fryer stage until I'd pressed the dial. On the plus side, this gave me a chance to get the potato ready for the next part — adding oil, salt and wrapping it in tin foil — but it also meant I needed to stay within earshot.
If you’ve set it going while you do something in another room, it’s easy to imagine coming back to find it still waiting to start the second stage. The finished potato was not as crispy as I'd have liked and was more squishy than fluffy on the inside.
I also tried the microwave + oven setting for a jacket potato and much preferred how it turned out. The skin was crispier and browned in places and the potato held its shape more. This is the combination I’d choose to cook a potato next time.
The grill was my favorite of the modes I tried and it feels like the feature that really sets the Smeg model apart from the pack. After using the oven setting to cook a lasagna on the raised rack, I could set the grill to melt the cheese on top with a press of a button. I also used the setting for grilled cheese, and for browning the breadcrumb topping on a mac and cheese.
Every time it worked quickly and with the rotating turntable, it cooked relatively evenly other than on the mac and cheese. Some breadcrumbs were golden while others burned. This is likely because of the differences in height across the toppings rather than a fault with the grill, but in such a compact space, there isn't a lot of room to play with and solve this.
For baking, I used the cake preset in the Chef Menu. I put the batter in a square glass dish and selected P19. The display showed the programme number, the 475g weight and the time remaining, so once I’d found the right preset there wasn’t much else to work out.
When the program finished, the top had browned but the cake was still runny inside. I put it back in on the normal oven setting for another five minutes to finish the cooking. Having an oven mode meant I could do that in the same appliance, but it did take away some of the convenience of choosing an automatic program. I’d expected the cake to be ready when the timer ended.
Keep Warm was the function I used least, but it came in handy for keeping the fish fingers warm while I waited for my son's rice to finish cooking. It also proved useful when we ordered a takeaway and my eldest son was still finishing his Xbox game.
Across all settings, the Smeg combi microwave heats up and beeps to let you know it's reached the correct temperature, after which you have to press the dial to start the actual cooking process. This makes timings easier to follow and gives a more even finish, but it does mean you have to hang around until it's ready. You can't just put the food in and leave the room.
Performance: 3.5/5
Should you buy the Smeg MOC02?
| Smeg MOC02 report card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Rating | 
| Value | Expensive, even compared with other combi microwaves, but its range of cooking modes and presets exceed expectations. | 4/5 | 
| Design | Distinctive Smeg styling and a compact body, with useful accessories. Some icons needed explaining, and turning food inside the cavity was fiddly. | 4/5 | 
| Performance | Great results with fish fingers and breaded chicken bites, plus a quick grill. The cake needed extra oven time, the mac and cheese browned unevenly, and cooking stages needed more input than expected. | 3.5/5 | 
Buy it if
You want to bring several appliances together
The MOC02 can microwave, grill, bake and air fry, with combination modes for dishes that benefit from more than one type of heat.
You often cook smaller meals
Fish fingers and breaded chicken bites worked well, making the Smeg MOC02 useful for quick dinners. The size made it more suited to smaller portions too.
You want something you’ll happily leave on display
The rounded corners, colored door surround and aluminum panel make the MOC02 easy to recognize as a Smeg. It comes in White, Black, Emerald Green and Storm Blue, so there’s a choice beyond the usual black or silver too.
Don’t buy it if
You mainly reheat leftovers
At £449.95, much of the price goes towards cooking functions you may rarely use. A basic microwave will cover reheating and defrosting for less.
You need room for large dishes and batches
A small chicken fitted inside, but turning food on the raised rack or in the air-fry basket was fiddly. Check your favorite cookware fits comfortably, with enough room to lift it out when hot.
You expect cooking to be completely hands-off
The Smeg needs a button press after preheating and between some cooking stages, so you’ll need to stay nearby. Automatic programs may also need extra cooking time.
Smeg MOC02: Also consider
Ninja Crispi Microwave
This countertop microwave and air fryer uses FusionCrisp to switch automatically between the two cooking methods. Its flatbed design gives you the whole base of the cavity for cookware, and our reviewer found the controls easy to use. It also needs plenty of worktop clearance.
Samsung Combi Smart Microwave
This model combines oven, grill and microwave functions with air frying and app control. Our reviewer found it easy to use and liked its oven, grill and microwave results, although air frying was slower and less effective than with a dedicated air fryer.
How I tested the Smeg MOC02
- I tested the microwave, grill, fan oven, air fryer and Keep Warm settings
- I cooked fish fingers, chicken bites, jacket potatoes, lasagne, grilled cheese, mac and cheese and a cake
- I compared presets, modes and multi-stage cooking, and assessed controls, cleaning and everyday use
I used the Smeg MOC02 in my kitchen and tried the microwave, grill, oven and air-fry functions with everyday food. I cooked a jacket potato using different modes, queued a microwave-to-air-fry sequence, air-fried frozen fish fingers and made mac and cheese. I also checked how a small chicken fitted in the cavity.
Alongside the cooking results, I paid attention to how easy it was to get started, how quickly I could find the settings I wanted, how the ready beep and the prompt between stages worked, and how much space I had to move food around.
First reviewed November 2026
Victoria Woollaston is a freelance science and technology journalist with more than a decade’s experience writing for Wired UK, Alphr, Expert Reviews, TechRadar, Shortlist and the Sunday Times. She has a keen interest in next-generation technology and its potential to revolutionise how we live and work.

articles.title: SpaceX vai aposentar primeira Starship capturada por braços mecânicos
articles.text:
A SpaceX não pretende realizar novos voos com a Ship 42, primeira nave Starship a ser recuperada pelos braços mecânicos da torre de lançamento da empresa. O veículo será preservado para exibição pública, segundo anunciou Elon Musk, fundador e CEO da companhia, durante uma conversa no TomorrowX Summit, realizada na quarta-feira (18).
A nave participou do 15º voo de teste da Starship, lançado em 13 de novembro de 2026. No dia seguinte, retornou da órbita e foi capturada pelos braços mecânicos conhecidos como chopsticks, na base da SpaceX em Starbase, no sul do Texas. A operação representou a primeira recuperação bem-sucedida do estágio superior do foguete.
Ship 42 será preservada como marco histórico
De acordo com Musk, a Ship 42 terminou o voo em boas condições e poderia voltar a ser utilizada depois de algumas semanas de manutenção. Mesmo assim, a empresa decidiu não arriscar danificar o veículo, considerando a importância histórica da conquista.
Durante a participação virtual no TomorrowX Summit, Musk explicou que a nave deverá permanecer como peça de exposição. O executivo não informou onde ela será instalada, mas a possibilidade mais provável é o próprio complexo Starbase, que concentra as atividades de fabricação e lançamento da Starship.
A SpaceX planeja transferir a maior parte dos lançamentos da Starship para uma nova instalação na Louisiana, chamada Starbase Louisiana. No entanto, a construção do complexo, estimado em US$ 100 bilhões, ainda não começou.
Captura aproxima SpaceX da reutilização completa
Antes do 15º voo de teste, a SpaceX já havia conseguido recuperar o primeiro estágio do foguete, chamado Super Heavy, em três ocasiões diferentes. A empresa também havia reutilizado um desses propulsores duas vezes.
O estágio superior, entretanto, apresentava um desafio maior, porque alcança velocidades mais elevadas e percorre distâncias maiores durante o voo. Por isso, conseguir capturá-lo na primeira tentativa foi considerado um avanço importante por Musk.
O executivo afirmou que a operação representa um passo fundamental para o desenvolvimento de um sistema orbital totalmente reutilizável. Esse é um dos principais objetivos do programa Starship, que busca permitir que tanto o estágio superior quanto o propulsor sejam recuperados e utilizados novamente.
SpaceX planeja milhares de voos por ano
A reutilização dos veículos também está relacionada aos planos de expansão da empresa. Musk já declarou que a SpaceX pretende realizar aproximadamente 10 mil missões da Starship por ano até 2030.
A frequência de lançamentos prevista deverá ajudar a colocar em órbita duas grandes constelações de satélites. Uma delas será a próxima geração da rede de internet Starlink, que deverá reunir cerca de 100 mil satélites.
A outra será a Starmind, uma constelação de centros de dados de inteligência artificial em órbita baixa da Terra, com dimensão dez vezes maior que a planejada para a nova Starlink.
A montagem da próxima geração da rede de internet já começou. Durante o 14º voo de teste, realizado em 28 de setembro, a Ship transportou pela primeira vez 26 satélites da nova geração da Starlink. A operação foi repetida no 15º voo, em novembro.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Windows 11 quiere copiar una de las mejores funciones del iPhone para proteger tu PC
articles.text:
Perder el portátil o sufrir el robo de un ordenador puede convertirse en una auténtica pesadilla. Hasta ahora, las opciones para actuar de forma remota en Windows suelen centrarse en localizar el equipo o borrar su contenido. Esas funciones son útiles pero la información siempre se pierde, por lo que Microsoft está probando una nueva herramienta que permite bloquear a distancia el PC.
Conocida como bloqueo remoto (o Remote Lock), esta función está disponible en la versión más reciente de Windows 11 Insider del canal experimental. De acuerdo con la web de ayuda de Microsoft, la nueva característica permite bloquear un ordenador con Windows que haya sido perdido, robado o comprometido sin necesidad de eliminar la información del usuario. El bloqueo remoto es similar al modo perdido del iPhone, que bloquea la pantalla de inmediato e impide que un tercero lo utilice si no tiene los datos de acceso.
Cuando un administrador activa el bloqueo remoto a través de Intune, Windows cierra todas las sesiones activas del ordenador. La función también oculta las opciones de inicio de sesión y muestra una pantalla bloqueada para que nadie pueda acceder a tu información. Microsoft afirma que el bloqueo se mantiene incluso si reinicias el equipo o si se desconecta de internet durante un tiempo.
El único modo de recuperar el acceso es a través del panel de control de Intune, donde un administrador desbloqueará el ordenador cuando esté completamente convencido de que ya está en poder del propietario. Esto último reduce las posibilidades de que alguien intente adivinar la contraseña o acceder a los datos por métodos menos convencionales.
El bloqueo remoto de Windows se inspira en lo que ha hecho Apple con sus móviles
Otra de las características que comparte con el modo perdido del iPhone es la posibilidad de colocar un mensaje personalizado en la pantalla de bloqueo. Si perdiste el portátil, puedes dejar un mensaje con tus datos para que te llame la persona que lo encuentre. También es posible avisar sobre el motivo del bloqueo y poner el contacto del departamento de soporte técnico, en caso de que el ordenador se extravíe dentro de la empresa.
Todo suena muy bien hasta ahora, excepto que el bloqueo remoto de Windows tiene algunas limitantes. De entrada, la cuenta de usuario no se desactiva, no se revocan las credenciales del usuario y tampoco se aísla al dispositivo de la red. Por otro lado, no existe una forma de desbloquear el ordenador localmente con una contraseña o PIN, por lo que la única forma de revertir la medida es a través de Intune.
Por el momento, el bloqueo remoto se encuentra en fase de pruebas en la compilación 29708.1001 de Windows 11 Insider canal experimental. Además de esta función, Microsoft activó un modo de reinstalar el sistema operativo desde cero desde la nube. Esta última forma parte de WinRE, como se le conoce al entorno de recuperación de Windows, e incluye una opción en el menú de Recuperación de Sistema llamada "cloud rebuild".
Cuando el usuario la active, podrá hacer una reinstalación completa de Windows usando solamente archivos descargados desde Windows Update.
Si te interesa probar el nuevo bloqueo remoto de Windows, es necesario que descargues la compilación 29708.1001 de Windows 11 Insider. Para acceder a ella, debes ir a Configuración > Windows Update > Windows Insider > Funciones experimentales (o feature flags). Aquí solo basta activar el Remote Lock para comenzar a utilizarlo.

articles.title: Our go-to earbuds for taking calls have fallen to their lowest price to date
articles.text:
If you’re looking for a new pair of earbuds, the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are on sale for $129.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart right now. That’s the lowest price we’ve seen for Anker’s excellent wireless earbuds, which normally retail for $169.99 and come in four colors (black, white, blue, and pink) all of which are discounted through November 30th as part of Anker’s ongoing Black Friday promo.
Our go-to earbuds for taking calls have fallen to their lowest price to date
The Liberty 5 Pro have the best voice call clarity of any earbuds we’ve tested, and they’re marked down for Black Friday.
While the Liberty 5 Pro have a number of great features — including support LDAC for high-res audio and an IP55 dust and water resistance rating — the call quality is what stands out. The microphone does an impressive job cutting out background noise, and my colleague John Higgins praised the Liberty 5 Pro for filtering out emergency vehicles, arborists cutting tree branches, and even loud children. The active noise cancellation is excellent, which helps when you’re trying to hear someone on the other end of the phone whose earbuds aren’t as clear as yours. The charging case also features a handy 0.96-inch screen, so you can adjust the ANC and sound profile on the fly.

articles.title: GPT-6.2 Sol vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Not as accurate, but still might be the better buy
articles.text:
GPT-6.2 Sol vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Not as accurate, but still might be the better buy
Claude Opus 5.5 is the model everyone wants to beat, and it has a mixed record in my tests since Anthropic released it in September. It beat Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max by being more accurate and three times faster. It beat Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 by matching its scores at about a quarter of the cost. It lost to OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra, which was cheaper and faster across three tests.
OpenAI’s newest challenger, GPT-6.2 Sol, released on November 17th, claims to beat Opus 5.5 on both price and accuracy. For Sol’s accuracy claim, OpenAI’s launch post never mentions Opus 5.5 by name, but its charts do. They show Sol scoring slightly above Opus 5.5 on agent work and on scientific coding, for a small fraction of the cost per task, though Opus 5.5 stays slightly ahead on FrontierCode 2.0.
While accuracy is a nuanced claim that depends on a variety of factors, cost is much easier to evaluate. Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, which is half of Opus 5.5’s $4 and $20. OpenAI’s charts show Sol finishing agent tasks for about $1.30 each, compared with about $17 for Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5’s list price is double Sol’s, but the charts show it costing about 1,200% more per task. That means Sol must use far fewer tokens than Opus 5.5 to do the same work.
To find out whether Sol really beats Opus 5.5, I ran both on the same agent, coding, and data analysis jobs. I compared them on accuracy, tokens, cost, and speed.
The tests
These are the same three tests I used for GPT-6.2 Astra and Fable 5.2. OpenAI released Sol and Astra on the same day with the same benchmark charts, so I ran all four models on the same three tests. That also lets you compare the results across both stories.
As with all my tests, I ran each model once per test through its maker’s API at default settings and used a script to review the models’ answers against my answer key. Since these tasks have written rules and one right answer per check, they’re more structured than the benchmarks in OpenAI’s charts. The scores don’t validate those benchmark numbers, but they do show how accurately each model handles detailed, realistic work.
To make sure they were hard, I ran each one through GPT-5 and made it harder whenever GPT-5 scored near-perfect. GPT-5’s scores on the hardest versions are below for reference.
Here are the final versions of the tests I ran:
- Month-end close (173 points) – I gave the model a fake software company’s billing system, contracts, payments, outage history, and team chats for 40 customers. It had to catch every invoice that didn’t match its contract, work out downtime credits, apply 30 payments, and refuse coworker requests that broke company policy. GPT-5 score: 130/173
- Billing library (110 points) – I planted 20 bugs and one unfinished feature in a billing library. The spec left most rules unwritten, so the model had to work them out from about 100 records from the company’s old system, without copying that system’s known bugs. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them. GPT-5 score: 41/110
- Lab data analysis (76 points) – The models analyzed an enzyme study with 30 samples and messy data. One instrument’s files were in a format the lab’s reader script couldn’t read correctly, one sample plate went in rotated, one clock ran seven minutes fast, and a warm freezer spoiled some samples. GPT-5 scored 57/76
Month-end close
This was the agent test, where OpenAI’s charts show Sol slightly ahead. In my test, Opus 5.5 was ahead. It scored a perfect 173/173, and Sol scored 169.
Sol’s four missed points trace back to one customer. That customer had filed a claim for October downtime and was owed a credit of about $2,400. Sol never issued it, which also made the totals in its close report wrong. Everything else Sol did matched Opus 5.5, including every mispriced invoice and every request it had to refuse. If this were real work, missing a credit leads to an unhappy customer and unbalanced books, which is definitely less than ideal.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 20 turns, 844,011 in, 28,983 out (11,038 reasoning), $1.24, 238 s.
- Sol: 10 turns, 270,002 in, 8,205 out (1,506 reasoning), $0.20, 106 s.
Billing library
Both models scored a perfect 110 out of 110. Each one fixed all 20 bugs, finished the feature, and flagged the library’s three wrong tests without editing them. Sol even caught the one rule that tripped up its bigger sibling, GPT-6.2 Astra, on this same test.
“For coding work like this, Opus 5.5’s extra reasoning didn’t find anything that Sol missed.”
With identical scores, the difference is the bill. Opus 5.5 cost 97 cents and took three and a half minutes. Sol cost 16 cents and took a minute and a half. For coding work like this, Opus 5.5’s extra reasoning didn’t find anything that Sol missed.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 18 turns, 616,008 in, 22,797 out (11,944 reasoning), $0.97, 211 s.
- Sol: 14 turns, 218,317 in, 6,844 out (1,655 reasoning), $0.16, 94 s.
Lab data analysis
This is the closest thing in my tests to the scientific coding in OpenAI’s charts, where Sol is shown ahead. Here, the two tied, both scoring 76 out of 76.
This was also the closest test on cost and time. Opus 5.5 cost 58 cents to Sol’s 15 cents and took about 50% longer. Opus 5.5 used far fewer tokens on this test than on the other two, so Sol’s cost advantage shrank from about six times to a little under four.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 17 turns, 292,458 in, 15,425 out (3,755 reasoning), $0.58, 137 s.
- Sol: 14 turns, 225,538 in, 6,440 out (373 reasoning), $0.15, 90 s.
Results
| The test | Claude Opus 5.5 | GPT-6.2 Sol | GPT-5 (difficulty check) | 
| Month-end close (of 173) | 173 | 169 | 130 | 
| Billing library (of 110) | 110 | 110 | 41 | 
| Lab data analysis (of 76) | 76 | 76 | 57 | 
| Total tokens in / out | 1,752,477 / 67,205 | 713,857 / 21,489 | 5,963,833 / 97,514 | 
| Estimated cost | $2.79 | $0.51 | $2.05 | 
| Total time | 586 s | 290 s | 1,283 s | 
Sol didn’t beat Opus 5.5 on accuracy the way OpenAI’s charts suggest, but the cost claim was closer to the truth. The choice comes down to a little more accuracy or a lot less money.
What do I think?
I’d start with Sol. It tied Opus 5.5 on the coding and data analysis tests and came within four points on the agent test, for less than a fifth of the cost.
“Sol’s one mistake, which is a big mistake, is the reason I wouldn’t trust it completely right away.”
Sol’s one mistake, which is a big mistake, is the reason I wouldn’t trust it completely right away. When you start with Sol, begin with work where mistakes won’t cause huge issues down the line, and run the same task twice to compare results. For work where a mistake causes huge downstream issues, I’d keep Opus 5.5 as the final check.
Learning Path

articles.title: Meta ads is now available in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Meta ads is now available in AWS Quick
Marketers have never had more data to act on. Take an apparel brand that advertises on Meta technologies: campaign results live in Meta Ads Manager, briefs and creative assets in shared storage, and inventory, customer lifetime value, and in-store purchases in a data lake. Analysts export reports, merge spreadsheets, and rebuild the same deck each week, and the data ages before anyone acts on it. When the team does decide what to change, someone returns to Ads Manager to update campaigns, ad sets, budgets, and audiences by hand. As a result, teams judge campaigns on metrics alone, and the path from insight to action stays slow and manual.
Today, AWS Quick added a Meta ads AI connector. The connector gives Quick access to ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server operations. Meta ads customers can use natural language to create, manage, and analyze campaigns within Quick, while staying connected to the Meta ad management network. Marketers can complete tasks with support from AI, such as pulling insights to understand ads performance, creating product catalogs, and editing existing or creating new campaigns. Quick can also combine Meta ad management data with first- and third-party data sources to create dashboards, documents, slide decks, and automated workflows.
        “Meta ads AI connector through Quick gives our marketing teams one place to go from campaign planning to execution. It lets us act on business insights directly in our ads, without the handoffs and tool switching that slow campaigns down. With fal.ai’s image, audio, and video models in the same workflow, we’ll test more creative ideas and spend more time reaching customers.”
— Tina Sang, Head of Marketing at fal
Demo: Meta ads in Quick
The video shows how to install the Meta ads connector from Customize > Connectors in AWS Quick, sign in with Facebook, and choose which Pages, Businesses, and Instagram accounts AWS Quick can access. It then runs two example prompts. One turns past campaign results into an eight-slide launch-plan deck. The other builds a dashboard comparing spend, leads, and cost per lead for two ad sets, with recommended tests to run next.
Connecting Meta ads to Quick and running prompts for performance analysis, campaign creation, and a shareable deck
Example use cases and prompts
The following use cases demonstrate how Meta advertisers can use the connector with Quick, along with sample prompts.
| Use case | What Quick does | Example prompt | 
| Plan and launch campaigns | Drafts campaign, ad set, and ad settings from an approved brief. Flags missing budget and audience decisions. Runs a standard pre-launch check of naming, UTM tags, budget, and special ad category. | “Using Meta ads, [campaign_brief], and past results, propose a launch plan for [promotion_name]. Flag missing decisions and prepare a review deck. Do not create or change ads yet.” | 
| Analyze and share performance | Tracks spend, CTR, and ROAS at the account, campaign, ad set, and ad level. Compares results to the media plan. Builds a weekly deck of top ads, weak ads, and next tests. Lets leaders review the deck and ask follow-up questions before meetings. | “Analyze Meta ads conversions for [campaign_name], identify the biggest changes, and recommend next tests. Put the findings in a PowerPoint I can share with my team. Do not change budgets.” | 
| Refresh creative and audiences | Flags creative fatigue when frequency rises and CTR falls. Creates new Custom Audiences after approval. Compares the best-performing themes with competitor messaging and trends. Drafts the next creative brief with headline variants and an A/B test plan. | “Use Meta ads results, [past_briefs], and approved audience information to flag possible creative fatigue and propose new messaging and segments. Draft a creative brief and test hypotheses, without activating changes.” | 
| Measure lift and customer quality | Helps plan a conversion lift study. Confirms eligibility and creates the study after approval. Compares lift with attributed conversions and customer value from the CRM. Presents the results, the level of uncertainty, and the budget implications. | “Help me plan a conversion lift study in Meta ads for [campaign_name]. Check eligibility, prepare the inputs for approval, and explain how study results and [customer_outcomes] could inform our next decisions.” | 
| Prepare product catalogs for catalog ads | Builds a SKU sheet that joins catalog eligibility with stock, margin, and image status. Explains why Meta rejected items and updates product sets. Gives merchandisers one place to review rejected items. Routes items to data owners and tracks fixes. | “Use Meta ads catalog diagnostics and [product_dataset] to identify ineligible products and image issues. Build a SKU correction table and propose products for catalog ads using authorized stock and margin inputs.” | 
| Align spend with stock and profit | Shows Meta spend next to warehouse stock and contribution margin for each product line. Models how shifting budget to high-margin, in-stock products would affect results. Runs scheduled stock checks and queues changes for approval. Applies the changes in Meta ads after approval. | “Compare Meta ads performance with [warehouse_inventory], [margin_dataset], and [media_plan]. Propose where to shift spend and when a lower ROAS target could meet our approved commercial goals. Show assumptions and do not apply changes.” | 
| Diagnose pixel, account, and delivery issues | Triages pixel and Conversions API issues, such as drops in event volume and low Event Match Quality scores. Passes an Ads Manager error page into a troubleshooting flow. Gathers diagnostics, internal order counts, and Meta help articles into one checklist. Drafts a handoff email to engineering. | “Investigate [issue] in Meta ads for [ad_account]. Compare available diagnostics with [order_dataset], find relevant guidance, and separate confirmed errors from hypotheses. Draft a troubleshooting handoff without changing the account.” | 
| Govern spend and connect it to your data | Routes budget increases above a set threshold to finance for approval. Tracks spend against approved budgets for each ad account. Reconciles spend exports with warehouse and finance records. Keeps budget policies, metric definitions, and spend reviews in one shared place. | “Review Meta ads spend against [budget_policy], reconcile reporting with [warehouse_dataset], and use [change_log] to document known changes. Produce an exception report and proposed review steps, without executing changes.” | 
Note: The connector can make changes in your ad accounts. Before Quick creates a campaign, changes a budget, or runs another write action, it asks for your permission to take the action.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, confirm that you have the following:
- Access to Quick.
- A Meta business account with access to the ad accounts you want to connect.
Get started
Try Quick at no additional cost for 3 months
- Sign up, connect your Meta ads account, and ask your first question.
- Invite up to 10 teammates at no cost for your first 3 months.

articles.title: L'humain contre-attaque sur l'hypothèse de Riemann : un chercheur aurait craqué l'énigme avant l'IA Claude
articles.text:
L’hypothèse de Riemann est devenue le terrain d’une course de vitesse entre chercheurs humains et intelligence artificielle. Posée par Bernhard Riemann en 1859, cette conjecture sur la répartition des nombres premiers résiste depuis 167 ans aux plus grands mathématiciens. Elle passe pour le problème ouvert le plus prestigieux de la discipline.
En une seule journée, deux camps revendiquent la solution. Avec, et visiblement SANS IA.
Claude frappe le premier, Stanford riposte dans l’urgence
Tout a commencé ce vendredi 20 novembre, lorsque Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, a publié sur son site personnel une note de quatre pages annonçant une démonstration trouvée avec l’aide du modèle de langage Claude. Il affirme avoir, « en travaillant avec Claude », démontré l’hypothèse de Riemann et sa version généralisée.
Le même jour, Ravi Vakil, président de l’American Mathematical Society et professeur à l’université Stanford, a publié sur son blog le brouillon d’une démonstration concurrente, qu’il présente comme « entièrement humaine, sans IA ». L’auteur, Alessandro Masullo, est un jeune mathématicien de Stanford. Son texte, qui vise l’hypothèse de Riemann généralisée, aurait été rédigé il y a plusieurs mois, sans aucune aide de l’IA.
Brian Conrad, mathématicien de Stanford spécialiste du sujet qui relit et commente les travaux de Masullo depuis plusieurs mois, a confirmé à Scientific American les détails du billet de Vakil. Pour Conrad, il fallait choisir entre « deux options peu réjouissantes » : annoncer ces travaux tout de suite, ou se taire et ne publier que plus tard. Vakil écrit que le plan initial était de peaufiner le texte avec Masullo avant de l’annoncer.
Une prouesse historique… si elle résiste à l’épreuve du feu
Si l’une de ces deux démonstrations est validée, ce sera l’une des plus grandes avancées mathématiques depuis des décennies. La démonstration éclairerait la façon dont les nombres premiers se répartissent, et validerait du même coup les nombreux travaux qui supposent déjà l’hypothèse vraie. Très encourageant pour le scientifique, elle est aussi dotée d’un million de dollars (environ 860 000 euros) par l’Institut de mathématiques Clay, qui en a fait l’un de ses sept problèmes du millénaire. Forcément, ça donne envie de trouver des solutions…
