articles.title: FBI reportedly hacked again, this time targeting nationwide police database
articles.text:
FBI systems have reportedly been breached for the second time in two months, this time targeting the agency's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which is used to share information between local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies.
The National Crime Information Center is an FBI-operated database used by law enforcement agencies across the United States to share information about wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, protection orders, and other criminal justice records.
Police officers routinely use the system during traffic stops, criminal investigations, and background checks.
According to CNN's reporting, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the NCIC system, citing two people briefed on the investigation.
The intrusion was reportedly discovered in recent days, although it is unclear when the breach occurred, how the attackers gained access, or whether any information was stolen.
The FBI has not publicly confirmed the incident and did not respond to CNN's request for comment.
The reported breach comes just two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed to have breached the FBI's systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability.
The earlier attack targeted a third-party platform associated with the FBI's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov, with ShinyHunters claiming to have stolen sensitive information from the agency's systems.
The FBI subsequently launched an investigation that led to the arrests of suspected ShinyHunters members, including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attacks.
There is currently no indication that the latest NCIC incident is connected to ShinyHunters or the earlier breach.
It remains unclear whether the attackers accessed sensitive law enforcement records stored in NCIC or whether the intrusion affected the system's availability to law enforcement agencies.
BleepingComputer contacted the FBI on Friday evening with questions about the reported breach but has not received a response.
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

articles.title: Sabrent Voltik 252W 8-port USB PD 3.0 Charger Quick Look
articles.text:
Sabrent sent us this charger, and while we do not generally review USB chargers, we thought we would take a few photos and share it since it has been pretty useful. The Voltik 252W 8-port USB PD 3.0 Charger is a desktop charging station with four USB-C ports and four USB-A ports, and Sabrent rates it at 252W of total output. That is a lot of power for something that sits on a desk, and the port layout is what makes it worth a closer look.
Here is the unit via an Amazon Affiliate link.
Sabrent Voltik 252W Hardware Overview
The enclosure is a black rectangular block that is not really what we would want from a travel charger, but it works well on a desk.
The front face has a display at the top, then the four USB-C ports, then the four USB-A ports below them. There is also a button for the LCD.
The USB-C ports are arranged in two rows of two. The upper row is labeled C1A and C1B, and the lower row is labeled C2A and C2B. Sabrent rates each USB-C port at up to 100W, which is enough for a laptop on its own. The 252W figure is the station’s combined output, so the four USB-C ports cannot all deliver 100W at the same time. Sabrent lists support for PD 3.0, PPS, QC 4.0, and QC 3.0.
Below the USB-C ports are the four USB-A ports, also in two rows, with the Sabrent logo underneath. Sabrent rates each USB-A port at up to 18W.
Here is a shot of the LCD lit up and showing eight port boxes labeled C1A, C2A, A1A, and A2A across the top and C1B, C2B, A1B, and A2B across the bottom. The screen can cycle through each port to show current wattage, voltage, amperage, and internal temperature by using the button between ports C1A and C1B. Other chargers do that, but if you do not have something like that yet, then it is something that if you read STH, you will like.
The power-input panel has the AC inlet, a printed rating label that includes the model AX-8PTC and the per-port and shared output modes. It is nice that the unit directly takes AC power rather than through an external power brick.
Of course, if you want to use it on the road, it is pretty easy to find a different input cable for this one.
The rear face has two long raised strips along its edges and two rectangular recesses in the center for a mounting plate.
The mounting plate has four fixing holes and two rectangular hooks, shown here with two black fixings in front and the charger behind. That hardware points to mounting the station rather than leaving it loose on the desktop.
Final Words
The Sabrent Voltik 252W is interesting because it consolidates a desk full of chargers into one unit with eight ports and a display that shows the status of each port’s voltage, current, temperature, and time. It is quite useful to know if something is charging, or if it is on, and how fast. On the other hand, we have seen notebooks that draw over 100W via USB Type-C, so even though this is a huge USB charger, it cannot charge everything.
For a desk with several devices that need to charge, that combination of port count, power, and feedback is the practical case for a single station in place of a drawer full of separate adapters. We now have four of these.

articles.title: El Gobierno de España aprueba cuatro medidas urgentes para acelerar la soberanía en IA, semiconductores y cuántica
articles.text:
"Soberanía es no depender de multinacionales ni intereses extranjeros". Con esa frase anunciaba Pedro Sánchez el real decreto-ley que el Consejo de Ministros de España aprobó este viernes y que tienen como objetivo, en palabras del actual presidente, convertir la ciencia española en líder en Europa gracias a un paquete de medidas urgentes para el impulso de la competitividad y la soberanía tecnológica en el ámbito científico e investigador.
Las medidas. Esencialmente son cuatro:
- La creación de una red de hasta 20 centros públicos de "interés nacional" en 10 áreas estratégicas, entre ellas IA, semiconductores, energía o tecnologías cuánticas y les otorga más autonomía y flexibilidad para contratar, comprar equipos o llevar resultados al mercado. La novedad no son los centros en sí, sino su estatus especial, que durará cinco años prorrogables hasta 10.
- Convierte el Barcelona Supercomputing Center en una fundación pública adscrita a la Administración General del Estado y podrá crear una empresa para comercializar sus resultados.
- Menos trámites en convenios de I+D+I y contratos y permite mayores retribuciones a investigadores financiados con fondos externos y elimina autorizaciones previas en ciertos contratos.
- Las empresas que más innovan pagan menos impuestos: la deducción pasa del 12% al 15%, las startups sin beneficios podrán cobrar hasta tres millones al año en deducciones en lugar de uno y las bonificaciones por contratar personal de I+D duran cinco años en vez de tres.
Por qué importa. Porque quien domine la IA, los chips y la cuántica tendrá más poder económico y de decisión y ahí Europa parte en desventaja respecto a Estados Unidos y China, entre otras cosas por la brecha de innovación en tecnologías avanzadas o la financiación dividida entre estados miembros y la UE.
A esta fragmentación europea se suma el punto de partida de España, que invierte menos en I+D que la media de la UE: el 1,50 % del PIB en 2024 frente a cerca del 2,2 % europeo. Para quien investiga en su día a día, el paquete toca cuestiones muy concretas, como contratos, burocracia y deducciones fiscales para las empresas que contratan investigadores para facilitar esa labor.
A contrarreloj antes de las elecciones. El paquete llega a poco más de una semana para las elecciones generales del 29N, pero no es desde luego una medida aislada: ya en mayo el gobierno español aprobó la Estrategia Deep Tech España, que movilizará más de 8.000 millones de euros hasta 2030 y en junio aprobó una aportación de 300 millones a las gigafactorías de IA europeas, de las que España tiene dos. en el BSC y en el CESGA. Y hasta agosto de este año, los fondos europeos Next Generation impulsaron la I+D.
El problema está en que con las Cortes disueltas, el decreto debe convalidarse por la Diputación Permanente dentro de un plazo de treinta días, según el artículo 86 de la Constitución, por lo que el próximo Gobierno podría cambiarlo.
Sigue haciendo falta dinero. El real decreto-ley habla de medidas urgentes concretas, pero no de dinero, algo esencial para que verdaderamente la innovación española de un paso adelante. Y la realidad es que haría falta mucho para ponerse no solo en la media europea, sino también para cumplir el objetivo del 2,12% del PIB en 2027. Según la Fundación COTEC serían necesarios crecimientos anuales de la I+D cercanos al 24%, bastante por encima del ritmo actual.

articles.title: En Japón, un hombre se encuentra con un Toshiba Libretto 50 con Windows 95 que era un ordenador portátil de lujo a su salida en 1997
articles.text:
En una tienda de electrónica de segunda mano de Akihabara (uno de los barrios más conocidos de Tokio) un hombre encontró un Toshiba Libretto 50, un clásico con Windows 95 instalado que estaba a la venta por unos 140 euros. Lo curioso es que este pequeño portátil no era precisamente barato cuando llegó al mercado en 1997, ya que su versión más cara costaba 248.000 yenes o lo que es lo mismo: 1.730 euros.
Según recoge Les Numériques, aunque el PC fue localizado en septiembre de 2026, su historia comenzó el 7 de enero de 1997 cuando Toshiba lo presentó en Japón. Por aquel entonces, los portátiles podían pesar varios kilos y lo sorprendente de este modelo es que se quedaba en solo 850 gramos con unas dimensiones de 21 centímetros de ancho, 11,5 de fondo y 3,4 de grosor, unas medidas impresionantes para la época.
Tener un ordenador tan pequeño en 1997 no salía precisamente barato
Y eso que su tamaño no era lo único llamativo. El Libretto 50 incorporaba un procesador Intel Pentium de 75 MHz, 16 MB de memoria RAM y un disco duro de 810 MB, además de una pantalla a color de 6,1 pulgadas con resolución de 640 x 480 píxeles. Todo ello funcionando con Windows 95, por lo que también podía ejecutar programas como Word 95, Excel 95 o Internet Explorer 3.
Para meter todos esos componentes en una carcasa tan pequeña, Toshiba tuvo que buscar soluciones bastante particulares. Por ejemplo, utilizó la propia placa base para ayudar a disipar el calor e incorporó unas cubiertas de magnesio de apenas 0,7 milímetros de grosor. Eso sí, la batería ofrecía entre una hora y media y dos horas de autonomía, aunque podía acercarse a las cuatro con una batería de mayor capacidad.
El precio tampoco ayudaba a que cualquiera pudiera comprarse uno. En Japón se vendía por entre 228.000 y 248.000 yenes, dependiendo de la versión, mientras que en Estados Unidos llegó en junio de 1997 por 1.999 dólares. Además, para utilizar determinados accesorios, como una disquetera externa o un módem, había que recurrir a conexiones y adaptadores adicionales.
Toshiba incluso llegó a fabricar una versión más exclusiva, el Libretto 50M, con pantalla táctil y destinada a la aseguradora japonesa Meiji Life, aunque nunca se comercializó para el público general. Casi tres décadas después, encontrarse uno de estos ordenadores por 140 euros resulta curioso, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta lo que costaba llevar Windows 95 en un dispositivo que apenas llegaba al kilo de peso.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

articles.title: FBI Investigating Apparent Hack of Its Key National Criminal Justice Database, AP Source Says
articles.text:
The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday.
The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics.
The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The scope of the problem was not immediately clear.
Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good.”
News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages.
The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers.
In September, for instance, a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters revealed that it had obtained a massive trove of data on FBI employees and applicants and had compromised the bureau’s jobs portal.
And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations.
Related: Ransomware Response Expert Arrested in ShinyHunters FBI Hack Probe
Related: ShinyHunters Claims FBI Hack, Demands Retraction of Threat Report

articles.title: Palmer Lucky's planned floating city is designed to escape state and local laws
articles.text:
Palmer Luckey wants to build a floating island that can last 1,000 years — Oculus Rift founder says SLAB will work outside of 'state/local laws that cripple critical American industries'
How difficult is it to develop US land? American tech billionaire wants to build a floating city
- Palmer Luckey wants a floating industrial island designed to last 1,000 years
- SLAB could accommodate oil refineries, metal processing plants, and desalination facilities
- The proposed offshore platform aims to avoid restrictive American state regulations
Palmer Luckey, the entrepreneur behind Oculus and defense technology company Anduril, has revealed he wants to develop a massive offshore platform designed to support industrial operations.
The proposed project, called SLAB, would provide space for activities including metal production, medical research, water desalination, oil refining, and chemical engineering.
Luckey says the structure could remain operational for 1,000 years, offering American industries an alternative to conventional land-based facilities.
SLAB could accommodate heavy industries without conventional land restrictions
Unlike floating offshore settlements and data centers, SLAB is an industrial installation capable of supporting activities requiring substantial infrastructure and specialized equipment.
Its proposed facilities include metal processing plants, medical research and treatment centers, desalination installations, petroleum refineries, and chemical engineering operations.
These industries frequently require considerable space, expensive infrastructure, and access to resources that can make conventional facility development financially demanding.
Establishing installations offshore could provide another location for such operations while reducing dependence on expensive industrial land and existing municipal arrangements.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The financial argument also forms an important part of the proposal, with offshore construction intended to cost less than acquiring suitable conventional property.
Avoiding certain state and local restrictions is another stated objective, particularly regulations that can constrain industrial activities within established American jurisdictions.
The project's development follows an approach associated with seasteading, which involves establishing permanent or long-term human infrastructure on bodies of water.
However, SLAB differs from many previous proposals because its primary purpose involves industrial production rather than just another sovereign AI territory.
Its design also raises substantial engineering requirements, particularly concerning structural durability and the conditions associated with continuous exposure to seawater.
Concrete construction, offshore maintenance, corrosion affecting associated equipment, and the logistics of supporting industrial operations would all require careful consideration.
SLAB has secured funding
SLAB originated in 2014, following Facebook's acquisition of Oculus, the virtual reality company founded by Luckey.
The acquisition provided financial resources for his various experimental projects, including helicopter flight training and the development of an offshore industrial platform.
Luckey subsequently established the initiative with several associates, who reportedly financed its development at a $1 billion valuation in 2017.
Recent additional funding has also supported the effort, although the amount raised and identities of the latest financial contributors remain undisclosed.
The project also carries an explicitly American industrial ambition, rather than the separation from established national governments associated with some seasteading proposals.
Its stated purpose involves creating additional capacity for domestic industries while providing an alternative to regulations considered restrictive by its financial backers.
“The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing, medical research/treatment, desalination, oil refining, chemical engineering, and more,” Luckey said.
The proposal has attracted reactions from social media users, with some questioning why American industrial development might need to move offshore in the first place.
An X user suggested that the growing interest in building entire cities at sea reflected serious difficulties associated with conventional land development in the U.S.
Palmer Luckey was also asked how far SLAB would need to sit from the American coastline to avoid falling under US jurisdiction, and his response was “three miles”.
SLAB remains under development, with no publicly confirmed construction schedule, installation location, or detailed engineering specifications.

articles.title: Voyager 1 e os 350 anos da velocidade da luz
articles.text:
A Voyager 1 acaba de alcançar um marco histórico em sua jornada pelo Cosmos. Esta semana, a espaçonave lançada nos anos 70, alcançou a distância de um dia-luz da Terra. Isso significa que a luz gasta um dia inteiro, 24 horas, para percorrer essa distância que a Voyager 1 precisou de quase 50 anos para alcançar. São praticamente 26 bilhões de quilômetros de nós, uma distância que só conseguimos medir hoje graças a um estudo apresentado ao mundo 350 anos atrás. Foi naquela época que conseguimos medir pela primeira vez a velocidade da luz.
Já havíamos tentado fazer isso antes. Até mesmo Galileu Galilei realizou um experimento com lanternas em montanhas distantes para tentar medir essa velocidade. Mas, por maior que fosse a distância entre as montanhas, a luz era rápida demais para ser percebida pelos instrumentos e métodos disponíveis na época. Por isso, muitos cientistas acreditavam que a velocidade da luz era infinita.
Até que em 21 de novembro de 1676, o astrônomo dinamarquês Ole Rømer apresentou à Academia Real de Ciências de Paris as primeiras evidências científicas de que a luz se propaga com uma velocidade finita. Mais do que isso, ele conseguiu, pela primeira vez na história, medir essa velocidade. Uma medição ainda imprecisa, mas que mudaria para sempre a maneira como observamos e compreendemos o Universo.
Rømer só alcançou esse feito graças a uma ideia de Galileu, não àquela das lanternas e montanhas, mas uma ideia que ele teve ao observar a dança das luas ao redor de Júpiter: os eclipses das luas de Júpiter aconteciam em intervalos tão regulares que poderiam funcionar como um relógio astronômico. Qualquer pessoa, em qualquer parte do mundo, poderia observar o momento em que Io, a lua mais interna, se escondia atrás de Júpiter, para acertar seu relógio com precisão. E isso seria fundamental, inclusive, para a medição das longitudes aqui na Terra.
Ole Rømer tentou aplicar esse método na prática e por isso, resolveu medir exatamente qual o período entre os eclipses de Io. Para sua surpresa, ao fazer essa medida, constatou que ela não era tão precisa assim. Ao longo dos meses, percebeu que os eclipses pareciam se atrasar progressivamente em relação ao horário previsto. Depois, os atrasos diminuíam, até que os eclipses começavam a acontecer cada vez mais cedo do que o esperado.
Como todo bom cientista, buscou os motivos. Ele percebeu então que, nos momentos em que a Terra se aproximava de Júpiter, os eclipses de Io ocorriam mais rapidamente. E quando se afastava, demoravam mais. A conclusão que ele chegou é que isso só poderia acontecer porque a luz de Júpiter e suas luas demorava mais tempo para chegar aqui quando o planeta estava mais distante. Isso significava, que a velocidade da luz não era infinita e poderia ser, finalmente, medida.
Pra compreender isso, imagine que temos um relógio preciso e acertado pelo horário de Brasília. Se ele for levado longe o suficiente para que a luz demore 5 minutos para chegar à Terra, ao olharmos para esse relógio através de um telescópio, veríamos a hora com 5 minutos de atraso. Isso significa que, se pudéssemos vê-lo se afastando até essa distância, veríamos seus ponteiros girando mais lentamente. E ao trazê-lo de volta, veríamos eles girando mais rapidamente até chegar na Terra, mostrando o horário correto com que foi acertado antes da viagem. Foi exatamente isso que Rømer observou, mas ao invés de um instrumento convencional, de ponteiros, o relógio utilizado era aquele, astronômico, proposto por Galileu: as luas de Júpiter.
Em setembro de 1676, Rømer fez uma previsão ousada: o próximo eclipse de Io aconteceria com aproximadamente dez minutos de atraso em relação ao horário esperado. Em 9 de novembro, a observação confirmou sua previsão. Duas semanas depois, em 21 de novembro, ele apresentou suas conclusões à Academia Francesa, estimando que a luz levava cerca de 22 minutos para atravessar o diâmetro da órbita terrestre.
Naquela época, a medição mais precisa da distância entre a Terra e o Sol, havia sido calculada por seu colega Christiaan Huygens. Usando sua medida e a estimativa de Rømer, Huygens calculou a velocidade da luz em 220.000 km/s. O valor é 27% abaixo das estimativas atuais e mais precisas. Mas é surpreendentemente próximo para uma primeira estimativa.
O mais importante é que Rømer havia demonstrado que a luz precisava de tempo para percorrer distâncias muito longas. Nos séculos seguintes, outros cientistas aperfeiçoaram essas medições. Em 1849, o francês Hippolyte Fizeau realizou um experimento utilizando uma roda dentada e um espelho distante. Depois, Léon Foucault aprimorou o método utilizando espelhos rotativos. Finalmente, experiências cada vez mais sofisticadas permitiram chegar ao valor que utilizamos atualmente: 299.792 km/s, no vácuo.
Um número com consequências extraordinárias. A luz do Sol, por exemplo, leva pouco mais de oito minutos para chegar à Terra. Isso significa que nunca vemos o Sol como ele está neste exato instante, mas como era oito minutos atrás. Quando observamos Júpiter, estamos vendo como ele era dezenas de minutos antes.
Essa relação entre a distância que a luz alcança em determinado período de tempo, levou à criação de unidades de medidas como o ano-luz, que corresponde a cerca de 9,46 trilhões de quilômetros, que é a distância que a luz percorre em um ano.
Por isso dizemos que, quando observamos estrelas e galáxias a milhões de anos-luz de distância, estamos literalmente olhando para o passado do Universo.
A velocidade da luz também estabelece um limite fundamental para a comunicação em viagens espaciais. Nenhuma informação pode ser transmitida mais rapidamente do que ela. É por isso que controlar uma espaçonave distante exige planejamento: não podemos simplesmente enviar um comando e esperar uma resposta imediata. No caso da Voyager 1, cada interação completa com a Terra exige agora, aproximadamente dois dias, sendo um para a informação ir, outro para voltar. Isso mesmo utilizando os sinais de rádio, que também viajam à velocidade da luz. Agora, precisaremos mandar o “feliz Natal” para Voyager 1 no dia 24, e só receber o “obrigado” no dia 26.
Quando Ole Rømer observava os eclipses de Io, provavelmente não imaginava todas as implicações de sua descoberta. Ele queria apenas uma maneira de acertar seu relógio, mas acabou abrindo caminho para uma nova compreensão do espaço e do tempo, que séculos depois seria fundamental para a própria teoria da relatividade.
Há 350 anos, Ole Rømer descobriu que a luz não chega instantaneamente até nós. Hoje, uma pequena espaçonave construída pela humanidade está tão distante que até mesmo uma mensagem enviada à velocidade da luz precisa de um dia inteiro para alcançá-la. São duas histórias separadas por séculos, mas unidas pela mesma descoberta. E enquanto a Voyager 1 continua avançando, levando consigo um pouco da história da humanidade para além das fronteiras do nosso Sistema Solar, a luz continua trazendo até nós notícias de mundos distantes, estrelas que já morreram e galáxias de um Universo ainda jovem. Porque, quando olhamos para o espaço, não estamos apenas contemplando a imensidão do Cosmos. Estamos viajando pelo tempo, lendo as histórias do passado do Universo que a luz ainda está nos contando.
Pres. Associação Paraibana de Astronomia; membro da Sociedade Astronômica Brasileira; diretor técnico da Rede Brasileira de Observação de Meteoros – e coordenador regional do Asteroid Day Brasil

articles.title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one
articles.text:
Xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one
The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.
The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, big batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.
Xiaomi 18 Pro
The Good
- Excellent main and telephoto cameras
- Privacy display
- Strong performance
- Compact
The Bad
- Rear display is limited
- Basic ultrawide camera
- Expensive
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max
The Good
- Excellent main and telephoto cameras
- Privacy display
- Strong performance
- Extended dynamic range
The Bad
- Rear display is limited
- Basic ultrawide camera
- Expensive
There are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
They come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.
The rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.
You can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.
Unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.
The only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.
It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.
Xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a new third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other big Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.
The ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Experte warnt: Nicht nur CEOs können in die Honigfalle tappen – auch für normale Angestellt besteht ein Risiko
articles.text:
Nach Huangs Rücktritt: Welcher Tech-CEO tappt als Nächstes in die Honigfalle?
Der Ex-Nvidia-CEO soll eine Affäre mit einer mutmaßlichen, chinesischen Spionin geführt haben – und ist daraufhin zurückgetreten. Er könnte also Opfer einer Honigfalle geworden sein. Dabei baut jemand eine Beziehung zu einer Zielperson auf, um Informationen zu erlangen oder Geld zu erpressen. Früher betraf diese Masche vor allem Politiker:innen und Geheimdienste. Laut einem Experten sind heute aber noch viel mehr Menschen gefährdet.
Huangs Affäre zieht ernsthafte Folgen nach sich
Huang führte Nvidia seit der Gründung im Jahr 1993 zu Rekordzahlen. Mit einer Bewertung von bis zu 5,8 Milliarden Dollar war Nvidia das wertvollste Unternehmen der Welt. Seit seinem Rücktritt ist der Aktienwert aber deutlich gesunken. Trotzdem fordern viele seine Rückkehr. Wie Wired berichtet, haben mehrere Mitarbeiter:innen auf Linkedin ihre Unterstützung bekundet. Eine Person soll ihr Vertrauen in Huangs Führungsqualitäten sogar als „unerschütterlich“ beschrieben haben. Eine Petition für seine Rückkehr haben inzwischen weit über 205.000 Personen unterschrieben, darunter auch Elon Musk (Stand: 21.11.2026, 12 Uhr).
Huangs Rücktritt macht deutlich, wie stark die Prozesse bei Nvidia auf seine Person zugeschnitten waren. Laut Bloomberg berichteten rund 60 Manager:innen direkt an ihn. „Nvidia ist Nvidia wegen Jensen“, sagte eine anonyme Quelle aus dem Unternehmen gegenüber Wired. Der Wunsch nach seiner Wiedereinsetzung sei intern weit verbreitet. Die Person befürchtet, dass der Chiphersteller ohne den Gründer leiden werde. Das zeigt, wie risikoreich es ist, wenn ein Unternehmen zu eng mit einer einzigen Führungskraft verwoben ist – und wie anfällig diese für Honigfallen sein können.
Nvidia-Chips könnten nach China gelangt sein
„Niemand klärt Gründer:innen über Spionageabwehr auf“, so Aaron Brown gegenüber Techcrunch. Der ehemalige CIA-Beamte hat inzwischen selbst ein Softwareunternehmen gegründet. Politiker:innen und Geheimdienstmitarbeiter:innen mit Sicherheitsfreigaben seien auf Annäherungsversuche von Spion:innen geschult. Heute lägen allerdings viele Geheimnisse bei Unternehmen, die Chips oder Software entwickeln. Spion:innen hätten es auf Kund:innenlisten und Informationen über Exportentscheidungen abgesehen. „Der CEO ist der kürzeste Weg zu all dem“, erklärt der Experte.
Huang könnte Opfer genau einer solchen Honigfalle geworden sein. Er soll eine Affäre mit Alice Huang gehabt haben, die im Verdacht steht, vom chinesischen Geheimdienst angeworben worden zu sein. Auch wird ihr vorgeworfen, Nvidia-Chips nach China geschmuggelt zu haben, für die strenge Exportkontrollen galten. Laut Will DePue gibt es tatsächlich Hinweise, dass chinesische KI-Modelle auf diesen Chips trainiert worden sein könnten. Der KI-Forscher hat ihre Gewichte analysiert. Diese spiegeln auch die Konfiguration der Chips wider, die für das Training verwendet wurden.
KI erleichtert das Aufstellen einer Honigfalle
Nach Huangs Rücktritt kursierten Witze darüber, welcher Tech-CEO als Nächstes in die Honigfalle tappen könnte. Gefährdet seien laut Brown allerdings alle Personen mit Zugang zu sensiblen Informationen – von Vorstandsmitgliedern bis zu Assistent:innen. Viele Spion:innen würden auch nicht zwingend eine Affäre eingehen, sondern sich mit ihren Opfern anfreunden. „Sie wollen, dass du dich im Gespräch wohlfühlst”, so der ehemalige CIA-Beamte. Wenn die Zielpersonen den Schwindel bemerken, könne die Lage eskalieren. Denn die Angreifer:innen würden oft versuchen, sie zu erpressen.
Die Ironie: KI macht Honigfallen heute viel einfacher und günstiger. Früher erforderte die Masche eine ausführliche der Recherche. Heute könnte das die KI übernehmen – ebenso wie das Erstellen von Fake-Profilen. „KI kann dabei helfen, eine ganze fiktive Hintergrundgeschichte aufrechtzuerhalten”, so Perry Carpenter, Kriminologe und Chefstratege für Täuschungsmanöver bei Knowbe4, gegenüber Techcrunch. Für Gründer:innen gehöre es zum Job, Risiken einzugehen, meint Brown. „Paranoia hilft nicht weiter. Zu erkennen, dass man ein Ziel ist, hingegen schon.“
) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Sicherheit im Heimnetz: Die offizielle Support-Liste für Fritzbox-Updates bis 2033
articles.text:
Fritzbox-Update-Check: Wie lange wird dein Router noch unterstützt?
Fast jedes Update bringt neue Funktionen auf Router, Repeater und andere Geräte von Fritz. Die FritzOS-Version 8.4o bringt etwa einen DNS-Filter auf Fritzboxen, mit dem sich bestimmte Werbeanzeigen, etwa auf Smart-TVs, ausblenden lassen. Die nächste Aktualisierung, FritzOS 8.50, steht auch schon für mehrere Router bereit. Doch wie lange geht das noch so? Nicht nur Smartphone-Besitzer:innen wissen, dass es irgendwann ein Ende hat mit dem Software-Support.
Bei Routern kann der besonders schwer wiegen, wenn kritische Sicherheitslücken nicht mehr geschlossen werden. Schon mehr als einmal hat ein Hersteller in diesem Fall zur Entsorgung geraten. Allerdings lässt sich schwer vorhersagen, wann ein Router oder entsprechendes Zubehör keine Updates mehr bekommt. Fritz hat deswegen für seine Kund:innen eine Liste veröffentlicht, die genau das beantwortet.
Fritz mit Software-Support bis in die 2030er
Die gute Nachricht: Wer ein halbwegs aktuelles Modell besitzt, muss sich in naher Zukunft keine Sorgen machen, plötzlich ohne Software-Updates darzustehen. Viele aktuelle Modelle unterstützt Fritz bis Anfang 2033. Seid ihr mit eurem jeweiligen WLAN-Standard zufrieden, braucht ihr euch also noch mindestens fünf Jahre keine Gedanken um einen Router-Neukauf zu machen. Bei einigen wenigen Modellen läuft dieser Updatezeitraum am 1. Januar oder Oktober 2032 aus. Selbst das ist aber mehr als genug Zeit, um sich Gedanken über das nächste Modell zu machen. Für Fritzboxen sieht die Liste wie folgt aus:
- Fritzbox 7590 AX: 1. Januar 2032
- Fritzbox 7530 AX: 1. Januar 2032
- Fritzbox 6690 Cable: 1. Januar 2032

articles.title: GTA 6 : tétraplégique, il joue sans manette uniquement par la pensée
articles.text:
Neuralink a publié ce vendredi 20 novembre sur X une vidéo de deux minutes où l’on voit un participant à ses essais cliniques jouer à GTA 6. Le jeu de Rockstar est sorti la veille, jeudi 19 novembre, sur PS5 et Xbox Series X/S. Le joueur ne touche aucune manette : ses commandes passent par l’implant cérébral de l’entreprise.
Sur un écran scindé en plusieurs fenêtres, un joueur immobile dirige avec précision un hors-bord sous un pont, s’engage dans un étroit chenal bordé d’arbres et suit les objectifs d’une mission de récupération de colis dans GTA 6. À côté de l’action, une manette virtuelle s’illumine en temps réel à chaque commande exécutée, tandis qu’un tableau de bord affiche le décodage en direct de son activité cérébrale.
Neuralink ne révèle pas l’identité du participant et ne dit pas sur quelle console tourne le jeu, même si la manette affichée à l’écran semble être une DualSense de PS5. La légende tient en une ligne : « Jouer à GTA 6 avec un Neuralink ». Neuralink soigne sa communication en profitant de la sortie du jeu le plus attendu de l’année pour mettre en avant son implant. La démonstration s’inscrit pourtant dans un essai clinique bien réel. Un autre participant, le vétéran britannique Jon Noble, jouait déjà à World of Warcraft par la pensée en mars.
Comment le cerveau remplace les pouces sur la manette pour GTA 6 ?
Cette démonstration s’appuie sur Telepathy, l’interface cerveau-machine développée par l’entreprise. L’implant capte directement les signaux électriques émis dans la zone du cortex moteur responsable des mouvements de la main. En imaginant simplement déplacer sa main ou presser un bouton, le patient génère une intention motrice que les algorithmes traduisent instantanément en commandes numériques.
Ces essais cliniques, menés auprès de personnes tétraplégiques à la suite d’une lésion de la moelle épinière, d’une sclérose latérale amyotrophique (maladie de Charcot) ou d’un AVC du tronc cérébral, visent d’abord à leur rendre une autonomie numérique sur ordinateur. Certains volontaires testent aussi des fonctions expérimentales pour piloter des consoles de jeux, des claviers, des fauteuils roulants électriques ou des bras robotisés.
Neuralink n’en est pas à son coup d’essai dans le jeu vidéo. Dès 2024, Noland Arbaugh, le tout premier patient de l’étude PRIME, jouait aux échecs, à Civilization 6 et à Mario Kart par la pensée. Noland Arbaugh pilotait donc déjà des karts en temps réel. Avec GTA 6, Neuralink montre surtout un jeu sorti la veille, contrôlé sur console par une manette virtuelle.
Une technologie encore strictement expérimentale
Aussi impressionnante soit-elle, cette séquence ne signifie pas pour autant que tous les patients équipés peuvent aujourd’hui lancer n’importe quel jeu du commerce en toute autonomie : selon Neuralink, ces contrôles avancés ne sont accessibles qu’à une partie des participants. L’entreprise rappelle elle-même que ses implants restent expérimentaux : ni la FDA, l’agence américaine du médicament, ni aucun autre régulateur ne les a autorisés.

articles.title: Steam Machine, déjà la fin ? Valve ne garantit plus ni le stock ni le prix de sa console — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pendant cinq longs mois, mettre la main sur une Steam Machine passait par une file d’attente : une réservation, puis l’attente fébrile d’un e-mail d’invitation à l’achat. Depuis ce jeudi 19 novembre, on peut ajouter le modèle 512 Go directement à son panier comme n’importe quel produit, ce qui a tout d’une bonne nouvelle.
Il n’y a pas d’offres pour le moment, découvrez :
- Sony PlayStation 5 Pro1 750,00 €Voir l’offre
- Nintendo Switch 2449,99 €Voir l’offre
- Sony PlayStation 5 Slim1 028,99 €Voir l’offre
Pourtant, Valve accompagne ce déblocage d’un aveu d’impuissance rare chez un constructeur : l’entreprise reconnaît ne plus savoir combien de consoles elle parviendra à assembler dans les prochains mois, ni à quel prix elle pourra les proposer.
Dans un billet publié sur la page Steam Hardware, le fabricant indique avoir honoré toutes les réservations du modèle 512 Go, facturé 1 039 euros sans manette (1 108 euros avec le Steam Controller). Cette déclinaison est donc disponible à l’achat direct, sans réservation, dans la stricte limite des pièces en stock, avant de basculer en rupture une fois le lot épuisé.
La version 2 To, affichée à 1 359 euros, subit un sort encore plus rude : les dernières invitations d’achat ont bien été expédiées, mais la file d’attente compte davantage d’inscrits que de machines disponibles, contraignant Valve à fermer la liste aux nouveaux candidats. Les joueurs déjà positionnés conservent leur rang sans garantie d’être servis, en attendant de nouvelles précisions promises par Valve pour le mois de janvier.
Valve prévient aussi qu’elle s’attend à produire moins de Steam Machine que prévu à l’origine, et que le modèle 2 To sera « particulièrement contraint ». L’entreprise ne dit en revanche ni combien d’exemplaires du 512 Go restent en stock, ni si elle en assemblera d’autres avant janvier.
    Pour aller plus loin
Steam Machine : fini les réservations, la vente libre est ouverte pour la console de Valve
            
Une console prise en étau par la crise de la mémoire
À l’intérieur de son boîtier compact, chaque Steam Machine embarque 24 Go de mémoire vive (DRAM) : 16 Go de DDR5 dédiés au système et 8 Go de GDDR6 réservés à la partie graphique. Ces puces gardent à portée immédiate les textures et les données du jeu en cours. Elles sortent aussi des mêmes usines que la mémoire des serveurs d’intelligence artificielle, aujourd’hui servis en priorité.
    Pour aller plus loin
Hausse des prix de la RAM, délais rallongés et pénurie, tout comprendre à la crise de la RAM
            
Les fabricants de mémoire (Samsung, SK hynix, Micron) réservent en effet une part croissante de leurs lignes de production à la mémoire HBM, une architecture empilée à très haut débit destinée aux serveurs d’IA, nettement plus lucrative que la RAM grand public. Selon le cabinet d’analyse TrendForce, les tarifs contractuels de la DRAM classique négociés entre fabricants et grands acheteurs ont ainsi bondi de 90 à 95 % au premier trimestre 2026, par rapport au trimestre précédent.
Fin septembre, le cabinet anticipait encore 10 à 15 % de hausse de la DRAM classique au quatrième trimestre. Pour la mémoire flash NAND qui équipe les SSD, il a revu sa prévision à la baisse le 19 novembre : 8 à 13 % de hausse sur le trimestre, contre 15 à 20 % annoncés auparavant. Avec quatre fois plus de stockage que la version 512 Go, la Steam Machine 2 To reste la plus exposée à cette hausse.
La « vente libre » du modèle 512 Go porte sur un stock limité, sans promesse de réassort. « Nous ne savons pas encore combien nous pourrons en fabriquer, ni à quel prix », écrit Valve. Sans officialiser de hausse, la marque ne garantit donc plus le tarif actuel, une perspective inquiétante pour une machine que notre test jugeait adorable mais plombée par son prix.
Valve l’a déjà fait sur son autre machine. Le 27 mai 2026, l’entreprise a remis en vente le Steam Deck OLED avec des prix relevés de plus de 35 % : 779 euros pour le modèle 512 Go (contre 569 euros) et 919 euros pour la version 1 To (contre 679 euros). Elle invoquait alors la hausse des coûts de la mémoire et du stockage.
    Pour aller plus loin
Test de la Steam Machine : une adorable petite console plombée par son prix
            
Que faire si vous voulez une Steam Machine
Si 512 Go vous suffisent, mieux vaut commander maintenant, au tarif actuel. La machine intègre un lecteur de carte microSD pour agrandir le stockage. Prévoyez la carte dans le budget : certains jeux récents dépassent largement les 100 Go. Les inscrits sur la liste d’attente du modèle 2 To ont un choix à faire : passer au 512 Go leur fait perdre définitivement leur place. Avant de débourser plus de 1 000 euros, relisez notre test complet de la Steam Machine pour vérifier qu’elle correspond à votre usage.
Autre option, monter soi-même son PC de salon. Notre guide pour construire sa propre Steam Machine détaille une sélection de huit composants pour obtenir une machine équivalente à moindre coût, en évitant un piège classique au montage.
Attention toutefois : les barrettes de mémoire vive et les SSD vendus au détail subissent la même flambée que les composants achetés par Valve. Vérifiez donc le prix du jour au moment de commander les pièces de ce PC de salon fait maison plutôt que de se fier à une estimation datant de quelques mois, à moins de patienter jusqu’aux annonces de Valve prévues en janvier.
Côté stockage, attendre peut se justifier. Dans sa note du 19 novembre, TrendForce prévoit une baisse des prix contractuels de la NAND dès le premier trimestre 2027 (de 0 à 5 %), et relève déjà une chute de plus de 20 % des prix spot ces dernières semaines. Le cabinet n’annonce rien de tel pour la DRAM.
    Pour aller plus loin
Nos conseils pour construire sa Steam Machine : 8 composants, moins cher et un piège

articles.title: The game of the year is finally here
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 153, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, thank you for tearing yourself away from GTA to be here, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
The game of the year is finally here
Plus, in this week’s Installer: A better YouTube Kids, new ways to get stuff done, the FTX story on Netflix, and more.
This week, I’ve been reading about nuclear radiation and F1 brains and phone scammers, watching about 10 minutes of Madden before bailing, playing a lot of Madden NFL instead, learning my way around Instagram Edits on the Mac, trying the 12-3-30 workout while watching Mission: Impossible movies in half-hour increments, getting my new Apple HomeView up and running (still don’t know why I bought one…), and dreaming up stuff to do with the Flipper One.
I also have for you the game of the year (decade? century?), a couple of great new productivity tools, a Netflix take on the FTX story, and much more. But mostly, it’s GTA week. Let’s do it.
Also, programming note: Installer is off next week. It’s Thanksgiving, there’s food to eat and football to watch. Hope you have a great couple of weeks, and we’ll be so back in December.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What have you been watching / reading / listening to / playing / adding to your holiday lists this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Grand Theft Auto VI. I mean, this literally could be the whole newsletter. But it appears this game is everything we’ve been waiting for, and I anticipate spending too much of the rest of my life playing it. No regrets.
- The GTA VI soundtrack. I can’t think of many games whose soundtracks have this kind of power: It’s a 34-song compilation, including a bunch of new music from huge artists. I’m going to listen to this while I work, which I assume will make all my writing cooler and more crime-filled.
- The Teenage Engineering EP/BC-1. I’ve been thinking about rebooting my physical media collection, and I can’t think of a better way to start than with this beautiful CD player. Like all Teenage Engineering gear, it is somehow retro and futuristic at the same time, and it’ll slide neatly into a synth setup or just look extremely rad in your living room.
- Alfred 6. A long-awaited update to the launcher and workflow tool so many Mac users love. I see some nice interface changes here but otherwise not a massively different product… but that’s actually probably the right call. Alfred is very good at being Alfred.
- The TRMNL Frame. A 31.5-inch, programmable color E Ink screen that you can hang on your wall. This either immediately excites you, and $1,299 is a small price to pay, or does nothing for you and is way too expensive. I accept both reactions equally. I also want one so badly.
- Tasks in Gemini. A stupid, stupid, stupid name for an otherwise useful product! Gemini now has a lot of the same “do stuff for you” tools that Muse and Dots offer — this time with much better access to your Google data. I’m slowly working through my inbox with this one.
- Who Wants This? Fun new podcast in which two writers and comedians attempt to make sense of current trends, and whether anyone actually… wants this. The first episode is about protein and proteinmaxxing, and I both enjoyed the hang and learned a lot. It also made me feel like everyone has just completely lost their minds.
- The Altruists. We are due for many, many fictionalized versions of the FTX story. I’ve heard and read some mixed things about this new Netflix series, but I dig the idea of trying to play it as both a love story and a scam story. It really is both those things!
- ClockwiseTV. Respect to Hank Green for being one of the few people bold enough to try and compete with YouTube. The pitch here is smart and simple: curated content for kids, on a timer, no ads, no autoplay. This is immediately going on all my iPads.
- “CIA Meeting Cold Open.” Last week’s SNL was really good overall (though maybe I just love John Mulaney?) but the cold open, with the tech billionaires learning how not to fall for a honeypot, absolutely slayed me. The spray bottle on Elon Musk makes me laugh every single time.
You may not know Tom Hovey, but I can practically guarantee you’ve seen his work. That’s because, in addition to many other cool projects, Tom’s also the artist behind those illustrated graphics of everyone’s bakes on The Great British Baking Show. His unique style has been all over that show, and my TV screen, for many years.
I found Tom’s work recently on Threads, when he went massively viral after debunking the idea that all those food drawings are AI with a video to prove how he does it. He’s been working with digital tools for a decade, he said, “but never ever AI.”
I asked Tom to share his homescreen with us to see how he might use his phone for his work, and also to see if I might learn any good GBBS spoilers. (Alas, none.) Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: iPhone 17 Pro.
The wallpaper: A sunrise photo of the Swan River, where I run most mornings in Perth Western Australia. We moved here permanently 6 months ago.
The apps: Apple Podcasts, Brick, Sonos, Strava, SoundCloud, Photos, Google, Google Maps, iNaturalist, Google Calendar, Chrome, NYT Games, Gmail, WhatsApp, Spotify, Discord.
Like many people I’m addicted to my phone, so bricking my phone when I get home from the studio has been amazing. I’m obsessed with running, so Strava and Runna are used every day for training and logging my runs but also hyping up my running pals.
Six apps for my kids’ primary school is too many apps.
I have weather apps but it’s kinda unnecessary now we live in Australia, because it’s either hot or really hot!
iNaturalist is my newest app and I love it. It’s for documenting nature — flora and fauna. As I’m in a new country, I’m enjoying discovering all the native flowers and plants I find on runs. I’ve also recently done some trial runs in Perth Hills, where I’ve run into tons of wild kangaroos and snakes. So fun! My kids also love bugs and birds, so learning all about them is cool. Also when you add your photos of nature, it geotags them and sends the details to some scientists who can understand the areas you are documenting.
I also asked Tom to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
- I listen to a lot of audiobooks while I’m at my desk drawing and also while running, and audiobooks are the only way I can “read” non-fiction as I just fall asleep immediately if I try and actually read them. Some recent audiobooks I’ve enjoyed: The Castle by Jon Ronson; Thirst: Twelve Drinks That Changed My Life by John Robins; Hidden Valley Road by Robert Kolker; London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe.
- TV shows I’ve recently watched: The Pitt, Widow’s Bay, This Is a Gardening Show, East of Eden, Star City, Pluribus.
- As an illustrator I’m always looking for excellent people making cool things and in a world where AI art is taking over I am seeking more and more analog art so here are some of the coolest creatives I’m currently enjoying: Natalie Andrewson, Sean Morris, Carla Adams, Ellis Parrinder, Azpeger Tat, and Kawafi.
- I have a WhatsApp chat with a bunch of my old illustrator pals which is a bunch of old men gossiping and sending each other Paul McCartney memes.
- Really enjoying the internet’s response to Damian Lewis’s foray into music.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Forget GTA VI, the game of the year is Queen’s Domain. It is only $20 instead of $80, made by two people instead of an army. It is all I have been playing this week.” — Mike
“In Meg Elison’s new novel, Foundling Fathers, some creepy tech billionaires clone Washington Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams and try to raise them in an ‘originalist’ setting. The satire is hilarious and all too plausible.” — aAron
“I’m not playing with it yet myself, but the FM-1 from M-Vave seems to be capturing the first wave of post-vibe-coding synthesized nerds, who are all replacing the stock firmware with homebrew. So a cheap Chinese generic keyboard is suddenly really hot hardware even though it’s like $50.” — Anil
“Reading John Scalzi’s The Kaiju Preservation Society and it is simple, honest sci-fi fun. Classic Scalzi.” — 4nd3rs
“Stick on Apple TV got me through the week until GTA VI!” — Justin
“Claude and I went around this week with a tape measure and built a to-the-inch accurate 3D model and floorplan of our house, which inevitably led to making it a Doom map.” — Michael
“I switched to ReadKit on my Mac and iPhone now that it has iCloud-based RSS sync.” — Todd
“Recently found the book The Canceling of the American Mind by Greg Lukianoff and Rikki Schlott at my local library. It is a well-written investigation into the effects of cancel culture on public debate and education. Wherever you fall on the political spectrum, this book will challenge you to think about how we should engage with ‘dangerous’ and ‘offensive’ ideas.” — Josh
“Been watching From since the first three seasons are available on Netflix right now. It’s a good show, has very Lost vibes to it.” — Bobby
Signing off
One of the most underrated strange things about the tech industry is how much The Social Network changed the way people think about Mark Zuckerberg. Yes, the movie takes huge liberties, and yes, every single person involved with the movie was quick to remind us that it was fiction. But for so many people, Jesse Eisenberg’s character just became who Zuck was.
I think Andrew Garfield in Artificial might be about to do the same thing to Sam Altman. The new trailer looks fabulous, all the early buzz about the movie seems to be great, and the movie absolutely could not be more perfectly timed. It’s apparently a pretty brutal look at Altman, OpenAI, and the whole AI movement — I wonder how Garfield and his handsomeness might bend the way the world responds. I cannot wait to see this movie.
See you in two weeks!

articles.title: En 2008, Steve Jobs a sorti un portable ultra fin d'une enveloppe : Richard Yu de Huawei y a glissé son PC pliant
articles.text:
En 2008, Steve Jobs a sorti un portable ultra fin d'une enveloppe : Richard Yu de Huawei y a glissé son PC pliant
18 ans après le MacBook Air de Steve Jobs, Huawei rejoue le coup de l'enveloppe pour lancer un PC pliant de 14,7 pouces doté d'un petit écran au dos. En précommande en Chine, il fonctionne sans Windows ni puce étasunienne.
San Francisco, 15 janvier 2008. Sur la scène de la MacWorld, Steve Jobs attrape une enveloppe de courrier interne en papier kraft et en sort le tout premier MacBook Air, présenté comme le portable le plus fin du monde. Ce 10 novembre 2026, Richard Yu, président de la division grand public de Huawei, a ressorti ce fameux accessoire dans une courte vidéo publiée sur Weibo.
L’enveloppe de Steve Jobs revisitée : un habile tour de passe-passe
Dans la séquence, il replie le MateBook Fold de 18 pouces, le glisse dans l'enveloppe, plie celle-ci en deux et en extrait un ordinateur bien plus petit, le MateBook Fold S. Plusieurs médias, dont le site espagnol 3DJuegos, ont titré sur “deux ordinateurs” logés dans la même enveloppe. Pas tout à fait… La vidéo montre une substitution digne d'un prestidigitateur : une fois plié, le nouveau modèle occupe environ moitié moins de place que son aîné. Le MacBook Air de 2008 se distinguait par ses 1,94 cm au point le plus épais et ses 1,36 kg ; Huawei met cette fois en avant la surface occupée.
MateBook Fold S : double écran Oled et Live Mini Display
Le Fold S reprend le principe d'une dalle Oled souple unique. Déplié, l'écran mesure 14,7 pouces. Replié, l'appareil prend le format d'un livre de 10,2 pouces, selon la fiche technique publiée par Huawei le 15 novembre. Les premiers articles, Notebookcheck en tête, avançaient 10,7 pouces. Le constructeur annonce un poids supérieur à 600 g, contre 1,16 kg (sans clavier) pour le modèle de 18 pouces.
Au dos, à côté d'un module photo marqué “AI Camera”, Huawei a installé un écran carré baptisé Live Mini Display. Celui-ci reste actif quand l'ordinateur est fermé. He Gang, directeur général de la branche terminaux, dit s'être inspiré de l'écran externe du smartphone pliant Pura X. Cette dalle sert à consulter son agenda, lire ses messages, faire défiler un réseau social ou lancer l'enregistrement de notes vocales de l'assistant Celia, et ce, sans même ouvrir la machine. Sa diagonale exacte n'a pas été communiquée.
L'utilisateur tape sur un clavier virtuel affiché sur la moitié basse de l'écran plié à angle droit, ou sur le clavier physique pliable fourni dans la boîte. Quatre configurations sont prévues, de 16 Go/256 Go à 32 Go/1 To, la plus onéreuse ajoutant le stylet M-Pencil.
HarmonyOS et puce Kirin : un PC portable sans Windows ni Intel
Comme ses aînés, le Fold S tourne sous HarmonyOS PC, le système que Huawei installe sur ses nouveaux ordinateurs depuis qu'il a dû renoncer à Windows en 2025. Le processeur, un Kirin de la série X9 conçu par sa filiale HiSilicon, n'a pas encore été précisé. Les logiciels Windows ne fonctionnent que dans une machine virtuelle fournie par un éditeur tiers. Les sanctions nord-américaines privent le groupe des usines les plus avancées : TechInsights a établi que la puce Kirin X90 du premier MateBook Fold sortait des chaînes du chinois SMIC en 7 nm, un procédé apparu en 2023 et en retard de plusieurs générations sur TSMC.
Sur son marché intérieur, ce handicap pèse peu. D'après Omdia, Huawei a expédié 1,8 million de PC en Chine au deuxième trimestre 2026, soit 82 % de plus qu'un an plus tôt, et détient 16 % de part de marché derrière Lenovo, dans un secteur tiré par les achats des grandes entreprises et des administrations.
Le Mac pliant d'Apple reste, lui, à l'état de rumeur. En 2024, l'analyste Ming-Chi Kuo évoquait un écran de 18,8 pouces et une production repoussée à fin 2027 ou 2028. Huawei en est, de son côté, à son troisième PC pliant en 18 mois.
Le prix sera dévoilé le 24 novembre lors de la conférence dédiée au smartphone Mate X8. Le grand MateBook Fold démarre à 24 999 yuans, soit environ 3200 € hors taxes. Aucune sortie européenne n'est annoncée et, sans Windows ni les logiciels professionnels habituels, elle reste peu probable.
